entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Blessed: The Hebrew term ’ashrey appears twenty-six times in the Psalms. While some translations use “blessed,” a different term (barak) is used for blessings (Psalms 5:12; Psalms 45:2; Psalms 107:38). 

• The godly are people who trust the Lord and try to live in ways that please him. They avoid living under the influence of sinners. 

Those who do not fear the Lord are “the wicked” (Psalm 36:1). They oppose those who love God, do right, and the poor and oppressed (see Psalms 10:2–13; Psalms 37:14). The wicked might seem devoted to God (Psalms 50:16). Sometimes they enjoy success, but it does not last long (Psalms 37:35). They will face sadness and ruin when they must deal with the results of their bad actions (Psalms 1:4–6; Psalms 9:16; Psalms 32:10). 

• People who turn away from God's path and rebel against him are sinners (Psalms 25:8; Psalms 78:17). They commit serious crimes like adultery (being unfaithful to their spouse) and murder (compare Psalm 51). 

• sit in the seat of: This expression describes a person who is controlled by sin (compare Psalm 1:2; Psalms 26:3–7; Deuteronomy 6:7). 

• Mockers are people who disrespect and reject God's wisdom. Mockers hate the Lord and insult anyone who tries to correct them (Proverbs 9:7–8). They seek only the “wisdom” that justifies their actions. These bold people have little respect for God, his plans, or his followers (see Psalms 86:14; Psalms 119:51, Psalms 119:69, Psalms 119:78, Psalms 119:85, Psalms 119:122). These three terms (wicked, sinners, mockers) describe all kinds of people who do not live in a way that pleases God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord brings true happiness to those who turn away from evil and find joy in him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Psalm 1 is a wisdom psalm. It sets the tone for the whole book of Psalms. The psalm clearly contrasts the happiness of godly people with the judgment of the wicked. In the end, the way of wisdom will triumph.

The psalm describes an ideal picture of a godly person, similar to Psalm 8. This picture shows what the Lord expects from his people. It also points forward to the coming Messiah, God’s chosen king (Psalm 2). 

The people of Israel did not live up to this ideal. The kings from David’s family also failed to meet it. Even the best kings could not bring about the lasting righteousness described in Psalms 1, Psalms 2:2, and 72. 

In the New Testament, the apostles use the Psalms to describe the life and work of Jesus the Messiah. Their teaching shows that Jesus alone fulfills the ideal of the godly person described in the Psalms. Only Jesus fully pleased God and secured redemption (rescue from sin), true happiness, and peace.

Psalm 1 also introduces a note of hope that continues through the Psalms. It looks forward to the final hallelujah in Psalm 150). At that time, the Lord will remove all evil from his creation and bring blessing and life to his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The first two psalms serve as an introduction to the whole book of Psalms (called the Psalter). Psalm 1 presents the Lord's guidance in wisdom, while Psalm 2 shows God's rule over a rebellious and sinful world. Together, these psalms invite people to abandon foolishness, which leads to destruction. These psalms invite people to follow God's path instead, which leads to wisdom and salvation. The New Testament confirms that God will govern the nations through Jesus Christ, his chosen representative (Hebrews 1:5; Revelation 12:5; Revelation 19:15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Psalms 1 and Psalms 8:8 form an inclusio (a literary pattern where the beginning and ending act like matching bookends). Together, they describe what God expects from the ideal person. These psalms compare the godly person with the wicked and praise the dignity and worth God gives to the godly (see Psalms 19; Psalms 33:33; Psalms 104:104; Psalms 145:145). 

Jesus the Messiah, introduced in Psalm 2, fully embodies this ideal. He is the Lord with complete power and authority, and the perfect example of true humanity. The New Testament applies Psalm 8 to Jesus, showing that God placed everything under his authority (Hebrews 2:6–8; see 1 Corinthians 15:27).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The law of the Lord is called torah in Hebrew. It means God’s instruction or teaching for his people (see study note on Deuteronomy 4:44). 

• Meditating involves inner reflection, which can be positive (Psalms 1:2; Psalms 63:6; Psalms 77:12; Psalms 143:5) or negative (see Psalms 2:1; Psalms 38:12). The Lord’s word is the object of godly meditation (Psalms 119:48). 

• day and night: This includes all times, whether walking, standing, sitting, or sleeping (see Deuteronomy 6:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Well-watered trees stay strong and produce plenty of fruit (compare Jeremiah 17:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The future belongs to those who follow a righteous path.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The future judgment (Psalm 1:5) will remove the wicked and everything they have done (Psalms 35:5; Psalms 83:13; Isaiah 17:13; see study note on Jeremiah 13:24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked cannot endure the Lord's judgment. They are already condemned (see Psalms 5:5; Psalms 7:6; Psalms 101:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• When God takes care of people who obey him and punishes people who do evil, it shows how God gives people what their actions deserve (see Galatians 6:7–10). This is called "retribution." The wicked might appear successful for a short while, but their lives are short and meaningless in the end. God and the people who remain faithful to him will have the final victory (see Psalms 9:5, Psalms 9:6, Psalms 9:18; Psalms 10:16; Psalms 37:20; Psalms 73:27; Psalms 92:9; compare Psalms 142:4; Isaiah 57:1). 

• People who live in a way that pleases God are happy (Psalms 1:1; Psalms 5:12; Psalms 14:5). They are happy because God protects and cares for them, listens when they ask for justice, and secures their future (see Psalms 121:3–4). 

• A person's path is their life and character.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: plot: The Hebrew verb translated as "meditates" in Psalm 1:2 suggests opposing the Lord through speech (Isaiah 59:13) or thought (Psalm 38:12; Proverbs 24:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Their useless paths lead to death (Psalm 1:4, Psalms 1:6), but sinful human beings join together to oppose the true God and his Messiah.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This royal psalm describes the Lord choosing a king descended from David. It celebrates the mission of all the kings in David's family line. It also introduces the hope of an ideal ruler. This ruler will accomplish the Lord's goal of bringing all nations into submission (Psalm 2:11) or to destruction (Psalms 2:9). The New Testament identifies Jesus as this descendant (see Acts 13:33; 1 Corinthians 15:25–27; Hebrews 1:5; Hebrews 5:5; Revelation 19:15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The kings hate the Lord's established order in the world, so they want to be independent of him (see Psalm 36:4). They plan to dominate the Lord's people (Psalm 31:13; see Psalms 83:1–4). Their goal is to undermine the Lord's rule by overthrowing his Anointed One (or his Messiah). 

The Lord chose the kings of David's family line to establish his kingdom on earth. The New Testament confirms that Jesus, the appointed and anointed Son of God (Acts 4:26; Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5; Hebrews 5:5), fulfills the role in which these earlier kings failed.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: break Their chains: These kings think that recognizing the true God and his chosen ruler will lead to their enslavement (Isaiah 28:22; Isaiah 52:2; compare Lamentations 3:7; Romans 1:1; 1 Corinthians 7:22; Titus 1:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: enthroned in heaven: The Lord's position in the universe is so secure that he laughs at humans who claim they can oppose his power and authority (see Psalms 3 7:13; Psalms 59:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord sees the human threat as unimportant. He offered a solution long before they rebelled. He will stop their unrest by appointing a human leader, a descendant of David, to rule the nations.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: My King: The Lord himself appoints and establishes his anointed ruler. The word anointed means chosen and set apart by God for a special purpose.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
today I have become Your Father: In the ancient Near East, people often believed in a father-son relationship between gods and kings. 

In Israel, the Lord adopted kings as his sons. God set David apart as his most excellent and exalted son (Psalm 89:27). All descendants of David were the Lord’s representatives or agents. 

Jesus is an eternal member of the Godhead (the one God who exists as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; John 1:1). He is also a descendant of David (Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5; Hebrews 5:5). Because he is both eternal and from David's family, Jesus uniquely fulfills God’s plan. He is fully divine and truly human. For this reason, he is rightly called the Son of God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord adopted the king from David's family to conquer rebellious nations by force (see Psalm 89:26–27).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• In the Old Testament, the relationship between the Lord and Israel’s king can be compared to a suzerain-vassal relationship. A suzerain was a great king. A vassal was a smaller king who served him.

In this picture, the Lord is the great King. Israel’s king rules under his authority (see Deuteronomy Book Introduction, “Literary Form”). The Lord invites his anointed king to ask for what he needs (see Psalm 21:2, Psalms 21:4). 

• All nations will be subject to David's descendant, the Messiah.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord grants his chosen ruler the power to conquer nations as his inheritance (Isaiah 11:4; Revelation 2:27; Revelation 12:5; Revelation 19:15), ending their rebellion, resistance, and independence.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord is pleased when people submit to him and seek his protection. Wise people accept the Lord's correction and want to change.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• rejoice: Leaders should accept the Son as their true and only King. 

• Kiss the Son: Kissing was an expression of submission (Hosea 13:2). 

• The Lord gives joy to those who fear him. To fear the Lord means to honor him, respect him, and obey him (Psalm 1:1–2). The Psalms also say that the Lord protects those who trust him (Psalms 18:30; Psalms 34:22; Psalms 119:1–3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This difficult time in David’s life (see 2 Samuel 15:2 Samuel 15–18) helps readers understand the promises of Psalm 2 better. The Lord gave victory to his chosen king (Psalm 2), but God controlled how and when this victory happened.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• A psalmist is the writer or speaker of a psalm. The psalmist here faces many enemies. Those enemies speak boldly and without respect (Psalm 4:6; Psalms 12:4; Psalms 40:15). They question whether the Lord can really save him (Psalms 10:11; Psalms 22:7–8; Psalms 71:10). Their words trouble the psalmist because it seems the Lord will not answer his prayer. 

• These enemies hold great power (compare Psalm 2:1–3). Unlike Psalm 2, this psalm does not resolve the crisis.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm expresses sorrow that the hopes from Psalms 1–2 have not been fulfilled. Even when surrounded by enemies, godly people should not doubt the Lord's just actions. Instead, they can trust in God's goodness and expect God to rescue them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This group of psalms moves from an orderly world to a troubled one. Psalms 1–2 describe stability. The righteous person is blessed, and the Lord’s anointed king rules with authority.

In the psalms that follow, the tone changes. The Lord’s anointed cries out for help. He faces enemies, strong opposition, and evil plans.

It even seems at times that the Lord is far away. The psalmist feels confusion and distress instead of confidence and calm.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist compares his enemies' arguments (Psalm 3:2) with the Lord’s help. The Lord acts as a shield for his people, turning their defeat and shame into victory and glory.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist looks away from his enemies and focuses on the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: By focusing on the Lord (Psalm 3:3–4) during his crisis, the psalmist can rest, confident in his safety (see study note on Psalm 4:8). The Lord cares for his servant. God protects him and keeps his mind and heart free from fear (Psalms 37:17; Psalms 54:4; Psalms 119:116; Psalms 145:14).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels peaceful and confident because the Lord protects and cares for him. This shields him from evil and gives him a new understanding of reality (Psalm 23:4; Psalms 27:1, Psalms 27:3; Psalms 46:1; Psalms 56:4, Psalms 56:11; Psalms 91:5–6; Psalms 118:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist does not seek revenge. Instead, he waits for the Lord to take vengeance. 

• Arise: The psalmist asks the Lord to act now.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Waiting for the Lord's answer helps you grow in patience and strengthen your faith (Psalm 38:15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This personal lament includes: 

• a prayer for rescue (Psalm 4:1)

• a rebuke of the enemy (Psalm 4:2–3)

• advice to the faithful (Psalm 4:4–5)

• a statement of confidence (Psalm 4:6–8)

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The opponents of those who follow God rely on false beliefs, deceit, and idol worship. 

• my honor (or my glory): The psalmist's honor, or possibly the Lord's, is being challenged.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Feeling angry is not a sin, but letting anger control you can lead to sin (see Psalm 37:7–8; compare Ephesians 4:26–27, Ephesians 4:31–32). 

• Instead of acting on their emotions, godly people think about their circumstances overnight. They might be disturbed as they sleep, but silence opens their hearts to trust in the Lord (Psalm 4:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Offer the sacrifices of the righteous: Redirecting emotions toward the Lord prevents a godly person from doing too much self-reflection (Psalms 40:6–8; Psalms 51:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
the light of Your face: When the psalmist speaks about God’s face, he is asking for God’s favor and peace (Numbers 6:25–26). God’s favor can change a situation from darkness to light (see Psalm 27:1). 

Confident faith protects against anger, resentment, jealousy, and a desire for wealth as the highest good. When God’s favor is enough, other desires lose their power.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Peace comes from God's blessing and protection (see Psalm 4:6 and Psalms 37:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The phrase give ear to my words appears in several prayers as a call for God's attention during difficult times (Psalms 39:12; Psalms 84:8; Psalms 143:1; compare Psalms 17:1; Psalms 54:2; Psalms 130:2). The needy ask their God, “Are you listening?”

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This morning prayer (Psalm 5:3) shows strong trust in the Lord's help and protection. The psalmist asks for God's response and waits for it (Psalm 5:1–3). 

He describes the plans of the wicked in detail but stays focused on God. The psalmist knows the wicked cannot be with God (Psalm 5:4–6, Psalms 5:9; see Psalms 1:5). 

He keeps returning to the Lord (Psalm 5:7–8, Psalms 5:10; see Psalms 5:1–3), and then he prays for the godly community (Psalms 5:10–12; see Psalms 3:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist starts and ends each day with prayer, looking for new signs of God's faithfulness and goodness (Psalm 143:8). 

• wait in expectation: The psalmist does not demand God's grace but hopes for it (see Micah 7:7; Habakkuk 2:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The boastful: Mockers (see study note on Psalm 1:1), the wicked (Psalm 73:3; Psalms 75:4), and the arrogant (Psalms 10:2) use their words to distort the truth and challenge the faith of the godly. 

• The Lord allows only the godly into his presence (see Psalm 1:5). His holiness and justice do not tolerate oppression or evil actions. 

• You hate: The Lord rejects proud sinners (see also Psalm 11:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God promises his loving devotion (his covenant goodness and faithfulness) to his people (see Psalm 25:6; Psalms 69:16; Lamentations 3:32). 

• Your house: The righteous desire to enter God's presence with awe and wonder (see Hebrews 12:28).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God guides those who are obedient, submissive, and patient as they wait for him to lead, provide, and protect them (Psalm 27:11; Psalms 43:3; Psalms 143:10). He does not guide those who expect God simply to approve their own decisions. 

• Following the right path of wisdom leads to the Lord (Psalms 47:11; Psalms 61:2; Psalms 139:24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist again describes the terrible acts of the wicked, who cannot stand in God’s presence.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist prays for the justice and retribution that God promised against the wicked (Psalm 1:6). The wicked are those who have rebelled against the Lord.

• The wicked set traps to harm (Psalm 38:12) or trick others (Psalms 140:4–5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• A blessing rests on all who take refuge in God (see Psalm 18:30). 

• Joy and praise go well together. The godly rejoice when they see evidence of God’s rescue. They sing joyful praises as a new song (see Psalm 33:3). 

When the Lord brings peace to the world, defeats evil, and rewards good people, they will have lasting joy (Psalms 9:2–4; Psalms 53:6; Psalms 90:14–15; Psalms 118:24). 

• The children of God, who find refuge in him, love his name. To love his name is to love his very character.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist cares not only for himself but for all the godly people. 

• A shield, here an image of God’s protection, deflects spears and arrows from the one holding it.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: do not rebuke me … or discipline me: The psalmist does not clearly connect God's discipline with sin here (compare Psalm 39:8–11), but it might be implied.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks for God’s favor and restoration at a difficult time.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The occasion for this lament might have been sickness or a mental or spiritual depression from which the psalmist sought healing.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist became physically weak while waiting for God's answer to his prayer (Psalm 6:6; see Psalms 77:3; Psalms 119:81; Psalms 142:1–3; see also Psalm 101). Fasting (abstaining from eating food) might have contributed to his suffering, but it is not mentioned.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The experience was so painful that the psalmist might as well have been dead, or perhaps he feared for his life.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: from Sheol?: In the Old Testament, Sheol is the place of the dead. It is not necessarily associated with punishment.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist feels deeply exhausted due to his spiritual distance from the Lord (Psalms 22:1; Psalms 31:9–10; Psalms 102:5). 

• When eyes grow dim, it means the body is failing (see Psalms 13:3; Psalms 31:9; Psalms 38:10; Matthew 6:22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In a closing note of triumph, the psalmist reasserts his confidence in the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Pursuers, a common term for enemies, actively look for people in order to harm or destroy them (Psalm 31:15; Psalms 56:1–2; Psalms 71:11; Psalms 143:3).

An unknown person from the tribe of Benjamin remained hostile to David.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This psalm includes the following: 

• A lament (Psalm 7:1–2): The psalmist cries out to God for help and protection from enemies.

• An oath of innocence (Psalm 7:3–5): The psalmist declares that he has done no wrong and maintains his integrity.

• A call for God's justice (Psalm 7:6–9): He asks God to act against evildoers and defend the righteous.

• An affirmation of God’s just kingship (Psalm 7:10–16): The psalmist praises God as a fair judge who rules the world rightly.

• A concluding hymn of praise (Psalm 7:17): The psalmist ends with a song of thanksgiving, honoring God’s righteousness and deliverance.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Like a lion, a wicked enemy relentlessly and violently pursues its prey (Psalms 10:9; Psalms 17:12; Psalms 22:13, Psalms 22:21; Psalms 35:17; Psalms 57:4), but God promises victory (Psalms 91:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist does not claim to be without sin, but he knows that he does not deserve the cruel attacks of his opponents (see Psalms 35:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist declares his innocence, opening himself up to examination (Psalm 7:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• trample: Compare Psalm 44:5; Psalms 60:12; Psalms 91:13; Psalms 108:13. 

• to the ground … in the dust: Disgrace and shame can lead to death and the grave (Psalm 143:3; see Psalms 13:3–4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s judgment brings justice, despite the chaos created by enemies (see Psalms 7:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: With this appeal to God for justice in the world, the psalmist also submits to God’s examination.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The judgment is against the defendants (the peoples) and in favor of the righteous plaintiff (the psalmist; see Psalm 43:1). 

• The psalmist, though not free from all sin, is a person of true integrity (see Psalm 15:2; Psalms 25:21; Psalms 41:12; Psalms 78:72; compare Job 1:1, Job 1:8; Job 9:20, Job 9:22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God knows the thoughts and intentions of every person. He does not see only outward actions. He examines what is hidden in the mind and the heart (see Psalms 11:3–4; Psalms 26:2; Psalms 139:1, Psalms 139:23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist moves from his own situation (Psalm 7:1–9) to speak for all the godly who seek redemption (Psalms 7:10–16). He protects and vindicates his people. When his followers cry out for help, God hears them and acts to rescue them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The righteous judge cannot be bought or bribed. He does not abuse his power (Psalm 9:4; compare Psalms 82:1–8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: sword … bow … deadly weapons … arrows with fire: As the Divine Warrior, God attacks to defend himself and his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Evil starts with small words or actions and leads to worse deeds over time (see Isaiah 59:4–5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• I will thank … sing praise: The laments in Psalms 3–7 usually shift from lament to praise, as does the entire book of Psalms. 

• Most High: This is an ancient title for God (see Genesis 14:19). 

• God is just and reliable, so his order prevails in this world.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The LORD (Hebrew Yahweh) is the covenant God of Israel (Exodus 3:15). This name emphasizes God’s faithfulness and relationship with his people.

He is also Lord (Hebrew ’adonay), which emphasizes his authority. As Lord, he is the king over the earth and all creation. 

• The word translated as majestic (and sometimes mighty) can describe: 

• kings (Psalm 136:18),

• heroes (Psalm 16:3),

• mountains (Psalm 76:4), or

• waves breaking on the seashore (Psalm 93:4).

While all these things are awe-inspiring and mighty, they are less impressive than the Lord. 

• A person’s name represents their reputation. 

• The earth and the heavens reveal the Lord’s splendor. All creation worships and praises the Lord (Psalm 66:4; Psalms 113:3; Psalms 145:21).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Psalm 8 begins the second part of Book One of the Psalms (Psalms 8–14). The psalmist praises God’s creation and the dignity of the ideal human (see Psalm 1). Instead of the world of enemies, wicked people, and unfair justice shown in Psalms 3–7, this psalm presents the world as God first made it. Someone who is tired (both physically and emotionally) can imagine a place of dignity in God’s world.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• silence: The loud noise of the adversaries contrasts with the praise of God. In the end, the praise of God will overwhelm the sound of evil (Psalms 31:18; Psalms 63:11; Psalms 101:5; Psalms 143:12). 

• Those who oppose God are filled with vengeful anger (Psalm 2:1–3; Psalms 44:16; compare Psalms 149:6–7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Many nations near Israel worshiped the sun, moon, and stars as gods. They thought these objects controlled life and events.

The psalmist reminds us that, while the sun, moon, and stars are great and beautiful, they are only created by God.

Because these things are his creation, they point to God’s power and majesty. They give a reason to praise the Almighty, who alone is worthy of worship.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
God’s glory is vast and awe-inspiring. At first, it might seem that people are too small or unimportant to matter to him.

Yet God has given humans honor and dignity. He has crowned them with glory and set them in charge of creation. 

This shows that every person has value. Humans are called to care for and rule over the world responsibly, reflecting God’s glory in their lives.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: son of man (literally son of Adam): This means "a human being." Through the influence of Daniel 7:13–14, son of man became a title with divine meaning in the New Testament. See Hebrews 2:6–8, where this passage is quoted.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
You made him a little lower than the angels: Humans bear God’s image. The Lord has given humans dignity and tasked them to rule (Genesis 1:26–27). 

Hebrews 2:6–8 applies these words to Jesus Christ, the ideal human who fully realized God’s purposes.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
made him ruler of the works of Your hands: The psalmist is still referring to humans in general. 

Paul applies these words to Jesus as the perfect man who has made the created order, and even death (1 Corinthians 15:25–27), subject to God and his glory. 

The New Testament connects these themes of creation and salvation with Jesus Christ (John 1:1–2, John 1:14; Colossians 1:16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Wild animals, including birds and fish, remind us of God's creation of the animal world in Genesis 1. Contrary to beliefs among Israel’s neighbors in the ancient Near East, animals are not sacred.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The verb translated as give thanks is also translated as thank in Psalm 7:17. This shows a strong connection between Psalms 7 and Psalms 9:9 (see Psalms 7:17; Psalms 8:1–2). 

The phrase with all my heart shows the psalmist’s deep devotion and commitment (Psalms 86:12; Psalms 111:1; Psalms 119:10; Psalms 138:1). 

• I will recount: These stories teach the next generation (Psalms 78:4; Psalms 145:4). If forgotten, a generation might easily turn away from the Lord (Psalms 78:11, Psalms 78:32). 

• Your wonders: These include the Lord’s judgments on the enemies of his people (Psalm 9:4) and his care for the oppressed (Psalms 9:9). The wonders in creation, redemption, and revelation show his character and power (Psalms 89:5; Psalms 111:4; Psalms 119:18, Psalms 119:27). His powerful acts inspire public praise (Psalm 9:1; Psalms 26:7; Psalms 75:1).

However, that tune (or song) is no longer known. The same is true for the tunes mentioned in Psalms 22, Psalms 45:45, Psalms 56:56–60, Psalms 69:69, Psalms 75:75, and 80.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This hymn celebrates the Lord's rule and triumph over evil. It may also respond to the laments in Psalms 3–7. 

Some believe that Psalms 9 and Psalms 10:10 should be read together as one psalm in two parts. This is because Psalm 9 has a title, while Psalm 10 does not. 

Despite some missing or inverted letters, the two psalms form an acrostic of the Hebrew alphabet. This means that each line or section begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

Other alphabetic acrostics include Psalms 25, Psalms 34:34, Psalms 37:37, Psalms 111:111–112, Psalms 119:119, and Psalms 145:145. 

The ancient Greek and Latin translations treat Psalms 9 and 10 as one psalm.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: rejoice … will sing praise: The psalmist often connects joy with praises, as one leads to the other (Psalm 5:11–12; Psalms 32:11; Psalms 67:4; Psalms 90:14; Psalms 92:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: retreat … stumble: The Lord overpowers even powerful enemies (see Psalm 27:2). Israel also experienced judgment when it resisted the Lord (Psalms 107:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist praises God's judgment of the wicked. This shows the Lord's promise to establish his kingdom on earth is trustworthy (Psalms 1:6; Psalms 2:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The throne represents the Lord’s royal authority.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
God created the heavens and the earth with a word (Genesis 1), and he can end nations with a word (see Psalm 2:5). 

Those who do evil will not endure forever. God promises that their power and influence will come to an end (Psalm 69:28; Psalm 109:13; Revelation 21:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The godly do not rely on human governments, which can be weak or corrupt. They understand that earthly rulers are limited and sometimes unfair.

Instead, they put their hope in God’s eternal rule. God governs with perfect justice and fairness (see Psalms 96–100).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Lord offers shelter in dangerous situations and protection from powerful and oppressive people. The psalms often describe the LORD as: 

• a fortress (Psalm 18:2; Psalms 31:2),

• a rock (Psalm 18:2; Psalms 42:9),

• strength (Psalm 18:1), and

• a strong tower (Psalm 144:2).

These images appear frequently in royal prayers (see Psalm 9:9; Psalms 18:30).

• Even oppressed, afflicted, and marginalized people (Psalm 10:17; Psalms 74:21) can receive divine protection. 

• Times of trouble (Psalm 10:1; Psalms 20:1) contrast with moments when the Lord openly shows favor to the afflicted (Psalms 69:13; Psalms 102:13; see Psalm 107:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
At times, a person may feel separated from the Lord. The psalms describe moments of spiritual alienation or distress (Psalms 22:1; Psalms 42:9; Psalms 119:8)

Even in these times, the psalms affirm God’s faithfulness. The Lord does not abandon his people (Psalms 16:10; Psalms 37:25, Psalms 37:28).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The psalm writers often connect the idea that God dwells (or sits, or is enthroned) with a specific place, such as: 

• heaven (Psalm 2:4; see Psalms 47:9),

• Jerusalem,

• "between the cherubim"(Psalms 80:1; Psalms 99:1),

• "on high" (Psalm 113:5), or

• "at my right hand" (Psalm 110:1).

Since the Lord rules the world, everyone must know about his unforgettable deeds of salvation (see Psalm 9:1; Psalms 64:9; Psalms 66:16; Psalms 105:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Understanding that the Lord judges some wicked people (Psalm 9:3–6) and promises to judge all evil (Psalms 9:7–10) inspires praise. The psalmist invites the godly community to join him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord saves his servants and punishes those who have harmed them (Psalm 18:46). He defends his servants by fairly judging his enemies on earth (Psalm 58:11). Those who follow God do not seek revenge. Instead, they wait for the Lord to defend them (Psalm 94:1–2; Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist returns from a vision of the glorious future to the reality of facing his enemies (Psalm 9:3). 

• The gates are a strong image of the powerful grip of death (see Psalm 13:3–4). 

• The gates of Daughter Zion (that is, Jerusalem) provide an intentional contrast to the gates of death.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Hope requires waiting for the Lord’s rescue or justice (Psalms 25:3, Psalms 25:5, Psalms 25:21). The godly experience hope, rest, and peace as they wait for the Lord (see Psalm 1:6; Psalms 27:14).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist concludes his lament by asking God to act on his behalf. He prays for the Lord’s intervention against those who do wrong. This includes a request for divine vengeance (God’s just punishment of evildoers). The psalmist trusts that only God can bring true justice.

• but men: People who gain power and honor can become oppressive and assume glory for themselves (see Psalm 8:4; Psalms 10:18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The opening questions set the mood. The Lord does not seem to hear the prayers of his people (Psalm 22:1, Psalms 22:19; see 2 Kings 4:27; Isaiah 1:15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The lament in Psalm 9:13–20 continues in Psalm 10 (see study note on Psalms 9–10). However, the mood shifts from confident statements to anguished questions. The psalmist prays for rescue, trusting that the Lord, as a just king, take care of the needy.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked openly defy God with their actions and words (Psalm 17:10; Psalms 31:18; Psalms 59:12; Psalms 73:8; Psalms 123:4). Although the Lord will deal with them (Psalm 31:23), they trouble the righteous (see Psalm 5:4–6) before their condemnation and judgment.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Wicked and oppressive people might succeed, causing harmful effects. Evil can be as dramatic as the psalmist portrays it here, or it could be more subtle.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Unlike those who have evil desires, the godly wait for justice (Psalm 10:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: there is no God: See Psalms 10:11; Psalms 14:1.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Even though they act wrongly (Psalms 5:9; Psalms 28:3; Romans 3:14), the wicked still hope for a future free of trouble like the righteous will enjoy.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked rely on violence (Psalms 11:5; Psalms 37:32) and deception (Proverbs 12:6; Proverbs 23:27–28).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: With confidence that the wicked will be held responsible for their deeds and that the Lord will care for the helpless, the psalmist prays intensely for rescue from evil.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord cares for those who suffer. He will notice and punish those who do evil (see Psalm 72:14; Psalms 116:15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist prays and calls for a strong curse (see “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note). 

• Arms represent the ability to wage war (Psalms 18:34; Psalms 44:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: As the true and just king, God will bring the wicked to an end, as he promises (Psalm 1:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist expresses his confidence in the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: People often misuse their power and enslave the very people God wants them to serve (see Psalms 9:19–20; Luke 22:25–26).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God offers protection (refuge; see Psalms 5:11; Psalms 9:9; Psalms 25:20) when justice fails.

• The mountains offer another place of refuge (see Psalm 121:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist affirms his faith in the righteous God. Even though the world appears hopelessly chaotic, both the godly and the wicked can depend on God’s justice. The godly can depend on him as a refuge and shelter.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked live in the shadows and create gloom for the godly (Psalms 82:5; Psalms 139:11; Psalms 143:3; Proverbs 4:19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In the ongoing struggle between those who do evil and those who follow God, the wicked often harm the righteous. This can leave the godly confused and full of questions.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked create a world of darkness (see Psalms 82:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The righteous King rules from heaven, where his throne remains free from human corruption (see Psalm 2:4). He examines everyone and sees everything that happens on earth (see Psalm 14:2–3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• hates: See Psalm 5:4–6; Proverbs 6:16–18. 

• Wicked deeds result in destruction and violence (Psalms 58:2; Psalms 73:6; Psalms 74:20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God sent fiery coals and burning sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19) as symbols of judgment (Psalms 18:8; Psalms 120:4; Psalms 140:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly are assured of the Lord’s favorable presence when they see his face (see Psalm 23:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Evil becomes so widespread that the godly pray for rescue (Isaiah 57:1; Micah 7:2; compare Psalms 1:6; Psalms 37:20; Psalms 58:7; Psalms 104:35).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This prayer from the community asks the Lord for help against the many evil acts in the world. Because God answers, the godly can face the future with confidence, knowing that God protects them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The words they say reveal the character of the wicked. They deceive and overpower the godly and arrogantly question the Lord’s purposes.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The godly can trust the Lord's promises, but not the lies of the wicked (Psalm 12:2–4). 

• Sevenfold means entirely or completely.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Those who follow God know that he cares, even when the wicked oppress them. God sees the corrupt and foolish people who praise those who do evil (see Psalms 9:19–20; Psalms 14:2–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: How long?: Repeating the question four times shows intense worry and deep pain (Psalm 79:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist’s loud cry for help becomes a confident song of hope.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A feeling of deep sadness and pain can make it hard to see any hope (Psalm 6:3). Without God’s answer to his prayers (Psalm 22:1), death seems unavoidable, painful, and slow (Psalms 6:6; Psalms 32:3; Psalms 55:4; Psalms 61:2; Psalms 102:5; Psalms 116:3). The psalmist struggles to pray and longs for God's redemption (Psalms 25:17–18; Psalms 31:10; Psalms 38:8; Psalms 39:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist's suffering feels like death (Psalms 22:15; Psalms 55:4; Psalms 88:15; Psalms 94:17; Psalms 116:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Only the Lord can provide understanding and comfort. The psalmist hopes for the Lord's justice so his enemies will not celebrate.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist no longer hears the mockery of his enemies. Instead, he feels joyful because he trusts in the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Also known as fools, the wicked talk to themselves, think, scheme (Psalm 10:4, Psalms 10:6, Psalms 10:11), and make claims. However, because they ignore God’s revelation, they lack understanding (Psalms 14:1; Psalms 39:8; Psalms 53:1; Psalms 74:18, Psalms 74:22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Paul uses phrases from the Greek translation of this passage in his description of the wickedness of all people (Romans 3:10–12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This wisdom psalm includes elements of lament and prophetic speech. The ideals of Psalm 8 clash with foolish human attitudes and sinful actions. Except for verses Psalms 14:5–6, this psalm is similar to Psalm 53.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: From heaven (Psalms 33:13; Psalms 80:14; Psalms 102:19), the Lord sees the wicked, who are clearly evil (Psalm 11:3–5). All humans lack wisdom and do not live in the way God originally intended for them (Psalm 10:4–11; see Romans 1–3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The evil live at the expense of others (Psalms 27:2; Psalms 44:11; Psalms 53:4; see Isaiah 5:8) and have no reverence or knowledge of God (Psalm 79:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Though the wicked perish (Psalm 1:5–6), God is with the righteous.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist prays for the renewal of God’s relationship with his people.

• Jacob is another name for Israel (see Genesis 35:9–10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Only those who follow God may be in the Lord’s presence (Psalm 5:4). As his guests, they experience his hospitality and protection.

• tent: In David’s time, God’s sanctuary was a tent (the tabernacle; see 1 Samuel 21:6; 2 Samuel 6:17; 2 Samuel 7:6; 2 Samuel 12:20; 1 Chronicles 6:32).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This wisdom poem contrasts the lifestyle of the righteous with the actions of fools (Psalm 14). The questions in this psalm invite people to examine themselves and not pay attention to problems with the wicked. The question of who dwells in God’s presence leads into a description of godly character qualities (compare Psalm 24:3–6; Isaiah 33:14–16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalms in this section emphasize integrity and purity (Psalms 17:15; Psalms 18:20–26; Psalms 19:13–14). They describe people as living in God’s presence (Psalms 16:9–11; Psalms 17:15) and remaining steadfast (Psalms 15:5; Psalms 16:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly speak truthfully and act faithfully in their relationships. Unlike the wicked, they are open and transparent (Psalm 12:2–4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Lord prohibited Israel from charging interest to people in need (Exodus 22:25–27). 

• The assurance of God’s presence keeps the godly from destruction (Psalms 16:8; Psalms 46:5; Psalms 125:1). Their situations may temporarily unsettle them, but they ultimately remain strong (Psalm 30:6; Psalms 94:18; Psalms 112:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The psalmist feels safe because only the Lord offers: 

• security (Psalm 16:5–6),

• guidance (Psalm 16:7–8), and

• the joy of his presence (Psalm 16:9–11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this psalm of confidence, the poet quickly transitions from a brief request (Psalm 16:1) to expressions of deep commitment to God and his people (Psalm 16:2–6). The psalm concludes with confident praise (Psalm 16:7–11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: I said to the LORD: The various writers of the psalms pray, lament, and praise the Lord throughout the Psalter (the book of Psalms). The Lord answers them (see Psalm 12:5–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist separates himself from unholy worship, rituals, and words (see Psalm 15:3–5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The cup of blessing represents how God supplies all the psalmist's needs (Psalm 23:5; see Psalms 116:13; compare Psalms 75:8; Isaiah 51:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The land is God’s gift for his people (Deuteronomy 18:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God's guidance gives life (Psalm 16:11; see Psalms 5:8; Psalms 23:1–3; Psalms 32:8; Psalms 73:24). 

• The psalmist relies on the Lord for strength and joy, feeling God's presence beside him (Psalm 16:11; see Psalms 73:23; Psalms 109:31; Psalms 110:1, Psalms 110:5; Psalms 121:5). 

• Peter quoted Psalm 16:8–11 in his sermon on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:25–28).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels confident because he knows that even death cannot separate him from the Lord. He fears separation (see Psalm 13:3–4), but he remains confident that he will see the Lord (see Psalms 11:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist shows belief that life goes on after death. The apostles applied this text to the resurrection of Jesus (Acts 2:25–33; Acts 13:35).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: at Your right hand: See Psalm 16:7–8; Psalms 110:1.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: comes from lips free of deceit: Deception characterizes the wicked. The righteous reject such deceit as a failure of character and pray for rescue from such people (Psalms 5:6; Psalms 43:1; Psalms 120:2). They love honesty, truth, and integrity (Psalms 15:2–3; Psalms 24:4; Psalms 101:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks for God's protection and justice, affirms his own integrity, and prays for the Lord to defeat his strong enemies.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Although he is not perfect, the psalmist dedicates himself to the Lord. He does not want to sin through lies, flattery, or gossip (see Psalms 10:7; Psalms 15:2–3; Psalms 17:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist declares his innocence (Psalm 17:1) and commits himself to integrity by being open to God’s examination.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This prayer for God's care continues the request begun in Psalm 17:1–2 for redemption from evil.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• as the apple of Your eye (literally as the pupil of your eye): This metaphor shows God's care and love for the psalmist (see Deuteronomy 32:10). 

• The shadow of God's wings is a place of his protection from enemies and hardship (Psalms 36:7; Psalms 57:1; Psalms 61:4; Psalms 63:7; Psalms 91:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays confidently for the Lord's victory, knowing God is more powerful than the evildoers. The psalmist finds joy in the Lord's inheritance (Psalm 16:5), whereas the wicked search for joy in this world.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: behold Your face: The psalmist does not allow temporary concerns raised by adversaries to stand in the way of his experiencing a real and lasting relationship with the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The servant of the Lord was given the duty to establish God's kingdom on earth (see Psalm 78:70; Psalms 132:10; Psalms 144:10). 

• The Lord rescued David from all his enemies by helping him defeat them (see 2 Samuel 8:1–14).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This psalm describes a royal story of God rescuing his king. A similar version of this psalm appears in 2 Samuel 22:1–51. The psalm encourages those who hear the earlier prayers for help in Psalms 16 and Psalms 17:17. 

The psalmist describes the dramatic nature of God’s rescue in three different ways (Psalm 18:7–15, Psalms 18:16–19, Psalms 18:30–36). The psalm also offers hope that a future Son of David will completely defeat evil (Psalm 18:43–50; compare Psalm 2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A shield symbolizes protection, salvation, and victory (Psalms 7:10; Psalms 18:2, Psalms 18:30, Psalms 18:35; Psalms 84:11; Psalms 91:4; Psalms 115:9, Psalms 115:10, Psalms 115:11; Psalms 119:114; Psalms 144:2). It inspires trust, patience, and confidence in God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God deserves praise for his greatness and faithfulness (Psalms 48:1; Psalms 96:4; Psalms 145:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God lives in his sanctuary, the heavenly temple (Psalm 102:19; see Psalms 14:2–3). He knows everything and sees every person. He will defend and vindicate those who live in a faithful and righteous way (see Psalm 11:3–7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The destabilization of the whole earth will be a means of God’s judgment (Psalm 77:17–18; Psalms 96:9; Psalms 97:4; Psalms 99:1; Psalms 104:32; Isaiah 29:6; Micah 1:3–4; Nahum 1:2–6; Haggai 2:7, Haggai 2:21).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The psalmist describes the Lord coming down from heaven to earth. This moment includes powerful signs such as earthquakes, fire, smoke, darkness, and rain. All creation trembles when God appears.

The psalm shows God as the Divine Warrior (a title that describes God fighting for his people, see Psalm 97:2–5) and as the Judge who rules with justice (see Psalms 50:1–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• His nostrils … His mouth: The psalmist compares God to an angry person or a fierce creature (see Job 41:12–22).

• The frightening images of smoke, flames, and glowing coals show God’s anger against sin.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord rules over all of nature (see Psalm 104:2–4; Psalms 148:5–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: a cherub: See study notes on 1 Chronicles 28:18; 2 Chronicles 3:10–13.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God loves and delights in the psalmist (see Psalm 18:1), so he will save him (Psalms 37:23; Psalms 41:11; Psalms 91:14–16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist states that loyalty brings rewards. He trusts in the Lord (see Psalm 16:1) and promises to live with integrity (see Psalms 1, Psalms 15:15, Psalms 24:24; see also Psalms 19:12–14).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• kept the ways of the LORD: The psalmist follows God's instructions faithfully (see Psalm 25:8–10). 

• have not wickedly departed: The psalmist avoids foolishness (see Psalms 1 and Psalms 14:14) and chooses wisdom (see Psalms 1 and Psalms 15:15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The faithful God remains true to his character. He loves faithfulness, innocence, and purity, and he hates wickedness (see Psalm 1:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The pure have clean hands (see Psalm 18:20–24). 

• to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd: The Lord understands everyone's character and responds to them fairly.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: haughty: The Lord hates pride (Psalm 101:5; Psalms 131:1; see Proverbs 6:16–17; Proverbs 21:4; Proverbs 30:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: light my lamp: The Lord renews the psalmist's life, helping him overcome the darkness of difficult times (see Psalms 112:4; Psalms 119:105).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: scale a wall: God helps his servants fight their battles.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• perfect: God’s character is full of integrity. He is completely trustworthy (see Psalm 18:26). 

• God promises to protect his people, and he keeps this promise. 

• Seeking God's protection requires trust and faith. Despite his feelings or external circumstances, the psalmist makes a deep commitment to the Lord. He experiences joy (Psalms 5:11; Psalms 64:10) as he waits for the Lord's rescue (Psalm 57:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist experiences God’s rescue and provision of victory.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist’s victories come from the Lord. He completely depends on God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A wide path represents freedom and safety (see Psalms 4:8; Psalms 119:35).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: With help from the Divine Warrior, the psalmist experienced victory over his enemies.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Placing a foot on the necks of the enemy represents total victory (see Joshua 10:23–26).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
With God’s help and victory, the psalmist gained success in battle and in ruling the nation. In this way, the psalm reflects the promise about David’s royal line in Psalm 2. 

This psalm also answers some of the earlier prayers for help. The laments in earlier psalms begin to find resolution here.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist again reflects on the Lord’s victories. God’s amazing rescue and the king’s victory are cause for celebration.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God defends and vindicates his servant. In this way, God fulfills the mission he gave him (Psalm 2; see Psalms 47:3; Psalms 144:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist's vision of praise among the nations inspired Paul in his mission to the Gentiles (Romans 15:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God appointed David, his chosen leader, to bring order to God's world (see Psalm 2). Both David and his descendants received this responsibility.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The glory of God refers to the Creator's splendor or visible presence (Psalm 113:4). 

• God (Hebrew ’el): El is an ancient name for God. It shows his power as the Creator.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The created world shows God's wisdom, and the heavens are where God lives (Psalm 2:4; see Psalms 8:1; Psalms 57:5; Psalms 89:6; Psalms 115:3). From heaven, God watches over people (Psalms 11:4; Psalms 14:2; Psalms 33:13; Psalms 53:2; Psalms 80:14; Psalms 102:19) and helps his followers (Psalms 18:6–8, Psalms 18:13; Psalms 20:6; Psalms 57:3; Psalms 76:8; Psalms 144:5). 

The heavens remain unaffected by human failures and rebellions (see Psalm 2:1–4). They show God's faithfulness, righteousness (Psalms 36:5; Psalms 50:6; Psalms 57:10; Psalms 85:11; Psalms 89:2, Psalms 89:5; Psalms 97:6; Psalms 108:4), and wisdom (Psalms 136:5; see Psalms 119:89–90). The heavens reveal the Lord’s glory (see Psalm 19:1) and prove his presence and work.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
God's wisdom is clearly shown in many places:

• It appears in the heavens (Psalm 19:1–4),

• in nature (Psalm 19:4–6),

• in his teachings (Psalm 19:7–11), and

• in the life of the psalmist (Psalm 19:12–14)

Like Psalm 8, this hymn uses creation to lead people to reflect on God. It offers a calm moment after the intense prayers and victory songs in earlier psalms.

The psalm begins with creation as a source of wisdom. It then moves to God’s word as the perfect source of wisdom. Finally, it ends with the human need for redemption.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God’s wisdom does not need to be spoken. Through creation, it is seen, felt, and experienced. Paul applied this text to condemn Israel for its lack of receptivity to Jesus Christ (Romans 10:18).

• The sun is part of God’s creation, but it is not a god, as people of other nations in the ancient Near East commonly believed.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God's instructions to humans show his character and wisdom. His guidance is valuable and enjoyable (Psalm 119:103). It nurtures the individual (Proverbs 16:24; Proverbs 24:14) and holds more value than material possessions (Psalm 81:13–16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist knows his weaknesses, so he prays to remain faithful and commits himself to the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• A person who commits deliberate sins does so with a proud and defiant attitude (Psalm 86:14; Psalms 119:21, Psalms 119:69). 

• The great transgression is rebellion (see Psalm 32:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart: The psalmist desires to please God in everything he says and thinks (see Luke 6:45; Romans 12:1–2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The title God of Jacob shows God's long-standing relationship with his people (see Psalms 46:7, Psalms 46:11; Psalms 75:9; Psalms 76:6; Psalms 81:1, Psalms 81:4; Psalms 84:8; Psalms 94:7; Psalms 114:7; Psalms 146:5). 

• protect you: See Psalm 59:1–2.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The community prays for the king’s protection and victory.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This royal prayer asks God to give victory to the king (Psalm 20:1–5). It then expresses confidence that God will bring rescue (Psalms 20:6–8). The psalm ends with the people asking God to answer their prayer (Psalms 20:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This series of psalms shows a journey from confidence and commitment (Psalms 20–21), through anguish and abandonment (Psalm 22), and finally to comfort, insight, and hope (Psalms 23–24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Gifts and burnt offerings show submission to the Lord (compare Psalm 40:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: make all your plans succeed … grant all your petitions: These requests might be those mentioned in Psalm 21:3–6 (compare Psalms 27:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Troops carried a victory banner to battle. They gathered under it and encouraged each other to act (see Isaiah 11:10, Isaiah 11:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God chose his anointed king to be ruler (see Psalm 2:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A community member (Psalm 20:1–5) responds with words of assurance and confidence in God's help.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: chariots and … horses: These were tools used in war (see Psalms 33:16–17; Psalms 76:6; Psalms 147:10; Isaiah 30:16; Isaiah 31:1–3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s people thank him for giving victory to the king.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God has given the king what he desired. God protected him and blessed him (see Psalm 20:5; see also Psalms 2:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: rich blessings: See Proverbs 10:6.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The king returned victorious from battle and received honor from the people. His greatest honor came from God, who gave him blessings, life, and his presence.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
God offers a rich quality of life (Psalms 61:6–7; Psalms 91:14–16; Psalms 128:4–6). This life is characterized by:

• God's presence (Psalms 16:11; Psalms 23:6; Psalms 27:4; Psalms 36:9),

• joy (Psalm 16:11)

• goodness (Psalm 23:6; Psalms 34:14–15), and

• protection (Psalm 41:2; Psalms 61:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God's eternal blessings also bring a full life now (see Psalm 133).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The king was victorious not because of his strength or goodness, but because God honored his faith.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: As long as even a single enemy opposed the king’s authority, God’s kingdom was not fully present. This prayer requests victory over all evil in the world.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The fiery furnace and fire represent the seriousness of God's judgment on the wicked. In the Old Testament, fire often represents God’s anger against sin and destructive judgment (Psalms 11:6; Psalms 18:8; Psalms 50:3; Psalms 68:2; Psalms 78:21; Psalms 79:5; Psalms 80:16; Psalms 89:46; Psalms 97:3; Psalms 104:4; Psalms 140:10; see Isaiah 66:24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: descendants … offspring: Evil will end when God destroys all opposition to himself (Psalm 109:13; compare Psalms 18:50; Psalms 22:30–31; Psalms 25:13; Psalms 102:28).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Be exalted (compare Psalm 57:5, Psalms 57:11; Psalms 108:5) expresses communal praise and joy in God’s greatness and power.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels deeply separated from God (see Psalm 10:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist switches between thinking about his current difficult situation and remembering the Lord's past faithfulness. He ends the psalm with a prayer for rescue.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
All previous laments seem minor compared to this outcry against the enemy and God's abandonment. The psalm has two main sections: 

• the lament (Psalm 22:1–21) and

• praise for redemption (Psalm 22:22–31).

This naturally leads to Psalm 23. 

The apostles saw this psalm as expressing the sufferings of Jesus Christ. He ultimately fulfilled the purpose of David's humiliation, rejection by people, and divine abandonment (Matthew 27:35, Matthew 27:39, Matthew 27:43, Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34; John 19:23–24, John 19:28; Hebrews 2:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God, the holy King, is set apart from all his creation, but he chooses to reveal himself to Israel. 

• God strongly desires that his people praise him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Both the Lord and the people reject the psalmist. He clearly describes his pain (Psalm 22:1–2). He lives like a humble animal.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: People ridicule the psalmist's trust in the Lord (see Psalm 3:2; Matthew 27:43), which shames him (Psalms 44:13–14; Psalms 74:10; Psalms 89:50; Psalms 109:25).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord took care of the psalmist before the psalmist could do anything for himself (see Psalm 71:6; Psalms 139:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist thinks about his past relationship with God (see Psalm 22:3–5). The Lord has been his very life.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Bashan, a region famous for its herds and plants, produced strong bulls (Psalm 68:30).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist again shares his deep pain and suffering (see Psalm 22:1–2, Psalms 22:6–8). His trouble comes from human beings who act like wild animals.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels like he is poured out like water. This describes a temporary and empty life that leaves him drained.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Facing adversity is as terrible as dying of thirst (see Psalm 137:6). 

• Jesus might have thought of this verse when he said, “I am thirsty” (John 19:28).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wild pack of dogs represents aggressive and dishonest people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• I can count all my bones: The psalmist's enemies have shamed him by taking his clothes. Jesus also faced this humiliation (see Matthew 27:35). 

• stare and gloat over me: Enemies make the psalmist a target of their ridicule (see Psalms 35:24, Psalms 35:26; Psalms 38:16; Psalms 55:3; compare Psalms 59:10). 

• cast lots: Casting lots was sometimes a way for religious people to seek God's guidance (Leviticus 16:8; Numbers 27:21; Acts 1:24–26). Here, the lots are thrown as a game of chance. The soldiers threw dice for the clothing of Jesus after the crucifixion (Matthew 27:35; Mark 15:24; Luke 23:34; John 19:24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays to God for help with his troubles. Only the Lord can protect him from dogs, lions, and oxen.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The sword shows that the enemy wants to kill.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: • I will proclaim Your name: The writer of Hebrews applies these words to Jesus (Hebrews 2:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist praises the Lord and calls for the godly to join him. He tells of God’s goodness to the needy, including himself.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly respond with awe (see Psalm 22:25).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Unlike how he responds to the wicked (see Psalm 21:8–12), God cares for the needy and listens to their prayers (Psalm 51:17; Psalms 69:33; Psalms 102:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The great assembly might include all nations (Psalm 22:27; Psalms 26:12; Psalms 35:18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist promises to praise the Lord, the great King of the earth (Psalm 22:27–28), who helps those in need. Only God deserves praise.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God understands what his people need and provides for them (Psalm 63:5; Psalms 81:16; Psalms 103:5; Psalms 107:9; Psalms 132:15; Psalms 145:16; Psalms 147:14).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: families of the nations: All clans and tribes of humanity (see Genesis 12:3; Revelation 5:9–10) will submit to the Lord (Psalm 96:1–3; see Psalms 2, Psalms 72:72; Isaiah 2:2–4; 1 Corinthians 15:25–27).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God alone rules over the whole world (Obadiah 1:21).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord invites everyone, both rich and poor (Psalm 22:26), to the banquet as long as they worship him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Future generations will join those from the past in praising the Lord (Psalm 22:3–5). The descendants of the godly will receive blessings (Psalm 22:30–31), unlike the children of the wicked (Psalms 21:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord's acts of redemption (Psalms 40:9; Psalms 50:6; Psalms 71:15, Psalms 71:16, Psalms 71:24; Psalms 97:6) show that he is righteous (see Psalms 4:1). His righteousness gives him the character needed for leadership, making fair decisions, and building relationships. This virtue brings harmony and order (see Psalm 50:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord promises to care for his children (Psalm 34:9–10; Isaiah 51:14). He showed this ability to Israel in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 2:7) and in the promised land (Deuteronomy 8:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: People in the ancient Near East commonly viewed their rulers as shepherds.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm, which expresses trust and confidence in the Lord, has been a favorite of God's people for generations. It assures us of God's presence during difficult times. It brings to mind images of the Good Shepherd (Psalm 23:1–3; see Ezekiel 34:12; John 10:11) and the messianic banquet (Psalm 23:5–6; see Isaiah 25:6; Revelation 19:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
These psalms develop the importance of: 

• integrity (Psalms 25:4–7, Psalms 25:12–14, Psalms 25:21; Psalms 26:6, Psalms 26:11; Psalms 27:7–12),

• God's care as a shepherd (Psalms 23:1; Psalms 28:9),

• God's guidance (Psalms 23:2–3; Psalms 25:5; Psalms 27:11),

• God's goodness (Psalms 23:6; Psalms 25:7–8; Psalms 27:13), and

• living in his house (Psalms 23:6; Psalms 26:8; Psalms 27:4, Psalms 27:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Sheep rest after they have eaten enough (Zephaniah 3:13; see Isaiah 11:7; compare Isaiah 13:20; Isaiah 27:10). 

• The Lord guides the sheep for their benefit (see Psalm 5:8). 

• Sheep drink only from still water, so the shepherd finds peaceful streams for them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Compare Psalm 19:7; The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul.

• The Lord guides by: 

• rescuing his people from evil (Psalm 23:4–5; see Psalms 31:3),

• bringing them back to himself (Psalms 5:8; Psalms 61:2),

• caring for his people (Psalms 48:14; Psalms 139:10),

• ruling his people (Psalm 67:4),

• counseling his people (Psalm 73:24),

• protecting his people (Psalms 78:53; Psalms 107:30; Psalms 143:11), and

• instructing them in wisdom (Psalm 27:11; see Proverbs 4:11).

• The Lord’s name guarantees the relationship. He protects his reputation against any claims of abandoning his people or allowing them to sin (see Psalms 25:11; Psalms 31:3; Psalms 106:8; Psalms 143:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The shepherd used his rod and staff to protect against danger.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• A feast shows the Lord’s care and mercy for his people (see Psalm 22:26, Psalms 22:29). Enemies may watch, but they cannot disturb the guests. 

• The ritual of anointing the head with oil honored guests (Psalm 92:9–11), and provided hospitality and refreshment (Psalms 104:15; Psalms 133:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord shows his unfailing love through his presence and the unique benefits he provides (Psalms 69:16; Psalms 86:17; Psalms 109:21; see Psalms 18:6; Psalms 61:4). He gives care that surpasses the temporary challenges from enemies (Psalm 7:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord made the earth and everything in it, and now he rules over it (see 1 Corinthians 10:25–26). He sees all its people (Psalm 33:14), no matter their status (Psalms 49:1–2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The kingdom belongs to the Creator, the Great King (see Psalm 22:27).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The shepherd from Psalm 23, who is also the King of the world, takes control of Zion.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God created everything in an orderly and stable manner (see Psalm 89:11; Psalms 102:25; Psalms 104:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• These questions encourage people to stop focusing on their issues with the wicked and to reflect on themselves (see Psalm 15:1). 

• God's holy place is the holy mountain, referring to both Jerusalem and heaven.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The citizens of the King’s realm include all who seek him. The Lord invites them to enter his presence.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• People with clean hands have not caused harm or damaged relationships (see Psalm 9:12; Psalms 15:2–5).

• People with pure hearts dedicate themselves completely to the Lord. This is shown through strong character, honesty, and selflessness (Psalm 51:10; Psalms 73:1; see Matthew 5:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The LORD of Hosts rules from his home, the temple in Jerusalem (Psalm 84:3–5). He keeps out sin and sinners (Psalm 24:326) but protects everyone living in Zion.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist commits himself to the Lord instead of to idols (see Psalm 24:3–4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist is confident that the godly will be proven right and his enemies will fail (see Psalm 25:15–22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This personal lament includes wisdom teachings and a community lament. It starts and ends with a declaration of trust in the Lord (Psalm 25:1–3, Psalms 25:15–22). The psalmist prays for guidance (Psalm 25:4–7) and urges the godly to live wisely (Psalms 25:12–14). 

In addition to the enemies who trouble him, the psalmist confesses his sins(Psalm 25:7, Psalms 25:11, Psalms 25:18) as part of his distress. Trust grows by understanding God's nature: He is compassionate, faithful, and good (Psalm 25:8–10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Enemies would rejoice by singing a victory song.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The right path, the path of wisdom (see Psalm 5:8), involves being open to instruction that leads to life (Psalms 27:11; Psalms 43:3; Psalms 73:24; Psalms 119:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this prayer for guidance, compassion, and forgiveness, the psalmist asks the Lord for wisdom. He admits his past mistakes and recognizes that his hope is in his merciful Savior.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Biblical hope is not just wishing for a good outcome. It means trusting in the Lord's will and having the courage to face disappointments (Psalm 33:22; Psalms 130:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: compassion: See also Psalms 51:1; Psalms 57:1; Psalms 103:8.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord keeps his people close to himself.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks for forgiveness for his many sins (Psalms 25:7; Psalms 32:1–5). The sins of Israel’s kings showed the weaknesses in David’s family line and why it failed in Old Testament Israel (see Psalm 89).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Those who fear the Lord will receive further instruction and experience God’s presence (Psalm 25:14) and blessing (Psalms 25:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• prosperity: See Psalm 23:6. 

• inherit the land: Unlike the wicked, who will perish (Psalm 1:6), the godly have a secure future. In the end, God will bless them, and their blessings will last (see Psalm 37:9, Psalms 37:11, Psalms 37:22, Psalms 37:29, Psalms 37:34; Isaiah 57:13; Matthew 5:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: free my feet from the mesh: See Psalm 5:9–10; Psalms 31:4; Psalms 140:5; Proverbs 3:26.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist expresses confidence in the Lord, commits to a life of integrity, and prays for rescue.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist finds no relief (see Psalms 4:1; Psalms 13:1–2) as his problems worsen. He connects his anguish to sin but does not explain the nature of his sin (see Psalm 25:7, Psalms 25:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks God to handle these enemies, knowing that the Lord hates violent people (see Psalm 11:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalm ends with a promise of trust and hope, just as it began (see Psalms 9:18; Psalms 25:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist opens himself to divine examination of his life, especially in the areas of his character and devotion.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this personal lament, the psalmist prays for redemption because of his innocence and the Lord's justice.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: For God’s truth to become part of one’s character requires a habitual commitment.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Because of his devotion to the Lord (Psalm 26:1–3), the psalmist separates himself from evil people (see Psalm 1:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Ritual purity required the worshiper to wash their hands. This act symbolized separating from evil and evildoers (see Psalm 73:13). 

• The altar symbolizes God's presence (Psalm 43:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist demonstrates his loyalty to the Lord through pious rituals, praise, and acknowledgment of the Lord’s presence in the temple.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The sanctuary represented the visible presence of the Lord (see Psalm 18:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Do not take my soul away with sinners: The end of the godly cannot be the same as that of the wicked.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist standing on solid ground represents salvation (compare Psalm 143:10). 

• in the congregations: This means in the great assembly at the temple (Psalms 26:6–8; Psalms 22:25).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Light shows the Lord's goodness (Psalm 27:13; see Psalms 4:6; Psalms 23:6; Psalms 31:19; Psalms 38:10; Psalms 43:3; Psalms 56:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist acknowledges the Lord at the center of his life (Psalm 27:1). Because of God’s presence, he engages his adversaries with confidence. They cannot intimidate him or disrupt his inner peace.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm combines two types—a psalm of confidence (Psalm 27:1–6) and an individual lament (Psalms 27:7–14)—united by the theme of longing for the Lord's presence. The psalmist focuses on the Lord, making his own circumstances less important. The psalmist shows strong faith by being open to the Lord's guidance, timing, and priorities.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist's enemies want to take advantage of him and live off his resources (see study note on Psalm 14:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: keep my trust: See Psalms 25:2; Psalms 26:1.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Seeking and enjoying the Lord's presence gives the psalmist confidence and security. He trusts in God's protection and looks forward to giving thanks and praise (see Psalm 18:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: tent (or tabernacle): This early shrine was where the Israelites worshipped before they built the temple.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• my head will be held high: This is a sign of victory. 

• The granting of the request of Psalm 27:4 leads to sacrifices with joyful shouts.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Unlike the wicked (Psalm 10:4), who only want a temporary advantage (Psalms 78:34–36), the godly search for the Lord like a thirsty person seeks water in the desert (Psalms 63:1; Psalms 105:4; Psalms 119:2, Psalms 119:10; Matthew 6:33). They act wisely (Psalm 34:10, Psalms 34:14) while waiting for the Lord to resolve their crisis (Psalms 34:4; Psalms 69:6; Psalms 77:2; Psalms 119:58).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks for the Lord's mercy, presence, and guidance. For the psalmist, God is the greatest good, while enemies and other situations are less important.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist shows confidence and hope in the Lord's presence. Living in faith means waiting patiently, knowing the Lord is good. This life is not always easy for the faithful (Psalm 42:2–3; Psalms 43:5), but their future is secure (Psalms 37:9; Psalms 130:7; see Psalms 9:18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: if You remain silent: The psalmist asks the Lord to act (Psalm 35:22; Psalms 50:3; Psalms 83:1; Psalms 109:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks the Lord to listen. His urgent request comes from the tension between his close relationship with the Lord and the trouble he is facing.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this personal lament, the psalmist asks for justice and mercy. He trusts in the Lord's strength and faithfulness and prays for the Lord's people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: People often raised their hands as a sign of devoted prayer (Psalms 63:4; Psalms 134:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks God to punish his enemies and prove his innocence.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked do not acknowledge the difference between the sacred and the common, so they have no respect for the Lord’s creation, redemption, or revelation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist anticipates rescue because of his confidence in the Lord’s justice.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: my strength and my shield: The Lord protects the psalmist (see Psalm 59:9, Psalms 59:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The poem closes with intercession for the Lord’s people. 

• bless Your inheritance: See Psalms 29:11; Psalms 133:3.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist issues a call to honor the Lord for his power (see Psalm 96:7–8). 

• O heavenly beings: Angels or deities who, some believed, held special powers. The psalmist did not believe in other gods but called on people who thought they were real to look to the Lord as the only God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This nature hymn in praise of the Creator declares that the Lord holds all power over nature. God uses the same unsurpassed strength to care for his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Hebrew word qol can mean "voice," "noise" (1 Kings 1:45), or "thunder" (Joel 3:16). The Lord's voice is awe-inspiring and overpowers any sounds people might attribute to other gods.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The cedars of Lebanon were famous for their large size and high quality (see Isaiah 2:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Lebanon’s mountains and Sirion (another name for Mount Hermon) are high mountains to the north of Israel. 

• The Lord can make even huge mountains shake when he commands it (see Psalm 114:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Wilderness of Kadesh was south of Judah. People could hear God's voice across the land, from the north (Psalm 29:6) to the south.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The image of strong floodwaters relates to the great flood (Genesis 6:17). The Lord rules as king over all creation. No one challenges his kingdom.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The ruler of nature blesses his people with peace (see Psalms 28:8–9; Psalms 37:11; Psalms 133:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• I will exalt You is a call to praise and thank the Lord (Psalms 34:3; Psalms 81:1; Psalms 99:5, Psalms 99:9; Psalms 107:32; Psalms 118:28; Psalms 145:1; see Exodus 15:1; Isaiah 25:1).
