• You have lifted me up: God saved the psalmist from death (Psalm 30:3).

• God, in his justice and care, did not let the psalmist’s enemies win (see Psalms 26:9; Psalms 27:12; Psalms 28:3; Psalms 31:8).

Perhaps David wrote this psalm before the dedication of the temple, making his own experience representative of the nation’s.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist praises God for his victory over difficult circumstances, comparing it to being saved from death.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This individual thanksgiving psalm begins by praising the Lord for his salvation (Psalm 30:1–3). It then contrasts God's favor with his anger (Psalm 30:4–7) and ends with a transformation from mourning to dancing (Psalms 30:8–12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly should celebrate the Lord’s acts of rescue with song and praise (Psalms 33:21; Psalms 97:12; Psalms 103:1; Psalms 105:3; Psalms 145:21).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• I will never be shaken: The psalmist admits his overconfident attitude (compare Psalm 32:3–4). 

• my mountain stand strong: In the psalms, this phrase powerfully symbolizes stability and God's control (see Psalms 11:1; Psalms 18:7; Psalms 36:6; Psalms 46:2; Psalms 72:3; Psalms 76:4; Psalms 83:14; Psalms 97:5; Psalms 114:4, Psalms 114:6; Psalms 125:2). 

• I was dismayed: The absence of God’s favor destroys the security of the proud (compare Psalm 104:27–30).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist faced death (also in Psalm 30:1–3), either literally or figuratively. When he turned to the Lord, the Lord rescued him and changed his mourning into joyful dancing. Only God's favor can permanently and powerfully overcome human failure and deep despair.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord provides safety to anyone seeking his protection. The psalmist trusts and submits to the Lord. See also Psalm 71:1–3.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist urges the faithful to seek safety in the Lord and wait for his salvation. After experiencing something like death, he shares how the Lord remained faithful. This psalm points ahead to the suffering of Jesus (Luke 23:46).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist urgently asks the Lord to notice his desperate situation (PSalms 71:2; Psalms 88:2; Psalms 102:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Into Your hands I commit my spirit: The psalmist will trust his Lord, whether he lives or dies. Jesus said these words on the cross before he died (Luke 23:46).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Trusting the Lord means believing he cares about our well-being.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: in the open: This means a wide area, unlike a narrow or tight place that causes distress (see Psalm 18:19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this prayer for mercy, the psalmist places a description of his intense suffering and the pain of rejection between two statements of trust in the Lord (Psalm 31:6, Psalms 31:14).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: my bones are wasting away: This phrase powerfully describes how despair can harm our physical health.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Hope does not trust weak and unreliable human beings. It trusts only in the Lord. The suffering person places his life in God’s hands while he waits for the Lord to bring justice.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: My times are in Your hands: To give up control of timing is one way to express submission.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist, who did not deserve to be disgraced, invokes the principle of retribution (see study note on Psalm 1:6; see also “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist, who did not deserve to be disgraced, invokes the principle of retribution

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist thanks the Lord for answering his prayer and rescuing him (Psalm 31:1–18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Blessed be the LORD: The psalmist expresses his joy at the experience of God’s goodness and love. Throughout his struggles, the Lord has cared for him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Out of his own pain and renewed awareness of the Lord’s goodness, the psalmist turns to others who suffer. He holds out the promise of God’s loving care for those who persevere in hoping for the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord’s forgiveness brings people back into a relationship with him, removes their guilt, and gives them joy. Paul quoted this text when explaining justification by faith alone (Romans 4:4–8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This wisdom psalm of confession and thanks urges the godly to learn from the psalmist’s journey through sin, denial, confession, and forgiveness. The early church used this psalm as one of the seven penitential psalms (psalms of repentance, see also Psalms 6, Psalms 38:38, Psalms 51:51, Psalms 102:102, Psalms 130:130, Psalms 143:143).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist admits his sin (see Psalms 19:12–13; Psalms 25:7, Psalms 25:11, Psalms 25:15–22) and his resistance to confessing sin. The Lord pressed him hard until he confessed his guilt.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist believes his suffering comes directly from the Lord's discipline (compare Psalms 38:2; Psalms 39:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God has forgiven the guilt and rebellion mentioned in Psalm 32:1. The Lord’s nature is to reconcile and forgive (Psalms 78:38; Psalms 85:2; Psalms 130:4), but he requires people to confess and repent.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly will learn from the psalmist’s experience to pray for forgiveness before it is too late.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord promises to be a safe place for his people (Psalm 31:20). Instead of feeling terrified (Psalm 31:13), the psalmist hears songs of victory all around.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God interrupts the psalmist's teaching with a message inviting the godly to receive the Lord's wisdom (see Psalms 5:8; Psalms 23:3; Psalms 25:4–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The foolish person lacks wisdom. Ignoring the Lord’s advice harms life and makes a person like an animal (see Isaiah 1:3; James 3:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Difficulties common to all of life will come to the wicked, whereas the Lord promises to protect the godly with his care.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist urges the godly to praise the Lord with melodies, with a new song, and with skillfully-played music.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This hymn of creation (see also Psalms 8, Psalms 19:19, Psalms 104:104, Psalms 145:145) might be a continuation of Psalm 32. It urges readers to praise God (Psalm 33:1–3), to recognize the power of his word in creation (Psalms 33:4–7), and to respect the Creator (Psalms 33:8–11). It gives hope to forgiven sinners (Psalm 32) that they can live a new life in the fear of the Lord and under divine protection.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God's word shows his character and power.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The nations surrounding Israel thought that the sea had divine power, but it is under God’s control, within boundaries that he set (see Psalm 104:8–10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The power of the Lord extends to all the nations (see Psalm 22; Psalms 96:123).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Fear of the Lord begins with awe for God and for his powerful word. His word created everything and continues to order and sustain creation. He frustrates the plans of people who oppose his will.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The plans of powerful people will only succeed if God allows it (see Isaiah 8:9210).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God’s word still orders creation and will do so forever.

• God's purposes are wonderful (Psalms 40:5; Psalms 92:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: People who fear God are chosen as his inheritance (see Psalm 33:13–19). This does not include rebellious people (Psalm 78:62).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: From the heavens, the Lord searches out and cares for anyone who fears him (see Psalm 14:2–3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: army …great strength. … horse: Even military power is under God's control (see Psalm 33:10–11; Ecclesiastes 9:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God watches over all who live by his counsel (Psalm 32:8). He protects, rescues, and stays close to them (Psalm 34:15–22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The faithful see God's power in creation and world events. They respond with trust, commitment, joy, and hope as they pray and wait for God's help.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist uses wordplay to contrast his people's certain hope (Hebrew yakhal) in the Lord with the supposed strength (Hebrew khayil) of the wicked's horses.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Abimelech is another name for Achish (see 1 Samuel 21:10–15). The body of the psalm makes no explicit connection to this event.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist encourages those in need to join him in praise.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This wisdom psalm includes a thanksgiving song of praise (Psalm 34:1–7) that celebrates the Lord for caring for and protecting godly sufferers. It also includes an invitation to wisdom (Psalm 34:8–14) and explains wisdom concerning the Lord’s care for the needy and the suffering of the wicked (Psalm 34:15–22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist describes his experiences of answered prayer.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The angel of the LORD showed God's presence during the journey through the wilderness. He protected Israel from Egypt's forces (Exodus 14:19–20), and he will guard all those who are godly (Psalm 91:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly encourage everyone to seek wisdom, to fear the Lord, and to place themselves under the protection of the Lord’s angel.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Fear of the Lord includes reverence and respect, and it motivates a life of wisdom (see Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Anyone who listens, even children, can become wise followers of God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Wisdom has three parts: 

• fearing the Lord (Psalm 34:11),

• doing good (Psalm 34:14), and

• rejecting evil (Psalm 34:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Peter quotes this passage in his instructions for peaceful living (1 Peter 3:10–12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Godly people choose their words carefully. Speaking evil and telling lies is unwise (see Psalm 10:7; compare Psalms 17:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The way of peace leads to harmony and order, whereas evil destroys them (see Psalm 37:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord distinguishes between wise and foolish people; he shows his concern for the wise by rescuing them from trouble (Psalm 34:15, Psalms 34:17–20). However, God destroys the foolish (Psalm 34:16, Psalms 34:21).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Those who are brokenhearted have a spirit of deep sorrow for sin and a strong dependence on the Lord. God accepts this humble spirit as a proper sacrifice (Psalm 51:17). The wicked hate people who are brokenhearted (Psalm 109:16). But the Lord heals them and restores them (Psalm 147:3; see Isaiah 57:15; Isaiah 61:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly might suffer, but the Lord will reward them in the end. Similarly, the wicked might prosper for a time, but ultimately they will perish (Psalms 1:6; Psalms 34:15–16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Bones represent a person's whole self (see Psalm 6:2). 

• not one of them will be broken: John applied this statement to Jesus at the crucifixion (John 19:36).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this lament, the Lord's troubled servant asks God to notice his situation and defend him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist desires the Lord's salvation. The language may seem harsh, but it comes from a wish for justice and for the Lord to help the needy and oppressed.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• A dark and slick path suggests instability and sudden disaster under the Lord's judgment (see Psalms 69:23; Psalms 73:18; Psalms 82:5; Psalms 107:10; Psalms 143:3). 

• The angel of the LORD is an agent of judgment as well as salvation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Nothing in the universe can compare with the Lord (see Psalms 86:8; Psalms 89:6, Psalms 89:8; Isaiah 40:18, Isaiah 40:25).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: False witnesses want nothing but violence (see Psalms 11:4–6; Psalms 54:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist presents the Lord with the reasons for his suffering. Evil has many faces. He is tired and worn out, and he knows that only the Lord can help him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist's attackers gnashed their teeth to show their jealousy.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: John applied this claim of innocence (see also Psalm 69:4) to Jesus (John 15:25).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
In this prayer for justice, the psalmist faces a crisis so great that only the Lord can resolve it. The psalmist chooses the right path and believes that vengeance belongs to the Lord.

God’s patience allows the wicked to continue in their evil ways. Because of this, their hearts grow harder and they find reasons to justify their behavior.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Aha, aha!: This Hebrew word (he’akh) expresses a feeling of joy.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist calls on the Lord to judge the wicked and to rescue the godly and bring them joy.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: no fear of God: Paul uses this phrase to describe how all people are morally corrupt (Romans 3:18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Foolish people reject wisdom and goodness while they chase after evil.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This lament contrasts the foolish world made by the wicked with the wise world created and maintained by the Lord. The wicked care only about themselves, while the Lord cares for all creation. He will step in to bring justice to his world. The righteous will enjoy his protection, but the wicked will die.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s all-encompassing goodness surpasses that of the created order. God graciously meets his people’s practical needs.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: As the source of wisdom, the Lord is reliable and incomparable. His faithful care extends to all parts of the created order.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: All creatures live by God's grace (1 Timothy 4:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God invites everyone to a feast in his house (compare Proverbs 9:1–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Light represents salvation and celebration (Psalms 18:25–29; Psalms 27:1; compare Psalm 35:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God's wisdom covers all of creation and protects those who follow him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist is sure that the chaos caused by the wicked (Psalm 36:1–4) will stop when they die.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: envy: The jealous desire to have what others enjoy leads to further sin (Psalm 73:3; Proverbs 3:31; James 1:14–15; James 4:1–2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The wise respond to evil by trusting in the Lord. Trust has five parts:

• Do not become irritated or jealous of those who do evil (Psalm 37:1–2).

• Delight in the Lord (Psalm 37:3–4).

• Submit to the Lord (Psalm 37:5–6).

• Practice patience in hope (Psalm 37:7).

• Avoid anger (Psalm 37:8–9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This psalm addresses the issues raised in Psalm 36: 

• How should the godly react to evil? 

• When will the Lord bring justice? 

• Why does he allow the wicked to harm his creation? 

Psalm 37 provides clear answers that reduce the tensions of life (Psalm 37:1–9, Psalms 37:34) and promise that the meek will have a future (Psalm 37:10–11, Psalms 37:39–40). 

The contrast between the godly and the wicked highlights the uselessness of foolishness (Psalm 37:12–24, Psalms 37:27–33). The psalmist's personal insights add a human element (Psalm 37:25–26, Psalms 37:35–38). He encourages viewing the land's inheritance with a long-term perspective: The earth belongs to the Lord, who will give it to those he blesses—the humble and godly who trust, hope, and follow him (see Psalm 37:9, Psalms 37:11, Psalms 37:22, Psalms 37:29, Psalms 37:34; see also Isaiah 57:13; Matthew 5:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Human life is limited and does not last long (see Psalms 90:5–6; Psalms 92:7; Psalms 102:4, Psalms 102:11; Psalms 103:15; Psalms 129:6; Isaiah 40:7–8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Doing good means developing a commitment to wisdom (see Psalm 34:14; Proverbs 3:5–7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Trusting in the Lord helps reduce irritability and envy (Psalm 37:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: To delight in the Lord means to follow the Lord’s ways and find joy in him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Justice occurs when the Lord’s will triumphs and the godly experience his rescue (Isaiah 45:8; Isaiah 51:5–6; Isaiah 58:8, Isaiah 58:10–11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Be still: We should let the Lord be God rather than taking matters into our own hands.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Irritability and anger can quickly damage a person’s character.

When someone becomes easily upset or angry, it affects the way that person thinks and acts. Over time, this can weaken good habits and harm relationships.

Learning patience and self-control helps protect and strengthen character.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked will not possess the land; those who trust in the Lord will. The Lord promises an inheritance because he is committed to caring for his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord creates peace (Psalm 85:10)—he brings peace to a chaotic world (Psalm 29:11; Psalms 37:11; Psalms 85:8; Psalms 147:14). His wisdom leads the meek to peace (Psalm 119:165; Matthew 5:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked show their envy by gnashing their teeth (an expression of anger and hostility). They make plans to harm the godly. But the Lord laughs at them because he knows they will fail (Psalm 2:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked seek to destroy the Lord’s order, but he defeats them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked prepare weapons, but those weapons will turn against them (compare Psalm 7:12–13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: It is better to be wise with little money than to be rich and evil (Proverbs 15:16; Proverbs 16:8, Proverbs 16:19; Proverbs 17:1; Proverbs 28:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord cares for the blameless in this life and for eternity, but the wicked will perish.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Smoke represents the temporary nature of life (Psalm 68:2; Psalms 102:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• To borrow and never repay shows a dishonest way of life.

• Generous givers freely share what they freely receive from the Lord (see Psalm 111:5; Psalms 112:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The honesty and strength of a godly person's life come from the Lord (see Proverbs 4:12; Proverbs 14:15; Proverbs 16:9; Proverbs 20:24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord does not abandon his children or their descendants.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly are wise; they do good and reject evil. The Lord cares for them, protecting them and ensuring that they receive their rightful portion of the land as their inheritance. The wicked might try to ambush the godly, but they will not succeed.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The righteous base their counsel on the Lord’s wisdom.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The law of his God is in his heart: The godly accept God’s instruction and live by it (see Psalm 119:11; Jeremiah 24:7; Jeremiah 31:31–34).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked might appear to be flourishing like a tree (compare Psalm 52:8; Psalms 92:12–13), but they eventually die and are forgotten (Psalm 37:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord provides strength for his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The meaning of this phrase is uncertain (also in Psalms 70:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist’s sins brought the Lord’s anger and rage. Because of this, the Lord disciplined and rebuked him, like arrows and blows striking him. As a result, his whole body is sick.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These verses introduce the psalmist's confession (Psalm 38:18) and describe his miserable state.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm is a lament and a prayer for healing. The psalmist's suffering is linked to his unconfessed sin. He admits his sin and trusts the Lord with his situation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Sin can lead to sickness and even death (1 Corinthians 11:30). The psalmist may have felt physically ill, or his sickness was a metaphor for emotional distress. He understood it came from God and endangered his life (see Psalms 32:3; Psalms 39:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels burdened because of sin (see Psalms 40:12; Psalms 41:4; compare Genesis 4:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The severity of God’s punishment brings anguish that affects every part of the psalmist’s being.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist wants to reconnect with God but feels distant. He feels lost and alone as his friends leave him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist suffers quietly before his opponents (see Isaiah 53:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord alone will resolve the conflict (Psalms 9:18; Psalms 27:14; Psalms 37:9, Psalms 37:34).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist, unable to bear his suffering and close to collapse (compare Psalm 15:5), admits his sin (see Psalm 32:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels more pain because his enemies hate him for no reason.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In the Psalms, people often ask the Lord to act quickly in times of great need (Psalms 22:19; Psalms 31:2; Psalms 40:13; Psalms 69:17; Psalms 70:1; Psalms 71:12; Psalms 79:8; Psalms 102:2; Psalms 141:1; Psalms 143:7). However, wisdom and experience show that God's people often need to wait for him to act (Psalms 27:14; Psalms 37:7; Isaiah 8:17; Isaiah 40:31).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Jeduthun was a Levitical singer who was appointed by David, along with Asaph (1 Chronicles 9:16; 1 Chronicles 16:38; 1 Chronicles 25:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Suffering in silence makes the psalmist's anguish, pain, and inner distress worse.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This prayer for rescue shows the psalmist's discouragement, which comes from not fully understanding his situation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: how fleeting my life is: This perspective comes out of suffering (see Psalms 78:39; Psalms 89:47–48; Psalms 90:3–10). The human lifetime is but a moment to God (Psalm 90:4), as temporary as a breath (see Psalms 39:11; Psalms 144:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Due to his suffering and sin, the psalmist concludes that life is meaningless and short (see Job 7:7–10; Isaiah 40:6–8). He had expected only a wicked life to be like that (see Psalms 37:2, Psalms 37:20; Psalms 103:15–16), but now it seems irrelevant whether a person is godly or not.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The idea that rebellion leads to suffering is a common theme in Psalms 32, Psalms 38:38–41.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist links suffering with God’s discipline, assuming that it is punishment for his sin.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord uses discipline to correct his children (Psalms 38:1, Psalms 38:3, Psalms 38:7; Psalms 40:12; see Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:5–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A foreigner could not own land (see Leviticus 25:23). The patriarchs had lived as guests in Canaan (Psalm 105:23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Earlier, the psalmist asked God to stay close to him (Psalm 8:21–22). Now, he wants God to leave him alone. This is similar to how Job felt (Job 7:17–19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist thanks the Lord for rescue and affirms that people can trust God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm has a thanksgiving song (Psalm 40:1–10) and a lament (Psalms 40:11–17). The thanksgiving song explains why the psalmist is thankful (Psalm 40:1–5), shows a promise to stay committed (Psalms 40:6–8), and shares a public testimony about God's character (Psalms 40:7–10). The lament talks about the psalmist's troubles due to his sins (Psalm 40:11–12) and includes two prayers asking for justice (Psalms 40:13–15, Psalms 40:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Lord delights in the attitude and character of the person giving an offering more than the offering itself. 

• my ears You have opened: The Greek text reads You have given me a body. In Hebrews 10:5–7, the writer quotes from the Greek version of Psalm 40:6–8. He presents these words as something Jesus said when he left heaven and came into the world.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: it is written about me in the scroll: Moses had recorded God’s requirements for Israel’s kings in Deuteronomy 17:14–15.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays that the Lord will be true to his character when answering this plea for mercy.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist is troubled by both his adversities and his own sins and prays for rescue.

• This passage is almost the same as Psalm 70.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The poor who suffer hardship have special protection under God's law (Leviticus 14:21; Leviticus 19:10). They receive God's justice and guidance (Psalms 72:13; Psalms 82:3–4). The word translated as poor often means the godly (Psalm 113:7; see Zephaniah 3:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
In this wisdom psalm, the psalmist: 

• asks for healing (Psalm 41:4, Psalms 41:10),

• laments his distress (Psalm 41:5–9), and

• expresses confidence in the Lord's blessing (Psalm 41:1–3, Psalms 41:11–12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: on his bed of illness: This illness might be physical or spiritual (see Psalm 6:2; Psalm 38).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist applies the blessing to himself (Psalm 41:12). He has helped the poor (Psalm 41:1), but he has sinned against the Lord in other ways. In his pain, he asks for healing and admits his sin. Only the Lord can provide the restoration that brings true joy (Psalm 30:2; Psalms 107:20–21).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: When will he die: The psalmist's enemies see his suffering as a judgment from God (see Psalm 1:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist’s enemies disguise themselves as friends, while his friends openly become his enemies.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: the one who shared my bread: Eating together was a sign of unity (Acts 2:42). Refusing to eat with someone was a sign of hostility (1 Corinthians 5:11). Jesus experienced the same kind of betrayal (John 13:1, John 13:18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist knows that the Lord has forgiven him and will bless him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This doxology (song of praise) ends Book One (Psalms 1–41). Compare with Psalm 106:48.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The sons of Korah were members of a Levitical choir. They were chosen by David to serve as singers in the temple (see 1 Chronicles 6:22–38; 1 Chronicles 9:19–34; 2 Chronicles 20:19). Their ancestor Korah was the rebel who opposed Moses and was swallowed by the earth (Exodus 6:24; Numbers 16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist's deep desire for God arises from being far away from the temple as he remembers the past. 

• The verb translated as "longs" appears only here and in Joel 1:20 (meaning "cry out"). In both instances, it describes extreme thirst in a dry desert (see Psalms 63:1; Psalms 143:6; see also Psalms 84:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
These psalms, like Psalms 9 and Psalms 10:10, form a unit with a lament and a bittersweet refrain of hope (Psalm 42:5, Psalms 42:11; Psalms 43:5). Many Hebrew manuscripts combine these two psalms into one. 

The historical context is unclear; these psalms might represent God's people in exile, expressing loyalty to God while he punishes them for their ongoing disobedience. 

The psalmist longs for the fellowship with God he had in Jerusalem (Psalm 42:4); his memories only deepen his discouragement. As the psalmist cries out to God, he remembers God's love and faithfulness (Psalm 42:8), which leads him to ask for vindication (Psalms 43:1–4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Crying so much that tears become food shows deep sadness (Psalms 80:5; Psalms 102:9; see Psalms 6:6; Psalms 56:8; Psalms 119:136; Psalms 126:5). 

• The wicked try to impose their timing on God and deny his power to intervene.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist remembers leading a large procession as part of the Levitical choir, possibly during the important holy days.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels sad, but he can still function. He remembers that the living God is his Savior. This verse appears again in Psalms 42:11 and Psalms 43:5.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist encourages himself with questions and answers.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Mount Hermon is a high mountain range northeast of Israel. The source of the Jordan is by Dan at the foot of Mount Hermon.

• Mount Mizar might be a peak in the Mount Hermon range.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The raging seas, waves, and surging tides bring to mind God's anger (see Psalm 88:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist sees rays of hope. A life focused on God includes joyful songs and prayers for justice and vindication (Psalm 42:9–10; Psalms 43:1–4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist brings his many doubts, discouragements, and questions directly to God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist turns to the Lord for rescue from his troubles, for guidance, for restoration, and for vindication.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: rejected me: Other psalms also ask if God has rejected his people (Psalm 44:9, Psalms 44:23; Psalms 60:1, Psalms 60:10; Psalms 74:1; Psalms 77:7; Psalms 88:14; Psalms 89:38; Psalms 108:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• This prayer for God's redemption sees light and truth as guides (see Psalms 18:25–29; Psalms 27:1; Psalms 85:10–13; Psalms 89:14–18; see also Psalms 119:105; John 3:19; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5–7). 

• The temple on the mountain in Jerusalem symbolized God's holy presence among his people (Psalms 15:1; Psalms 43:3; Psalms 99:5, Psalms 99:9; Psalms 132:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This verse is repeated in Psalm 42:5 and Psalms 42:11.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: We have heard … the work You did: The story of redemption includes God's favor and power in his past acts of rescue (see Psalm 78:1–4; see also Psalms 105–106).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This national lament after a defeat in battle continues the tone of the previous two psalms. It reflects on an unspecified moment in Israel's history and calls on God for salvation. The people: 

• recite God's past acts of rescue (Psalm 44:1–3),

• recognize God's power to save (Psalm 44:4–8),

• describe their humiliation in exile (Psalm 44:9–16),

• claim their innocence and lament the injustice of their current situation (Psalm 44:17–22), and

• cry for vindication (Psalm 44:23–26).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God drove out the pagan nations during the conquests recorded in Joshua.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Though the Israelites used swords and other weapons (Psalm 44:6), they would have lost their battles without the light of the Lord’s favor (see Psalms 18:25–29; Psalms 27:1; Psalms 89:15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s people feel confident about his mighty acts; he was with them in the past, and he is their king in the present.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The people have experienced defeat (Psalm 44:9–12), so they understand suffering and shame (Psalms 44:13–16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: scattered us among the nations: This likely refers to the exile (see Psalms 51:18–19; Psalms 89:38–51; Psalms 106:40–47; Psalms 137:137).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Paul quotes this verse as a parenthetical aside in his list of things that cannot separate us from Christ’s love (Romans 8:36).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Wake up: Biblical authors often call for God’s attention in a crisis (Psalms 35:23; Psalms 44:23; Psalms 73:20; Psalms 80:2; Mark 4:38).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In the end, God’s people can turn to the Lord and trust him for rescue. Their petition for God to remedy their situation is as strong as their lament about God’s rejection.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: To the tune of "The Lilies" is no longer known (see also Psalm 69).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm celebrates a royal wedding; it might have been sung on many occasions and not just at one wedding. As God’s representative, the king carried the responsibility of dispensing justice and maintaining order in God’s world (see Psalm 2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This general description of the king’s symbolic status anticipates his enduring legacy (Psalm 45:16). The Lord’s blessing and the charge to reflect God’s attributes are symbolized by his handsome appearance and gracious speech.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Glory and majesty belong to the Lord (Psalms 96:6; Psalms 111:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist describes the royal splendor the king showed when fighting his enemies.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: As God's representative of truth, humility, and justice (see Psalm 72:1–2, Psalms 72:4, Psalms 72:7), the king can perform impressive deeds (Psalms 65:5; Psalms 96:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Justice characterizes God’s rule, as it should characterize the king’s administration.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The king is like a god among humans. God anointed him, gave him a powerful throne, and he delivers justice as he rules eternally. 

• The writer of Hebrews uses Psalm 45:6–7 to describe Jesus, arguing that the Son is greater than the angels (Hebrews 1:8–9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Fine spices mixed with oil create unique perfumes. 

• The king's palaces had wood panels with ivory inlays (see Psalm 6:4; Amos 3:15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Royal marriages often confirmed diplomatic alliances between kings, and the women became part of the royal harem (see 1 Kings 11:1–3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The bride is a representative of the king. Powerful people and nations try to gain her favor in order to get close to the king. This is a great honor, and she is encouraged to give herself fully to her new position.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Daughter of Tyre: Israel traded with Tyre, a powerful city-state. The city's most noble woman brings a wedding gift to the new queen, who represents an honored kingdom.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: According to Alamoth (“maidens”; see also study note on 1 Chronicles 15:20). In worship, a choir or a group of instrumentalists performed this hymn.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Even during natural disasters, the citizens of Zion show no fear.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm of Zion celebrates God's special presence in Jerusalem (see also Psalms 48, Psalms 76:76, Psalms 87:87, Psalms 122:122). It encourages trust in the Lord because the people of Zion have his protection.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This river provides life, renewal, and healing like the streams flowing through Eden (Psalm 36:8–9; see Genesis 2:10; Ezekiel 47; Revelation 22:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The strong city, where God lives, protects its people. They enjoy the river flowing within the city. This river is calm, unlike the turbulent waters (representing the powers of the nations) outside the city.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: when morning dawns: In the ancient Near East, enemies attacked cities during the day. Even in dangerous times, the Lord will protect the place where his name is.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: People and nations live in chaos. They take every chance to benefit themselves (Psalm 83:2), stay busy with many things (Psalms 39:6), and fill the world with noise. They are unstable and can fall apart, unlike the city of God (compare Psalm 15:5). But when the godly are troubled, they cry out to God for help (Psalm 42:5, Psalms 42:11; Psalms 43:5; Psalms 55:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• This refrain reminds us who the God of Zion is. 

• with us: Hebrew 'immanu, part of the name Immanuel, meaning “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 8:8; Matthew 1:23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel witnessed the Lord's amazing works in the wilderness (Psalms 107:24; Psalms 111:2), but the wicked, who do not care about them (Psalms 28:5), end up desolate (Psalms 73:19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This invitation to trust in the Lord offers a perspective on God’s interactions with human powers.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• A message directly from the Lord confirms the truth of the psalmist’s vision (see also Psalms 12:5–6; Psalms 32:8). 

• know that I am God: The Lord will fulfill his promises (Isaiah 45:3; Isaiah 49:23; Isaiah 60:16). 

• God will be honored (Psalm 47; Isaiah 6:1); he will judge the nations and save his people (see Psalms 57:11; Psalms 89:13; Psalms 108:5–6; Psalms 118:16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: People clap their hands in praise and recognition of wonderful deeds (Psalm 47:3–4; see Psalms 98:8; Isaiah 55:12; compare Nahum 3:19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: As the ruler of all nations, God deserves praise.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm praises God's rule as king over the entire earth. It describes God's victory with Israel and other nations. Both Israel (Psalm 47:3–4) and the nations (Psalms 47:9) are part of God's kingdom.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord gave Israel victory, especially under David (see Psalm 18:40–50). God's powerful acts of redemption show his love for Israel.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• pride of Jacob: Jacob was the father of all Israelites (Genesis 32:28). The name Jacob often represents the nation of Israel. 

• God loves and commits himself to Jacob (see Psalms 78:68; Psalms 127:2; see Romans 11:28).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: horn: Or rams’ horns (see Psalm 81:3). People sometimes blew rams’ horns during celebrations (Psalm 98:5–6; 2 Kings 11:14; 1 Chronicles 15:28).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist describes the Lord as returning to heaven, having accomplished his victories. For a description of his descent, see Psalm 18:9–16.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: People from all over the world (see Psalm 96:1–3) will worship God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This song of Zion (see also Psalms 46, Psalms 76:76, Psalms 87:87, Psalms 122:122) clearly describes Jerusalem (Zion) as the city of the Great King, where the godly find protection (Psalms 48:1–3). God rules from Zion with faithfulness, righteousness, and justice, inspiring his people with confidence and joy (Psalm 48:9–11). They dedicate themselves to witnessing Zion's glory so they can share it with the next generation (Psalm 48:8, Psalms 48:12–14).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God lives in Zion to protect it from all enemies (see Psalm 46:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The ships of Tarshish were built for long voyages and represent human achievement (see also 2 Chronicles 9:21; Isaiah 2:16). Their destruction might be the event mentioned in 1 Kings 22:48.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist happily celebrates the Lord's presence with the community, thinking about God's faithful, righteous, and just rule.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: towers … ramparts … citadel: These structures show Zion's strength.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: No one is like God (Psalms 35:10; Psalms 71:19; Psalms 86:8; Psalms 89:6, Psalms 89:8; Psalms 113:5; see Isaiah 40:18, Isaiah 40:25). He is the shepherd King (Psalm 95:7) who will guide (see Psalms 5:8; Psalms 23:2) the sheep of his flock (Psalms 77:20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Anyone who will listen can gain wisdom (Proverbs 1:5, Proverbs 1:8, Proverbs 1:33).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wisdom teacher invites everyone to come and learn wisdom. He promises to teach them through a proverb and a riddle.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this wisdom psalm, a wise teacher warns about enemies who live richly and care only for themselves (Psalm 49:5–9). They cannot save anyone, not even themselves, from death or being forgotten (Psalm 49:10–12). Like fattened animals, they are led to slaughter (Psalm 49:14–20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The teacher used proverbs and riddles to teach wisdom (see Proverbs 1:5–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: If enemies who live for material rewards cannot sustain themselves, how can they give life to others?

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The teacher uses irony to teach wisdom. Everyone dies, and even those who give their names to lands or estates will be forgotten.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The teachers of false wisdom cannot rescue themselves from death. Only God has that power.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked might have rich, luxurious lives, but they forget that they cannot avoid death.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The whole universe must pay attention when God approaches to bring justice into the world.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God appears as judge. He reminds both the godly and the ungodly that sacrifices and reciting the law are worthless without thankfulness, repentance, and justice.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord is coming to bring justice. This hope encourages his faithful people. However, those who have been unfaithful will not receive blessings when the heavens and earth testify against them (see Deuteronomy 30:19; Deuteronomy 31:28; Deuteronomy 32:1; Isaiah 1:2). The Lord comes to restore order to the world (see Psalms 5:8; Psalms 22:31; Psalms 33:5; Psalms 40:9; Psalms 50:6; Psalms 71:16; Psalms 97:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist warns against valuing sacrificial rituals more than having the right attitude in your heart.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Unlike pagan gods, God does not need food. Instead, he wants his people to serve him with sincere hearts (Psalm 50:14–15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: the cattle on a thousand hills: God has no needs because he owns everything.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Thankfulness involves recognizing and appreciating God's blessings beyond personal gain (see Psalms 51:15–17; Psalms 54:6). 

• True sacrifice means dedicating oneself to honor God (Psalm 50:23; Romans 12:1–2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s response to his people’s cry is to rescue them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This message is against the wicked, who only pretend to listen to God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: My instruction … My words: The wicked may observe rituals, but they reject more important matters such as justice, mercy, and faithfulness (compare Matthew 23:23–24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Because he is patient, God remained silent.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God will destroy the wicked like a lion tearing its prey (Isaiah 5:29; Isaiah 31:4; Ezekiel 19:3; compare Psalms 7:2; Psalms 22:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked will experience God’s justice, while the godly will see God’s everlasting salvation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
A prayer for God's mercy and kindness is a type of lament. Sometimes, the psalmist asks for mercy because he recognizes his own weakness and sin (see also Psalm 6:2; Psalms 9:13; Psalms 25:16; Psalms 31:9; Psalms 41:4, Psalms 41:10). Other times, the plea comes from the psalmist's dedication to the Lord (see Psalm 26:11; Psalms 27:7; Psalms 119:29, Psalms 119:58, Psalms 119:132). In every situation, God's mercy leads to inner renewal.

See 2 Samuel 11:1–27. The psalm does not directly mention this event.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The person who regrets their wrongdoing cannot offer anything to God. They need God's favor, mercy, forgiveness, and blessing to experience renewal and restoration.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This heartfelt prayer for restoration seeks God's favor, mercy, forgiveness, and cleansing. With a broken spirit, the psalmist admits his sin and takes responsibility (Psalm 51:3–6). He then asks God to remove his guilt and renew him internally (Psalm 51:7–12). The psalmist commits again to living wisely and joyfully while serving God and others (Psalm 51:13–17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These psalms of David share a common theme. They reflect on the experience of evil. In Psalm 51, the psalmist admits his wrongdoing and asks for God's forgiveness. Psalms 52–64 express sorrow over specific evils David faced. A song of praise (Psalm 65) brings David's laments to an end.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Wash me … cleanse me: The psalmist asks for cleansing and freedom from the guilt of his sin (Psalm 51:7; see Psalms 26:6; Isaiah 1:16, Isaiah 1:18; Isaiah 4:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist accepts the results of his sin against God. He understands that he has no goodness without God's renewal.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Against You, You only: This is an exaggeration. The psalmist knows he also sinned against people (2 Samuel 11:2–4, 2 Samuel 11:15–17), but his sin against God is more important. He expects God to rebuke him and will accept whatever verdict God gives (see Romans 3:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: I was brought forth in iniquity: The psalmist is not making excuses but is admitting how deep his sinfulness is. From the time we are conceived, we all share in the human condition of sinfulness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Purify me with hyssop (literally Purify me with the hyssop branch; see Exodus 12:22; Leviticus 14:4; John 19:29; Hebrews 9:19): The psalmist relies on God to cleanse and renew him (see Isaiah 1:18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Regaining joy is a gracious gift from God. 

• You have crushed: The psalmist feels completely broken (Psalm 6:2; compare Psalms 34:20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A loyal spirit produces inner strength. It helps a person remain faithful and continue even during difficulty.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s Spirit renews and recreates the human spirit.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Your Holy Spirit: Only the Holy Spirit can change a person's will to make it "right" (Psalm 51:10) and "willing" to obey (Psalms 51:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: As he learns from his sin and its consequences, the psalmist wants to teach others.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: bloodguilt: This expression refers to any injustice, not only killing someone (Psalm 9:12; Psalms 58:10; see 2 Samuel 11:14–26; compare Isaiah 1:15–17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: build up the walls of Jerusalem: These verses were likely added as a prayer for national restoration after the exile (see Psalms 42–43). The entire community in exile shared the feelings expressed in this psalm.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Sacrifices made with the right intentions come from a heart that is right with God and others (see Psalms 15:2–5; Psalms 24:3–6; Psalms 50:14; Matthew 5:23–24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The accuser, Doeg the Edomite, is an example of a person who chose to do evil.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Liars deceive themselves by thinking they can be heroes with their words. They see themselves as innocent, even though they love evil and cause harm. Those who speak curses, sarcasm, bitterness, arrogant boasting, and lies (Psalms 31:18; Psalms 34:13; Psalms 59:7, Psalms 59:12; Psalms 120:2–3; Psalms 140:3, Psalms 140:9) create chaos, isolation, and destruction (James 3:5). Their sharp words cut like swords and daggers (Psalms 55:21; Psalms 57:4; Psalms 64:3), the fangs of a snake (Psalms 140:3), or a razor.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Wicked people use words to destroy relationships and communities. They foolishly think that they can be heroes by their words (Psalm 52:1–4), but their downfall comes suddenly (Psalms 52:5–7). In contrast, the godly renew their commitment to the Lord (Psalm 52:8–9) and find security in their future with him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Dishonest speech can change a person's character.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God will strike the wicked down like a pagan altar, idol, or unclean vessel (Exodus 34:13; Leviticus 11:35; 2 Kings 10:27).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s judgment on the wicked will come suddenly and forcibly. The godly rejoice in God’s justice, not in the misfortunes of the wicked.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: see and fear: In Hebrew, these words sound almost alike.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist commits himself to a life of trust in the Lord.

• An olive tree can live a long time with proper care (Psalms 1:3; Psalms 128:3). The psalmist wants to be near the Lord, who is his Savior and the source of his blessings (Psalms 18:6; Psalms 23:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Paul uses the Greek translation of this passage to describe the moral corruption of all people (Romans 3:10–12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm is similar to Psalm 14, with differences only in verse 5.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: scattered the bones: Israel's enemies would face a shameful defeat and would not have the peaceful rest of a proper burial (compare Psalm 141:7; 2 Kings 9:10; Jeremiah 8:1–2; Ezekiel 6:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Ziphites intended to use violence.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This personal lament was caused by violent and godless people (Psalm 54:3). The psalmist prays to God and focuses on God's help (Psalms 54:4). He asks God to save him from evil and judge his enemies (Psalm 54:5, Psalms 54:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The strangers were excluded from the covenant community (see Psalm 109:11; Proverbs 5:10). 

• Proud and violent people do not respect God or others (see Psalms 35:11, Psalms 35:25; Psalms 86:14; Proverbs 11:16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A voluntary offering is a sacrifice of praise. Sacrifices of praise are the kind of offering God most desires (see Psalm 50:14–15, Psalms 50:23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In anticipation of God’s response, the mood of the psalm changes from sorrow to thanksgiving.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The occasion for this prayer is an attack by an enemy.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The psalmist faces enemies led by a former friend (Psalm 55:12–14). This causes him great distress. He prays to the Lord and trusts him for justice (Psalm 55:22–23). 

Jesus went through similar pain when Judas, his friend, betrayed him. He also experienced the psalmist’s prayer being answered: 

• by taking the place of the wicked and receiving their punishment (Isaiah 53:7–9), and

• by trusting the Father, who saved (Luke 23:46) and rewarded him (Isaiah 53:10–12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In the experience of deep anguish, the psalmist confesses that his adversity has become unbearable and he seeks an escape.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist's enemy used to be a friend. Remembering their close relationship causes him pain (see Psalm 31:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God is good and faithful, but the psalmist’s enemies and so-called friend are deceitful and wicked.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist commits all his cares to the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: To die young means missing out on God's full blessings (compare Proverbs 3:2, Proverbs 3:16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• A Miktam: This may be a literary or musical term.

• David was seized by Philistines concerned about his loyalties and brought before King Achish (1 Samuel 21:10–15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this lament, the psalmist first asks for help and then expresses confidence in God. This pattern occurs two times (Psalm 56:1–4, Psalms 56:5–13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: man: Or mere flesh, in contrast to God, who is immortal and much more powerful (see Isaiah 2:22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist specifies his charge against his attackers as he prays for their evil to end.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist uses wordplay with two similar Hebrew words: wanderings (nod) and bottle (no’d).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
man (Hebrew ’adam): The psalm also uses two other words for man: 

• ’enosh (meaning “people,” Psalm 56:1) and

• basar (meaning “mere mortals,” Psalm 56:4).

All these words point to the short and limited nature of human life.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The light of God’s goodness and salvation will replace the darkness of death (see Psalms 18:25–29; Psalms 27:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
shadow of Your wings: Like a bird protects its young, God protects those who trust in him (see Psalm 17:8).

See 1 Samuel 22:1 or Psalm 24:1–8.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks for mercy and protection, then expresses trust and confidence in the Lord (Psalm 57:1–4). When the wicked fall into their own traps (Psalm 57:6), the psalmist will praise the Lord (Psalms 57:7–10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God Most High (Hebrew Elohim-Elyon) is a common title for God. He is more powerful than all real or imagined supernatural beings (see Psalms 91:1; Psalms 97:9; Genesis 14:18–22). 

• who fulfills His purpose for me: Or who will end my [trouble], or who deals kindly with me.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These verses are a prayer for rescue from strong enemies. The metaphor of fierce lions describes human foes. The psalmist feels unable to escape them without God's help (see also Psalms 35:11–21; Psalms 124:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• This verse appears again in Psalm 57:11 and Psalms 108:5. 

• God's glory, which is his visible presence that keeps out all evil (Psalm 8:1; Psalms 19:1–4; Psalms 24:7), will fill the entire creation (Isaiah 6:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist is sure that God will stop the night of evil (compare Psalm 56:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This section is repeated with a few changes in Psalm 108:1–5.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God's glory reaches the entire universe, and people will praise his constant love and faithfulness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: rulers (or gods): People used this term for high officials and administrators of justice (Psalm 82:1, Psalms 82:6). In other contexts, it might refer to angelic creatures (Psalm 89:7) or the gods of other nations (Psalms 82:1; Daniel 11:36).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The administrators of justice were furthering their own interests rather than those of the needy. The absence of justice gradually resulted in a violent society.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The administration of justice is a mark of good government. God expects nothing less from his people. The psalmist condemns Israel’s leaders for abusing their power, and he calls on the Lord to rain down his curses upon the wicked. The demonstration of divine justice will reassure the godly that God is just.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: All humans are born with a tendency to sin (see Psalm 51:5). However, the wicked follow their sinful desires, while the godly struggle against them (Romans 7:19–23; James 4:1–10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Venom here means harmful speech (see Psalm 140:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist calls on God to break the destructive power of the wicked.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: When moving over dry ground, slugs dry up.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s judgment will come suddenly. The certainty of vindication brings joy to the godly.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Being shown to be right is the reward for those who live for God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: See 1 Samuel 19:11–18.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: protect me (or lift me up high): When surrounded by evil, the godly pray for God to set them apart for himself and protect them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist laments the power of enemies who conspire with other nations.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks God not to show mercy to the treacherous, deceptive, and wicked traitors (see Psalm 25:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked threaten like aggressive dogs, but the Lord shows that he does not fear them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays that the wicked will suffer the same pain they have caused others.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked will remain unsatisfied, but the psalmist will praise the Lord's strength and loving devotion.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• This psalm was taught to young people as part of their education. 

• When: See 2 Samuel 8:13–14. 

• Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah refer to the Arameans of northwest Mesopotamia and Syria (see study note on Genesis 24:10). 

• The tune “Lily of the Testimony” is unknown today.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: When God’s people experience his discipline, they affirm their loyalty and await God’s answer.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist laments a national defeat and cries out to God for rescue.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: we are staggered from the wine: Yayin, the Hebrew word for "wine," is often associated with drunkenness (2 Samuel 13:28; Isaiah 5:11; Isaiah 28:7–8; see also Psalm 104:15; Deuteronomy 14:26; Isaiah 55:1). It symbolized God's judgment on the wicked (Psalm 75:8; Jeremiah 51:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God raised a banner over his people to serve as a rallying point and as a source of pride and confidence. 

• The fear of God that leads to wisdom (Psalm 111:10) is not weakness. It gives the perspective and strength needed to do what is right.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays for rescue based on the special relationship between God and his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This section is repeated in Psalm 108:6–13.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Shechem and Succoth represent the heartland of Israel.

These places were located in the central region of the land. Because of this, they can represent the center of Israel’s life and strength.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord responds with a message of promise. He shares his land with his people as spoils of war.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Destroying the capital (the fortified city) of a defeated invader would help prevent future attacks. Edom's capital was Bozrah, located to the southeast of Israel. Only God could grant victory.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks God to protect him and guide him into his presence (Psalm 61:4–5). He prays for God to extend and protect the king's rule and promises to praise God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In these royal prayers, the psalmist longs for God’s presence. All three psalms concern themselves with the king’s security.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• the ends of the earth: This phrase suggests a cry that comes from a place far away from God. 

• The psalmist feels deep sorrow and distress.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The poet desires God's presence and seeks entry into God's earthly home for protection and care. Being welcomed into God's sanctuary (tent) is the greatest blessing (see Psalms 15:1; Psalms 23:6; Psalms 24:3–6). The Hebrew word for tent refers to the tabernacle and the tent David built for the ark (1 Chronicles 15:1). See also study note on John 1:14. 

• The shelter of your wings represents God's protection and care (see Psalms 9:9; Psalms 17:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• You have heard my vows: The psalmist's vows might be part of ceremonial sacrifices (Psalms 66:13–15; Psalms 76:11; Psalms 116:14, Psalms 116:18). He praises and thanks God for rescuing him. 

• The inheritance refers to the promise of the land (see Psalm 60), the sacredness of the temple, the joy of God's presence (Psalm 119:111), or any similar reward (Psalms 16:6; Psalms 37:9, Psalms 37:11, Psalms 37:18, Psalms 37:22, Psalms 37:29, Psalms 37:34; Psalms 127:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: See 1 Chronicles 25:1; also in Psalms 39 and Psalms 77:77.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This psalm expresses trust in the king and includes a prayer for him. The king relies on God even during tough times. 

His tricky and strong enemies challenge him, but he stays strong. He urges himself and his people to trust God. 

He wants them to view their human enemies from God's perspective, where they seem weak, temporary, and deceitful (Psalm 62:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The enemies want to overthrow the king using lies and tricks.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: his lofty perch: This means the royal throne.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist encourages himself and others to place their hope in God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: are but a lie: People often try to appear stronger and better than they truly are.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Humans are temporary, unlike God. Even when successful, their prosperity does not last long.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Extortion involves using threats to force someone to give up their belongings. Stealing means taking what belongs to someone else.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Only God balances power and loving devotion. He cares for his people by removing those who do evil from the world (see Psalm 1:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Together, soul and body refer to a person's entire being. 

• dry and weary land: When David lived in the desert, he felt spiritually empty, away from God's people and the sanctuary.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The king deeply desires God's presence. He experiences God's goodness in everything he does. Despite being tired and troubled by the wicked, the king finds strength in God and praises him. God is his source of life (Psalm 63:3), while the wicked face destruction (Psalms 63:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist remembers that he had found God to be present in his sanctuary (see Psalm 18:6; Psalms 61:4; Psalms 62:5, Psalms 62:11–12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: better than life: The best life comes from a relationship with God (see Psalms 4:7; Psalms 63:5; Proverbs 16:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Meditating on God requires focus, concentration, thought, and reflection (see Psalm 1:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist thinks about and feels God's presence during the night. When it is dark, God is the light. The quiet night and the wait for morning offer time to reflect on the true meaning of life with the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The wicked planned to ruin the psalmist's life with lies and deceit, but they would fail. 

• the depths of the earth: This refers to the place of the dead.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Wild foxes and jackals are often associated with places that are ruined and abandoned (Isaiah 13:20–22; Isaiah 34:10–15; Jeremiah 9:11; Jeremiah 49:33; Jeremiah 51:37; Lamentations 5:18; Malachi 1:3). The wicked will not receive honor in death. Scavenging animals will consume their bodies (Ecclesiastes 6:3; Jeremiah 22:18–19; Jeremiah 36:29–30).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These verses form a prayer for rescue from bold and powerful liars.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This lament speaks against the destructive plans and arrogant attitude of the wicked (Psalm 64:1–6). The psalmist prays to God and finds comfort in God's justice because the righteous judge will undo the wicked's actions. The godly will rejoice and gain wisdom as they think about God's powerful deeds.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: their tongues … bitter words: Liars use their words to harm others. This description might also refer to practicing magic.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The enemies make a plan to harm the innocent without getting caught. 

• Human beings can act with extreme evil through words, actions, or plans (Psalm 83:3; see Jeremiah 17:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God acts righteously. God stops wickedness and gives the wicked what they intended for others.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God alone deserves praise and is worthy to have vows made to him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Praise is the right response to God's great acts in redemption (Psalm 65:3–5) and in nature (Psalms 65:5–13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm recounts the reasons why all people should praise and revere God for his almighty power and merciful care for his universe.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: all people: This means all humans.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: You atone: God graciously removes the guilt of sin (see Psalm 32:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• the one You choose and bring near: This includes people from Israel and other nations. 

• Only those God sees as blameless live in his holy courts (Psalms 15 and Psalms 24:24). 

• At the temple, God's earthly palace, all nations can gather to experience God's holy presence. No structure can separate humans from God (see Revelation 21:22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God brought order to the mountains, the roaring oceans, and the pounding waves (see Psalms 95:4–5; Psalms 104:6–9). 

• The psalmist compares the chaotic forces of nature with the rebellion of the nations (see Psalms 2:1–12; Psalms 33:6–11; Psalms 46:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: All over the world (Job 38:13; see Psalm 50:1–3), people should stand in awe of the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The streams of God and all rivers show God's power and goodness through nature's order and the regularity of the harvests (see Psalms 1:3; Psalms 36:8; Psalms 46:4; Ezekiel 47:6–12; Zechariah 14:8; Revelation 22:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The created world clearly shows God's power (Psalm 65:6–8). He shows his love by taking care of nature. Everything praises the Lord as all parts work together smoothly.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Nature praises the Creator (see Psalm 79:13; Psalms 96:11–13; Psalms 148:3–5, Psalms 148:7–12; Isaiah 55:12–13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist urges nature to join a powerful song to praise God's glory, name, and power.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This anonymous psalm includes two hymns (Psalm 66:1–12, Psalms 66:13–20) that praise God for saving his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The glory of his name represents the perfection of God’s character.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God defeats his enemies (see Psalm 18:44; Psalms 59:11; Psalms 81:15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The story of the exodus and God's victory over the sea causes the people to be amazed (Psalm 66:5) and to worship (Psalms 66:6). God performs miracles to redeem people for himself.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God's power brings redemption. The same word appears in Psalm 65:6 to describe God's power in creation (see also Psalm 80:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The orderly lives of the redeemed reflect the order of God’s world. The Lord protects them from evil and purifies them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God guides his people into wisdom and away from foolishness (Psalms 17:5; Psalms 37:31; Psalms 121:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: For You, O God, have tested us: Like a silversmith heats silver to remove impurities, God's discipline removes sin from his people (see Psalm 12:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God decrees and permits the many trying circumstances his people experience.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: You let men ride over our heads: Or You made people rule over us. This likely refers to a foreign ruler who controlled the Israelites.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Vows often included sacrifices of thanksgiving, including burnt offerings (see Psalms 20:3; Psalms 40:6; Psalms 50:8; Psalms 51:19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The private testimony at the end of the psalm matches the public praise at the beginning (Psalm 66:1–4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Confession leads to restoration (see Psalm 32:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This prayer is inspired by the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24–26. God's kindness to Israel influences his reputation among other nations (see Psalm 96:1–3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This anonymous prayer asks for God's blessing. The psalmist speaks about knowing and worshiping God among all nations (compare Psalms 64:9; Psalms 65:8). The prayer asks for God's name to remain holy and that his kingdom come (compare Matthew 6:9–13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God’s international reputation leads to his praise among the nations (see Psalm 138:4). Their chaos and rebellion will stop when they join Israel in praising God. 

• One God rules over everyone, and the nations will give thanks for God’s just rule (see Psalm 67:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God delivers the ultimate justice that people seek (Psalms 96:10; Psalms 98:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Large harvests show God’s blessing (Genesis 26:12; Isaiah 30:23). 

• all the ends of the earth: See Psalms 2:8; Psalms 96:1–3. 

• People from every nation will join Israel in acknowledging the God of Israel.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These verses form a prayer for God to rise and scatter his enemies, like when Israel entered the promised land (compare Numbers 10:35–36; Joshua 6–12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This prayer for God's victorious rule describes God's journey from Sinai to Zion (Psalm 68:7, Psalms 68:16–18, Psalms 68:24). He saved Israel from Egypt, led them through the wilderness, brought them to the promised land, and established his kingdom. He is a caring and victorious God, whose nature does not change. Therefore, the faithful hope and rejoice in the promise of God's universal rule.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Both smoke and wax represent a temporary existence (Psalms 22:12–18; Psalms 37:20; Psalms 102:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The fate of the godly is different from that of the wicked (see Psalm 1:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Him who rides on the clouds: This is an ancient description of Baal, a Canaanite god. The psalmist uses it to describe the Lord as the true God "who rides upon the highest heavens" (see Psalms 68:33; Psalms 104:3). God has power over the clouds and the rain.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist praises God’s powerful and compassionate reign.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God, the Father of all marginalized and needy people, shows them compassion and protects their rights (see Psalms 10:14, Psalms 10:18; Psalms 69:33; Psalms 82:3). 

• Like his dwelling, the Lord is holy. The supreme example of the holy God coming down to rescue humanity is Jesus Christ.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God freed Israel from slavery in Egypt (Exodus 20:2; see Psalm 69:33), and he continues to free prisoners today. 

• The sun-scorched land represents being far from God and separated from blessing.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The earth shook as it does during an earthquake (see Exodus 19:18). 

• the heavens poured down rain: Wells in the desert and rain showers in Canaan provided plenty of water.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: a great company of women proclaim it: A large group of women singers celebrates the victory in song (see Psalm 68:25; Exodus 15:20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The people who cared for flocks and moved from place to place were surprised to receive silver and gold ornaments from the battle.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Almighty (Hebrew Shaddai) is an ancient name for God (see Psalm 91:1; Genesis 17:1). 

• The exact location of Mount Zalmon is unknown; it might have been a mountain in Bashan (see Psalm 68:15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Bashan is a plateau northeast of Jerusalem and east of the Sea of Galilee. It was famous for its forests and pastureland (see Psalm 22:12; Isaiah 2:13). The mountains might have included Mount Hermon to the north of the plateau or Mount Zalmon, possibly Jebel ed-Druze to the east.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Why do you gaze in envy: Bashan is more impressive than the mountains around Jerusalem, but it was not the Lord's home. Only Mount Zion had the honor of being God's dwelling place.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Chariots were the top weapon of the military in the psalmist’s time. They represent the Lord’s power to give victory (Psalms 20:7; Psalms 44:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• You have ascended on high: The Most High victoriously established his reign in Zion. 

• captives … gifts: This image shows a victorious ruler leading a victory march after battle. Paul applied this image to Jesus Christ (Ephesians 4:8–13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Like a caring father or a shepherd, God carries his people in his arms (see Psalm 55:22; Psalms 68:5–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God cares for his people like a shepherd, and the people praise him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God will crush the heads of His enemies: Compare Genesis 3:15.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God will deal with all enemies, whether from high places (represented by Bashan) or low (the depths of the sea).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A great company joins together in the pilgrimage to Zion.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The people pray for God's help and victory over enemy nations (Psalm 68:1–3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The conquered kings will bring gifts to the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Hostile and rebellious people delight in warfare and insurrection (see Psalm 2:1–3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The phrase kingdoms of the earth refers to all nations and power structures.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist urges the people to praise God, who triumphs over his enemies.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: When the Lord shows his power, majesty, and strength to the nations, he makes his people stronger (see Psalm 96:4–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Psalm 45 also mentions this tune, but Psalm 45 praises the glory of kingship. In contrast, Psalm 69 is the cry of a tired king who feels abandoned by the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist sees himself as almost drowning but still surviving chaotic forces and his sense of separation from God (see Psalm 42:7; Psalms 69:14, Psalms 69:15; Isaiah 8:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this personal lament, the poet shares his vulnerability, humiliation, and deep pain. He asks God to defend him for the sake of the righteous.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These last four psalms of Book Two contrast with the earlier psalms that describe God’s mighty acts in creation and redemption, ending with God’s march to Zion (Psalms 65–68). Psalms 69–71 describe the king's suffering, and Psalm 72 responds with a prayer for God to bless the king.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: John applied this lament to Jesus (John 15:25).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist confesses his sins and prays that God’s response to him will encourage others in similar conditions to place their hope in the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Mistreated and abandoned by family, friends, and community, the psalmist seeks comfort, relief (Psalm 69:13–18), and justice (Psalms 69:22–28) from the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist is devoted to God and what is holy, yet people repay him with insults. Later, this verse was applied to the anger of Jesus at the temple’s money changers (John 2:17) and his undeserved suffering (Romans 15:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: When the psalmist denies himself normal comforts to seek God in prayer, the wicked ridicule him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist can only pray for rescue and relief from his enemies.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels alone and misunderstood. He cannot bear his doubts, and his troubles overwhelm him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: vinegar to quench my thirst: This description applies to the suffering of Jesus (Matthew 27:34, Matthew 27:48; Luke 23:36; John 19:28–29).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks God to give his suffering (Psalm 69:3) to his enemies. Paul applied these words to the unbelieving Jews of his day (Romans 11:9–10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Peter quoted this verse after the death of Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: May they be blotted out of the Book of Life: Compare Psalm 1:5–6; Psalms 9:5; Revelation 3:5; Revelation 20:15; Revelation 21:22–27.

entries.title: Psalms
