entries.content: The psalmist prays that his pain will turn to praise.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Making a vow often included a sacrifice (Psalms 20:3; Psalms 51:19; compare Psalms 50:13–14; Psalms 51:16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: despise: See Psalm 22:24; compare Matthew 25:36; Hebrews 13:3.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays for Zion, offering a new petition from a new circumstance. He applies the prayer (Psalm 69:1–33) to the desperate condition of Judah (see Psalms 51:18–19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s people will inherit the land because the wicked will perish (see Psalm 37:8–9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: To bring remembrance: The meaning of this phrase is not known (also found in Psalm 38:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm is almost exactly the same as Psalm 40:13–17. It has an urgent tone (Psalm 70:1, Psalms 70:5) that matches the nearby psalms (compare Psalms 69:17; Psalms 71:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The poet recognizes God as a dependable protector who will act justly towards him and his oppressors. See also Psalm 31:1–3.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This untitled lament by an aging believer is more a confession of confidence and hope than a cry of abandonment by God. The psalmist experienced God's power and protection in his youth (Psalm 71:5–8) and now prays for rescue from enemies who pursue him in his old age (Psalm 71:9–13). 

Even in danger, he continues to speak of God's past faithfulness and looks forward with hope to sharing with the next generation that God is faithful and righteous.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist has trusted God throughout his life (see Psalm 22:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The poet prays for continued fellowship with God (see Psalm 9:10; Psalms 51:11). In his weakness, the poet needs the Lord's strength even more (see Psalm 143:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The aging believer turns to the Lord for hope. As questions from his adversaries get under his skin and his own strength fails, he asks God to answer his prayers. He does not seek answers to prayer for himself but so that he can tell the story to the next generation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist's enemies plan and scheme together (Psalms 2:2; Psalms 21:11; Psalms 31:13; Psalms 35:4; Psalms 63:9–10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist compares his goodness to his enemies' evil. He focuses on the Lord, even in difficult times (see Psalms 9:17–18; Psalms 27:13–14).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s righteous character provides encouragement and strength in the midst of suffering. The wounded psalmist confesses faith in God’s ability to transform his misery and weakness into abundant life.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: You will bring me back up: The psalmist hopes for the renewal of an abundant earthly life. This later became grounds for belief in the resurrection of the dead.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Knowing God provides comfort also assures the poet of God's presence, care, and goodness (Psalms 23:4, Psalms 23:6; Psalms 86:17). God's comfort increases the psalmist's sense of being alive (see Psalm 119:50).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: As he awaits God’s rescue, the psalmist prepares himself to declare with instruments and voice that God is faithful and righteous.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: justice … righteousness: In the ancient Near East, kings were expected to represent justice. For Israel's kings, the standard was higher because they followed the Lord's example.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Justice brings balance to nature, leading to harmony, prosperity, and fertility.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This royal psalm concludes Book Two, with Psalm 72:18–20 serving as an epilogue for the entire book. The psalmist considers the future of David's royal line and Zion (see Psalms 46, Psalms 48:48). He prays that Israel's kings will be good and successful, spreading the Lord's blessing to all people worldwide. The exceptional righteousness and rule desired in this prayer hint at the future arrival of Jesus, the Son of David.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Justice makes the world fruitful, abundant, harmonious, and good (see Isaiah 32:16–17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A just ruler will defend the poor against injustice, rescue them from violence, and bring their oppressors to account for their wrongdoing.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: May they fear him: In Hebrew, this phrase appears to be a response to the enforcement of justice. The Greek version reads May they endure, which makes this a prayer for long life (Psalm 21:4; Psalms 72:15, Psalms 72:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The administration of justice is refreshing like spring rain, allowing the godly to thrive (see Isaiah 45:8) like flowers. 

• until the moon is no more: This phrase means forever (see Psalm 89:36–37).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• from sea to sea: This phrase represents the entire world. 

• Solomon's kingdom stretched from the Euphrates River in the east to the Philistine territory in the west (1 Kings 4:21; see Psalms 80:8–11; Psalms 89:19–25), where the Mediterranean Sea appeared to be at the ends of the earth (see Psalms 2:8). 

Everyone will bow before this king, including desert nomads (Psalm 72:9), his enemies, and all the world's kings (see Micah 7:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The anointed king will rule the entire world. Even enemy nations will obey him. In the ancient Near East, giving gifts to the king showed his success and reputation (see 1 Kings 10:1 Kings 10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The western kings of Tarshish came from a major colony in the western Mediterranean. The eastern kings of Sheba came from southern Arabia, home of the queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:1 Kings 10). 

• Seba was likely south of Egypt, possibly on the western shore of the Red Sea across from Sheba. 

• The gifts given to the king were a tribute and a sign of submission.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: All kings and nations must submit to the messianic king (God's chosen leader). The hope in Psalm 2:10–11 will come true (see Psalms 96:1–3; 1 Corinthians 15:25) when other leaders and peoples bow and serve this king.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: To deliver the needy means to bring an end to the rule of their oppressors.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The anointed king will help those in need. He is both a judge and a father to the poor (Psalms 10:14, Psalms 10:17; Psalms 68:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Like a father, the king feels pity for those in need (see Malachi 3:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The people will bless him, fulfilling God's promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3; see Psalm 133:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The just kingdom will be long-lasting and universal. The summary combines the themes of abundance of crops, longevity, tribute of the nations, and the prayer of the nations.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: the forests of Lebanon: Lebanon was famous for its wood (see study note on 2 Chronicles 2:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This doxology (song of praise) ends Book Two of the Psalms.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This parenthetical note ends Book Two, which consists mostly of prayers of David. Books Three to Five were probably compiled after Book Two; they include additional psalms of David (Psalms 86, Psalms 101:101, Psalms 103:103, Psalms 108:108–110, Psalms 122:122, Psalms 124:124, Psalms 131:131, Psalms 133:133, Psalms 138:138–145).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
People with pure hearts (people who are sincere and devoted to God) are renewed by God’s Spirit (Psalm 51:10). They choose to live in a godly way, turn away from sin, and enjoy God’s presence (see Psalm 24:3–4).

Asaph was a Levitical singer appointed by David (1 Chronicles 6:39). His descendants were singers and instrumentalists (1 Chronicles 15:16–17). Many of the Psalms of Asaph (Psalms 50, Psalms 73:73–83) were likely written by Asaph’s descendants later in Israel’s history (for example, Psalm 74).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This wisdom psalm looks at the injustice of the prosperity of the wicked. The psalmist states that God is good to the godly, but his own experience is different (Psalm 73:2–12). 

Almost overwhelmed by doubt (Psalm 73:13–16), the psalmist meets the Lord in the sanctuary. This meeting gives him a broader view and renews his trust in God (Psalm 73:17–26). His troubling doubts lead to a stronger desire for truth. He knows he can trust God and that God will save him (Psalm 73:27–28).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The seeming success of the wicked (Psalm 73) and God's apparent rejection of his people (Psalm 74) raise questions about his justice. God rules the entire world and decides when to judge (Psalm 75).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The poet thinks it is unfair that wicked people prosper (see Psalm 72:7) and feels upset about it. 

• The psalmist almost strayed from the path of wisdom and godliness (see Psalm 17:5; Psalms 37:31), but God prevented him from completely losing his way (Psalms 38:16; Psalms 66:9; Psalms 94:18; Psalms 121:3). 

• when I saw the prosperity of the wicked: Compare Psalm 72:3, Psalms 72:7.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist gives an exaggerated picture of the happiness of the wicked (compare Psalm 1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Proud people choose pride and cruelty over wisdom (Proverbs 1:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The proud boast, claiming that they own everything and are not subject to anyone (see Psalm 2:1–3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• These rhetorical questions expect a discouraging “yes” as an answer. The psalmist wonders if godliness has become a meaningless ritual (see Malachi 3:14–15). 

• my heart: This refers to his whole being. 

• The psalmist’s pain comes from discipline and rebuke (Psalm 39:11; Proverbs 1:23, Proverbs 1:25; Proverbs 12:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: When the psalmist sees the effect of his discouragement and doubt, he turns to the Lord and gains new understanding.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: If the psalmist had spoken about his doubts regarding the value of living a godly life, he might have discouraged God's people and given God's enemies a chance to speak against God (compare John 13:20). Instead, the psalmist keeps the problem to himself and thinks about it.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• During this period, God's sanctuary was the temple in Jerusalem. In God's presence, the psalmist receives special insight (compare Psalm 18:6). 

• God deals with the wicked over the long term. He waits patiently and gives them time to repent (Ezekiel 33:11; 2 Peter 3:9). Those who do not repent will get what they deserve.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist’s feelings about the prosperity of the wicked had given him a bitter spirit.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord leads the godly through their troubles and changes their misery into splendor.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Nothing in heaven or on earth is better than being near God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God rejected his people because their sin made him angry (Psalm 106:34–46). 

• Like a caring shepherd, God looks after his people, the sheep of his pasture (Psalms 23; Psalms 100:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In the aftermath of Jerusalem’s fall, it seemed that God had forgotten his special covenant relationship with his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist laments the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem. This happened in 586 BC. The psalmist uses vivid imagery, asks questions, recalls fresh memories, and directly asks the Lord to act (Psalm 74:19–23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Lord chose and redeemed Israel from Egypt in the exodus (compare Exodus 15:13). 

• Your congregation: This is another expression for "your people" (Psalms 28:9; Psalms 78:62; Psalms 94:14; Psalms 106:40).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Like a guide, the psalmist points out to the Lord what took place during the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: my King from ancient times: The psalmist acknowledges God’s power and his historical bond with Israel (Psalms 5:2; Psalms 44:4; Psalms 84:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Leviathan: See Psalm 104:26; Job 3:8; Job 41:1, Job 41:12, Job 41:22, Job 41:31; Isaiah 27:1. Here, the creature’s multiple heads suggest a mythical monster.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: ever-flowing rivers: God gave water in the desert to his people (see Psalm 68:8–9; Exodus 17:6). He dried up the Red Sea (Exodus 14:21) and the Jordan River (Joshua 3:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The poet urges God to act.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This hymn of thanksgiving includes two direct messages from God that assure us of his justice (Psalm 75:2–3, Psalms 75:10). The Lord warns arrogant people who defy him, promising to humble them by force (Psalm 75:4–8). Together, the community and the psalmist give thanks for God's character (Psalm 75:1, Psalms 75:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord will bring justice in his own time.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked proudly defy heaven, where God lives. By boasting, they claim that they are wiser than God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: No creature has the right to rebel against its Creator.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord alone is the Judge. He has the power to raise people up or bring them down (see 1 Samuel 2:7; Luke 1:52).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A song: The Greek version reads for the Assyrian.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God's victory over Zion's enemies hints at his future victory over all his enemies worldwide.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm appears to celebrate a victory. The victory might have been recent, such as over the Assyrians (see note on Psalms 76:1; see also Isaiah 37). Or, it might be remembering God's great acts of rescue in the past.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God brings an end to the attacks of his enemies (see Psalm 46:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The victorious king’s splendor, glory, and majesty are greater than anything in the created order (Psalm 8:1; Psalms 29:4; Psalms 111:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist praises God for his achievement and for his glorious majesty.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: feared: The Hebrew word nora’ sounds like the Hebrew word na’or, translated "resplendent," in Psalm 76:4.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The needy await their victorious God, while the wicked stand in fear of him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The night provides a special opportunity for prayer and meditation (Psalms 77:6, Psalms 77:11; see Psalms 6:6; Psalms 16:7; Psalms 17:3; Psalms 30:5; Psalms 63:6; Psalms 119:55, Psalms 119:62, Psalms 119:148).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist laments that God has turned away from him, even though he feels innocent. He reflects on his situation (Psalm 77:3, Psalms 77:6, Psalms 77:12) and finds hope (see Psalms 25:5) in remembering God's past actions (Psalms 77:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• I remembered You, O God: God's people often face hard times. Remembering God's powerful actions at the beginning of their relationship assures them of God's commitment.

• Feeling overwhelmed, the psalmist is unable to deal with the crisis (Psalms 142:3; Psalms 143:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: As the psalmist meditates at night, he feels so disturbed that he cannot sleep or speak. He has pleasant memories of the past, but he cannot look beyond the present moment into the future.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Feeling rejected (see Psalm 43:2), the psalmist asks if the situation is permanent.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist questions his status before God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist is afraid that God's hand of protection (Psalm 44:3; Psalms 77:15; Exodus 6:6) and favor (Psalms 16:7–8; Psalms 110:1) are now against him for no clear reason.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The memories of God’s mighty works in the past fill the psalmist’s mind.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This central section of the poem reflects on God as the holy and powerful redeemer.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: the waters saw You and swirled: The Canaanites attributed divine power to the sea, but God is the one who made the sea and uses it for his own purposes.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The introduction is an invitation to learn wisdom.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This wisdom psalm urges people to learn wisdom and share it faithfully.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist tells Israel’s story (Psalm 78:5–72) as a parable to teach wisdom and insight.

• Jesus quoted this verse to explain why he taught in parables (Matthew 13:35).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This story of what God has done should be told from generation to generation (see Deuteronomy 6:20–25; Proverbs 4:1–4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The telling of the story should motivate God’s people to obey what he commanded (Deuteronomy 6:4–9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God holds each generation responsible for its own actions. They should maintain faith and hope (see Psalm 9:18; Psalms 27:14) and avoid being stubborn, rebellious, and unfaithful (see Deuteronomy 9:6–7; Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6; Deuteronomy 31:27).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Ephraim was the second son of Joseph. He received a special blessing from Jacob (Genesis 48:15–20; Genesis 49:22–26; Deuteronomy 33:13–17). His descendants inherited land with fertile valleys and important roads (Judges 8:2). However, the people of Ephraim did not follow God's covenant.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wonders are the ten plagues against Egypt that God performed during Israel’s captivity (Exodus 7–12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The focus shifts from Ephraim (Psalm 78:9–11) to all of Israel. The psalmist thinks about God's power in Egypt (see Psalm 81:4–7) and in the wilderness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God split the sea when Israel crossed through the Red Sea (see Exodus 14–15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God used a cloud and a light of fire to guide and protect Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21–22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel rebelled in the wilderness despite God’s abundant provision.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Abundance comes through the doors of heaven (Genesis 8:2; 2 Kings 7:2; Malachi 3:10). 

• The Israelites ate manna for 40 years in the wilderness (Exodus 16:31–36; John 6:31).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God powerfully satisfied the people’s desires, but they did not respond with gratitude or faith. Therefore, God exercised his justice.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel’s rebellion resulted in God’s judgment, but even their short-lived and insincere repentance motivated God to exercise forbearance.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: An entire generation died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:22–23, Numbers 14:28–35).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: they repented: This strong show of effort was not sincere.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel continued to exist because of God's compassion, despite the people's rebellion and lack of belief (Psalm 78:7–8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Israelites remembered the correct teaching about God (Psalms 9:9; Psalms 91:1), but they did not let God change the way they thought and lived (Leviticus 26:41).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Israelites rebelled even though the Lord had rescued them from powerful plagues.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel’s rebellion defiled the promised land. During the time of the judges, the people built shrines to false gods and worshiped idols (Psalm 78:58; see also Judges 2:11; Judges 3:7, Judges 3:17–18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God abandoned his dwelling at Shiloh because of the people’s idol worship (1 Samuel 4:11; Jeremiah 7:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The tribe of Ephraim was not completely rejected, but God favored Judah (Psalm 78:68).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In the choice of Mount Zion instead of Shiloh as God’s sanctuary on earth, God moved from the north to the south (see Psalm 69).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The God who had turned against his own people (Psalm 78:62) chose David, a shepherd (Genesis 46:34; 1 Samuel 16:10–11), to lead them as their shepherd (Psalm 78:52; compare Psalms 23:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Your inheritance: This phrase might refer to the land, the temple (see Psalm 61:5), or the people (see Psalms 79:2; Psalms 78:71).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The poet laments the defilement of the temple and the success of the enemy.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This lament describes the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. Israel’s early history of rebellion, described in Psalm 78, angered God. As a result, Zion was destroyed. The temple was defiled, and the bodies of the dead lay across the land. 

The psalmist then prays for forgiveness and rescue (Psalm 79:8–9) and asks God to repay the nation's enemies (Psalm 79:12–13). Other psalms lamenting the exile include Psalms 42–44, Psalms 102:102, Psalms 107:107, Psalms 126:126, and Psalms 137:137.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The intensity of God’s judgment surprises the people; they cry out in despair for compassion, forgiveness, and relief. Verse Psalms 6:6–7 are nearly identical to Jeremiah 10:25.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The repentant among God’s people ask him to vent his anger not on them but on their wicked and unrepentant enemies.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The people’s many sins in the past helped lead to the exile (2 Kings 17:7–23; 2 Kings 24:3–4). However, each person also suffered because of his or her own sin (Jeremiah 31:30; Ezekiel 18:20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The people ask God to rescue them. Although Israel’s sins caused the tragedy, the pagan nations must also be held responsible for the bloodshed.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The exile resulted in national suffering and in individual searching for the Lord. 

• Pay back: See Psalm 1:6; Psalms 94:2; Jeremiah 32:18. 

• The phrase sevenfold means something is complete. 

• Israel's neighbors included Edom, Moab, and Ammon (see Psalm 137:7; 2 Kings 24:2; Obadiah 1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The tune of “The Lilies of the Covenant” is unknown today.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• O Shepherd of Israel: See also Psalm 23:1; Psalms 28:9; Psalms 78:52–53.

• shine forth … mighty power: These expressions (Psalm 145:11) refer to God's visible presence.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist urgently calls upon the Lord to act.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This psalm of lament may come from the remnant (the small group that survived) of the northern kingdom after it fell in 722 BC. The people call on God as their Shepherd and as the God of Hosts (a title that describes God as the ruler over the armies of heaven). They hope that he will return to them and restore them.

They remember the Exodus and their special relationship with the Lord. The psalm ends with a promise of renewed commitment to him (Psalm 80:18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This verse is repeated (with a growing intensity) in Psalm 80:7 and Psalms 80:19.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The people cry out for rescue from the shame of their recent defeat. The enemy’s victory is less devastating, however, than the knowledge that they themselves are objects of God’s wrath.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel had been like a fruitful grapevine (Genesis 1:28; Galatians 5:22–23) that God transplanted to Canaan at the time of the conquest. However, the people forgot the source of their prosperity and chose to do evil (Isaiah 5:1–7; Hosea 10:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel has a glorious past that began when God rescued the people from Egypt.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Solomon’s kingdom had extended west to the Mediterranean Sea and east to the Euphrates River (see Psalms 72:8–9; Psalms 89:25; 1 Kings 4:21).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: broken down its walls: God no longer defended Israel (Isaiah 5:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The surrounding nations were ceremonially unclean, like a wild boar or vicious wild animals.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel was the son that God had brought out of Egypt (see Hosea 11:1) and planted him in the Holy Land.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The community prays for God to change their desperate situation and restore them. They are still the Lord’s chosen people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The son God chose was probably the northern kingdom of Israel. But it may also refer to the king from David’s line (Psalm 110:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Before giving a warning, the psalmist calls Israel to think about their God through song and dance.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This warning message invites Israel to worship only the Lord and to enjoy the fullness of his blessing.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• An Israelite tambourine was a hand drum with a round frame and skin cover. People used it as a percussion instrument during celebrations, often to accompany dancing (Psalms 68:25; Psalms 149:3; Psalms 150:4). 

• The sweet-sounding harp and lyre, both stringed instruments, are the most frequently mentioned instruments in the psalms (for example, Psalms 33:2; Psalms 57:8; Psalms 71:22; Psalms 150:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The ram’s horn gathered armies and announced special holy days (Psalms 47:5; Psalms 98:6). 

• New Moon: The first day of each lunar month was a festival.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The festival, a time to celebrate and listen to the Lord, took place at God’s appointed time.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: for Joseph: The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh (the sons of Joseph) are used here to refer to the entire nation of Israel.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord heard Israel’s cry in Egypt and rescued them from oppressive slavery.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God pleads with his people to remember the covenant and the Ten Commandments.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God emphasizes that he and no one else rescued Israel.

• The nation should eagerly accept God's word (compare Deuteronomy 8:3; Ezekiel 3:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord helps Israel to understand that their failure was not because of his weakness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God wants to give his goodness to his children, but they must listen (Isaiah 1:18–19; Isaiah 28:12; Isaiah 48:18–19; see Deuteronomy 6:3). 

• God promises to defeat the enemies (Deuteronomy 9:3) of those who follow the paths of obedience and loyalty. He will also provide abundantly for his people (Isaiah 1:19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God is ready to give judgment (see Isaiah 3:13). 

• divine assembly: See Job 1:6.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God condemns those who mistreat the helpless.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Because justice defines God’s rule (Psalm 89:4), he does not support the wicked. The psalmist is confused by this situation and cries out to God to bring justice (Psalm 82:3–4, Psalms 82:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Unjust oppressors cannot bring or restore order. They wander about in darkness, unmoved by circumstances, even when the whole world order falls apart around them (compare Psalm 11:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The gods (see study notes on Psalm 29:1–2; 58:1), like mere humans, cannot escape the judgment common to human rulers. Jesus quoted from this passage in John 10:34.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The nations belong to God. He will take over the realms formerly ruled by local gods and give them to his people, just as he did with the promised land.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The enemy has successfully intimidated God’s people, so the poet prays that the Lord will hear and act.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This community lament asks God to rescue his people and give them victory. The short and direct poetry suggests a time of great trouble. A strong group of nations plans to destroy Israel (Psalm 83:1–4) and joins together against God (Psalms 83:5–8). 

The psalmist remembers what happened to other enemies who attacked Israel in the past (Psalm 83:9–12). He prays that the same thing will happen to these enemies (Psalms 83:13–16), so that they will recognize God’s power and give him honor (Psalms 83:17–18). 

It is not clear whether this psalm refers to one specific historical event or whether it gathers together several nations as a poetic picture of Israel’s enemies.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: they form an alliance: The allies agreed to fight against God and his people. The nations named in this alliance lived around Israel and Judah.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Edomites were descendants of Esau. They lived southeast of Judah (see Genesis 25:30; Genesis 32:3; Genesis 36:1–8). 

• The Ishmaelites were descendants of Hagar. They lived in the desert. 

• The Moabites and Ammonites were descendants of Lot. They lived east of Israel and Judah. 

• The Hagrites might have lived north of the Ammonites (1 Chronicles 5:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Gebal, also known as Byblos, was on the coast of Lebanon. 

• The Amalekites lived south of Israel in the Negev desert. 

• Philistia was southwest of Judah, near the Mediterranean Sea. 

• Tyre was a port city on the Mediterranean Sea, northwest of Israel.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Assyria was located northeast of Israel and north of the Persian Gulf. 

• Lot's descendants were the Moabites and the Ammonites (Psalm 83:6–7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Midianites, led by Oreb and Zeeb and ruled by Zebah and Zalmunna, were Israel's enemies during Gideon's time (Judges 7:1–8:5). Barak's alliance defeated Sisera and Jabin (Judges 4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays that God will miraculously destroy the new coalition as he did three other enemies; doing so would bring him glory.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The coalition wanted to destroy Israel to take over the land (see Jeremiah 3:19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: tumbleweed … chaff: This dry plant material blows away easily (see Isaiah 17:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: fire … flame … tempest: These images describe how God appears when he brings judgment (see Isaiah 29:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist is far from the temple. He turns toward it in hopeful reflection.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The psalmist deeply longs for God's presence. He feels weak with longing as he thinks about the temple and the pilgrims traveling to Jerusalem (Psalm 84:1–7). He prays for himself and the community (Psalm 84:8–9). 

The end of the psalm (Psalm 84:10–12) shows that the temple represents God. The psalmist truly desires God's presence. He understands that God's goodness is better than life and that only God can grant his people favor and honor (Psalm 84:10–11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The poet envies the birds that have nesting places in and around the temple.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The priests and those who worked in the temple also lived there.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Travelers needed strength to meet the challenges of pilgrimage by foot along unpaved paths, in all kinds of weather and with the possibility of assaults.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The pilgrimage to Jerusalem reminded people of the exodus, when God provided for his people in a wonderful way (see Psalm 78:15–16; Psalms 105:41). The psalmist describes how the hardships of the journey turn into joy when the travelers arrive.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Valley of Baca is also called the Valley of Weeping or the Valley of Tears. It likely symbolizes the sadness that lonely pilgrims felt (see Psalm 23:4), rather than a real place. 

• spring … autumn rain: Even when pilgrims feel completely worn out, the hope of getting closer to the Lord encourages them (compare Isaiah 35:6–10; Isaiah 41:18–20; Isaiah 43:17–20; Isaiah 49:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Both kings and priests were anointed to dedicate them for service (see Psalm 132:17; Exodus 28:41; 1 Samuel 9:16; 1 Samuel 16:1–13; compare Isaiah 61:1; Acts 10:38).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist viewed being in God’s presence as much better than being anywhere else.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Some people worshiped the sun as a god, but the true God provides all that anyone needs.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God brought Israel back from exile and restored its fortunes (see Psalm 14:7; Psalms 126:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Though the psalmist gratefully acknowledges God’s goodness, he also asks God whether his wrath will last forever.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The psalmist leads the community that returned from exile in a lament and a prayer for complete restoration:

• He remembers how God rescued Israel from exile (Psalm 85:1–3), 

• asks for clearer signs of God’s goodness, and

• leads the people in prayer for full renewal (Psalm 85:4–7).

God answers with a message of peace (Psalm 85:8–9). The psalm ends with a poetic description of the greatness of God’s salvation (Psalms 85:10–13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: When God forgave the guilt of their sins, he gave the people the possibility of fellowship with him (see Psalm 32:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This prayer for renewal is based on God’s unfailing love for his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• When God speaks, his faithful people listen. He promises them peace, meaning wholeness and well-being (see Psalm 37:11). They respect the Lord and know that he and his salvation are near. 

• The Lord does not tolerate foolish ways, such as those that resulted in the exile.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In the renewed world of salvation, all the qualities of God’s care (love, truth, righteousness, and peace) come together. They transform creation and make it new (see Isaiah 32:15–20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Righteousness is like a messenger preparing the world for God’s coming in response to the prayers of his people (Psalms 85:4–7; Psalms 89:14).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This is the only Psalm connected to David in the third book.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s devoted servant prays for mercy. The psalmist sees himself as a member of the covenant community and as a citizen of the world.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The psalmist cries out to God for help and praises God’s character while facing evil (Psalm 86:14, Psalms 86:17). He says that all nations will one day worship the gracious and powerful God (Psalm 86:8–10). Because of this hope, the psalmist commits himself to live in a right and honest way (Psalm 86:11) and to praise the Lord (Psalms 86:12–13). 

The final section contrasts the behavior of evil people with the character of the Lord (Psalm 86:14–17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist lists God's perfect qualities (Exodus 34:6–7), especially God's readiness to forgive sin (see Psalms 32:5; Psalms 85:2; Psalms 145:7–10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist appeals to God to remain true to his character, which is the basis for hope.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: All the nations must submit themselves to the Lord and worship him (Psalms 45:17; Psalms 117:1; Psalms 148:7–11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The poet responds to the Lord by seeking faithful instruction in the truth. 

• A person with an undivided heart has integrity and wholeness (see Psalm 73:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In anticipation of God’s rescue, the psalmist praises him and trusts in his goodness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Arrogant people exist both inside and outside the community. The psalmist asks God to show his character. God is so great that even a small glimpse of his goodness will silence the wicked.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
God shows mercy to his people (Psalm 51:1). God is compassionate (Psalm 25:6). God is slow to become angry (Psalms 103:8; Psalms 145:8). God is full of loving devotion and faithfulness (Hebrew khesed and ’emeth; Psalm 143:1)

This verse repeats a theme first expressed in Exodus 34:7; Numbers 14:18 (compare Psalms 103:8; Psalms 145:8; Nehemiah 9:17; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Jerusalem was Israel’s capital and the location of the temple, God’s earthly palace (see Psalm 84).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm presents Jerusalem as the city of God, where people from all nations are counted as citizens.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Zion is great, but it will be even greater as an international city where believers from all nations are citizens. 

• God keeps a record of everyone who confesses him as their Lord (Daniel 7:10; Revelation 13:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Jerusalem becomes the international city where all God’s children are citizens.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• A Maskil: This may be a literary or musical term.

• Heman the Ezrahite: Heman might have been:

• a wise person from the time of King Solomon (1 Kings 4:31), 

• a descendant of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:6), or 

• a member of the Levite family responsible for singing at the temple (1 Chronicles 15:17; 2 Chronicles 5:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist calls on the Lord for salvation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this lament, the psalmist sees himself as cast out from God’s presence. At first, he calls on the Lord. When he finds no relief from his suffering, he presents three charges against God (Psalm 88:6–7, Psalms 88:8–12, Psalms 88:13–17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• In his first complaint, the psalmist blames the Lord for his suffering. God’s overwhelming anger does not make sense to him.

• The phrase the darkest of the depths might refer to:

• the place of the dead (Psalm 143:3; see Lamentations 3:6), or 

• the deep sea (Psalms 68:22; Psalms 69:1–2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In his second charge, the psalmist claims that God has isolated him and caused his loneliness (compare Psalms 31:11; Psalms 38:11). In that culture, loneliness was a curse because relationships mattered more than personal success.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In his third charge, the psalmist accuses the Lord of rejecting him. The force and apparent cruelty of the psalmist’s suffering overwhelm him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist restates his second and first charges.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
God’s loving devotion gives reason to celebrate forever.

Ethan the Ezrahite was a wise man (1 Kings 4:31; compare Psalm 88:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Book Three (Psalms 73–89) starts and ends with serious questions. Psalm 89 begins with praise for how the Lord established David’s throne and kingdom (Psalms 89:1–37). But later the psalmist protests that the Lord seems to have rejected his covenant with David (Psalm 89:38–51; see 2 Samuel 7:8–16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord has sworn by his own holiness (Psalm 89:35; see Psalms 110:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist repeats God's covenant with David (see also Psalm 89:19–37).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Those in heaven praise God's greatness (see Psalm 8:1) because they witness his faithfulness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God is the absolute standard of faithfulness, commitment, and order. The angelic beings and the heavens testify to his constancy.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: heavenly beings: Literally son of God (see study note on Psalm 29:1–2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Lord rules over all parts of the created order, including evil. 

• You scattered Your enemies: The Lord will defeat (Luke 1:51) evil forces that oppose him (Psalm 2:1–3). 

• with Your mighty arm: This phrase represents God’s strength (Psalm 89:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this hymn, the psalmist celebrates God’s complete and powerful rule over nature.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Mount Tabor was in northern Israel. Mount Hermon formed the extreme northern border of the nation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God rules wisely over creation. The qualities of righteousness, justice, and faithfulness fit the description of a wise ruler. The happy people who live under his rule enjoy his protection.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Those who are wise worship God, walk in his light, rejoice in their relationship with him, and delight in his character.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord protects his people with the same power by which he established the created order.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord chose David as his son and king of Israel (see Psalm 2:4–6; 2 Samuel 7:8–16) to protect his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: I have anointed him: This is the verb from which comes anointed one (Hebrew mashiakh, which means “messiah”).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord adopted David as his son, appointed him as his commander over the nations, and promised to support him forever. Verse 26 recalls a verse from David’s song of praise (2 Samuel 22:47).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: David would become the greatest of earthly kings. The Hebrew word translated highest is the same word used for God as “Most High” (‘elyon).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord displays his faithfulness in the heavens, across his whole creation (see Psalm 89:2). In the same way, he confirms his commitment to the kings that would come from David's family.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord disciplines his children when they go astray, but he does not reject them. He knows they will break their trust and will need correction, yet he remains committed to keep his covenant. His faithfulness to David is like his faithfulness to the created world.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: holiness: The Lord is completely different from the created world (Psalm 22:3). His character is entirely pure. He acts according to his will (Psalm 115:3) and chooses to be faithful (Psalms 89:1; Psalms 115:1). Therefore, he cannot lie.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: You are enraged: The psalmist is confused by the severity of God's anger.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: broken down all his walls: The Lord’s people are completely vulnerable.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Although the Lord promised to strengthen David, he has made David’s enemies strong

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist wonders whether he will live long enough to see the Lord’s anger end. Human life is short and passes quickly before the Lord (Psalm 90:4, Psalms 90:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The phrase Your servants refers to the community loyal to the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This doxology (a short praise to God) ends Book Three of the Psalms (Psalms 73–89). It was not meant to be read as part of Psalm 89. Its words of praise stand in strong contrast to the pain and questions expressed in Psalm 89. Compare Psalm 41:13; Psalms 106:48.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Moses led God's people from slavery in Egypt to Mount Sinai. There, he received the law and established God's covenant with Israel. 

• the man of God: Moses had a special relationship with God (Deuteronomy 33:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord is the dwelling place for the godly. He has provided shelter for many generations. The word translated as dwelling place is rare in the Psalms. It describes a safe place where the Lord meets and cares for those in need (Psalms 68:5; Psalms 71:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Although the Lord’s people have lived in him for many generations, their sin creates distance between them and their eternal Lord. The Lord’s anger against human sin can seem to last a lifetime. Even then, it is only a small sign of his full displeasure with sin. This sad situation leads the community to seek the Lord’s light.

The first step is to ask the Lord to restore them because of his compassion and faithful love (Psalm 90:13–14). He alone can make his servants glad. He alone can bless the generations that come after them (Psalm 90:16–17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Lord is the eternal God. 

• The Lord created the earth.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Unlike God, humans are mortal and temporary.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Sinners cannot escape God’s anger against sin because the Lord sees their sins. Their lives pass quickly and are full of suffering.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• A groan of sorrow (Ezekiel 2:10) represents a life facing the consequences of sin. 

• Humans create trouble (see Psalm 10:6) and receive pain as a result.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In the search for wisdom, no one can fully understand the Lord (see Isaiah 40:13). The right human response to the Lord is godly fear (see Psalm 60:4). The Lord alone can teach humans to follow the path of wisdom (Psalm 25:4–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The phrase Your servants refers to the community of those loyal to the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays for the Lord’s favor and restoration.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist calls upon the Lord to give the people gladness to replace their mourning (see Psalm 92:4–5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The children represent future generations in contrast to the generations past (Psalm 90:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Humans waste their efforts unless the Lord makes them successful (Psalm 44:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Most High is an ancient title that expresses the Lord’s exalted status as the ruler and protector of the godly (see Genesis 14:19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord is an ancient shelter (see Psalm 90:1), open to those who seek refuge in him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This wisdom psalm expresses confidence in the Almighty God, who provides a shelter for those who take refuge in him. They receive redemption, life, and glory from the Lord, who loves and cares for those who seek him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God protects the godly from deadly disease and even a destructive word.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist invites the godly to trust in the Lord and find protection in him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The shield might refer to a large shield that covers the body. The rampart likely refers to a smaller shield, though the exact meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly should not be afraid, because the Lord watches over them. These promises do not guarantee an escape from trouble, but they create an expectation of the Lord’s goodness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The word pestilence here means any kind of suffering or trouble.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The poet again invites the godly to seek refuge in the Lord and enjoy the benefits of divine protection.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: He will command His angels: Satan quoted these words when he tempted Jesus (Matthew 4:6; Luke 4:10–11). However, God makes this promise for those who obey him (Psalm 91:14), not for those who arrogantly test him (Matthew 4:4, Matthew 4:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Those who love the Lord will follow his commands (Deuteronomy 30:20; 1 John 5:3) and look for his protection (Psalms 91:1; Psalms 145:18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly can trust the Lord’s protection and provision.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Lord promises to answer the prayers of his people. 

• The Psalms often mention people honoring the Lord (Psalm 50:15). Here, God promises to honor the faithful who risk everything for him (Psalms 62:7; Psalms 71:21; Psalms 84:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A long life on earth represents just a small part of the Lord’s goodness and eternal friendship (Psalm 23:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
In Jewish tradition, each day of the week has an assigned psalm: 

• Sunday (Psalm 24)

• Monday (Psalm 48)

• Tuesday (Psalm 82)

• Wednesday (Psalm 94)

• Thursday (Psalm 81)

• Friday (Psalm 93)

• Saturday, which is the Sabbath (Psalm 92)

This is the only psalm that indicates this use in its title.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist offers praise and thanksgiving for God’s loving devotion and faithfulness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This psalm begins with thanksgiving and praise. The Lord, the Most High, is fair and just in judging the godly and the wicked. The godly will have a bright and strong future, while the wicked will die. 

Wise people see and understand the Lord's actions, which show his justice (Psalm 92:6–7, Psalms 92:11, Psalms 92:15). The wicked, like grass, are quickly destroyed (Psalm 92:7–10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord acts and the psalmist responds in praise (Psalm 92:4). God’s actions come from his thoughts (Psalm 92:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Fools perish because they do not understand the Lord’s great works and his eternal plans.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord’s thoughts confuse those who lack understanding or act foolishly, and those who do not seek wisdom (Proverbs 1:22; Proverbs 10:23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Even when the ungodly appear to thrive (Psalm 73:3–5), they have no future (Psalms 92:9; see Psalms 1:6; Psalms 90:5–6; Isaiah 40:6–8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The Lord is above the world of human experience. From this exalted place, he rules and judges (Psalm 7:7). From there, he:

• celebrates his victories (Psalm 68:18; see Psalms 47:47), 

• comes to rescue the needy (Psalm 102:19), 

• brings an end to the wicked (Psalm 92:7–8), and 

• receives praise (Psalm 148:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The glory of the Lord is the reason the poet receives new strength and honor. It is also the reason the enemy will soon be defeated.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: like that of a wild ox: The Lord allows the psalmist to express his joy (Psalm 92:8). Because of this, the psalmist is strong and will overcome his enemies.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist understands the Lord’s mighty acts. He shares in the glory of the wise of heart.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Carvings of palm trees (1 Kings 6:29, 1 Kings 6:32, 1 Kings 6:35; 1 Kings 7:36) decorated the temple. Builders used many cedars (1 Kings 5:6). The trees represent the godly, who are planted in the very courts of the temple.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The temple area consisted of the Lord’s own house and the courts that surrounded it.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: in Him there is no unrighteousness: The Lord is always just. He rightly judges everyone (see Zephaniah 3:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: robed in majesty: The Lord stands victorious both before and after battle (see Psalm 45:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The everlasting Lord gloriously establishes his kingship (see Psalms 47, Psalms 99:99–100).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
These psalms challenge the doubts created by the exile (see Psalm 89) and answer the questions asked in Psalm 90:11, Psalms 90:13. The Lord has established a kingdom (Psalm 93) that is characterized by: 

• punishment of the wicked (Psalm 94),

• respectful obedience among his people (Psalm 95),

• justice for the poor (Psalm 96),

• celebration in Zion (Psalm 97),

• salvation for Israel (Psalm 98),

• holiness (Psalm 99), and

• praise (Psalm 100).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s victory over natural chaos gives the psalmist confidence that the Lord will also defeat his present enemies (compare Jeremiah 46:8; Jeremiah 47:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Through his stable rule and royal laws, the Lord orders the world.

• Your house: The house from which God reigns might be the Lord’s heavenly palace or the earthly temple.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: After the community suffers at the hands of the wicked (Psalm 94:5–7), they pray for the Lord to bring justice (see Psalm 7:11; Psalms 9:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This plea for the Lord’s justice includes both communal and individual expressions of sorrow (Psalm 94:1–7, Psalms 94:16–23). The psalmist speaks about the pain and suffering caused by the wicked. He also describes the comfort and stability of the Lord’s protection. He calls on the Lord to avenge the needy against the arrogant and foolish, he rebukes such people for their foolishness (Psalm 94:8–11), and speaks a blessing on the wise (Psalms 94:12–15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: When the Lord's enemies rise against him and his people (Psalm 3:7; Psalms 93:3), he must rise and punish the enemy (see Psalms 79:12; Isaiah 65:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: widow … foreigner … fatherless: The Lord’s law protects those in need (Deuteronomy 24:17; Deuteronomy 27:19), but they remain vulnerable in society.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked think that they can get away with their evil acts and speech, foolishly assuming that God is not looking or does not care.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The writer of the psalm corrects people for acting foolishly.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: It makes no sense for people who have ears and eyes to think that their Creator is deaf and blind.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: discipline: This word can also mean "admonished" (Psalm 2:10), "discipline" (Psalms 6:1; Psalms 94:12), or "instructs" (Psalms 16:7). The Lord disciplines his people to improve their character (Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:6–11). He punishes his enemies by giving them what they deserve (Psalm 1:6; Romans 6:23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: While the Lord’s thoughts are deep, people’s thoughts are worthless (compare Psalm 92:5; 1 Corinthians 3:20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Because the Lord is faithful to his character, he rewards those who live by his wise instruction. He makes them happy, just as he promised.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s relief includes his comfort and rescue.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Even when it seems that he has, the Lord will not reject his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Only God has the power to stand up to the wicked (see Psalm 2:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist resumes their prayer (see Psalm 94:1–7) with a desperate plea for the Lord's justice. It ends with the hope that evil will cease.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels like he is slipping, but God promises to stand with him (Psalm 94:12–13; see Psalms 15:5; Psalms 93:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This call to worship urges the people to respond to the Lord, the Shepherd, and to follow him faithfully. The previous generation, who refused to obey, did not receive the blessings of the promised land.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: above all gods: The psalmist argues against idol worship and pagan beliefs (Psalms 96:4–6; Psalms 135:15–18; see also Isaiah 46:5–7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord is the great King over the whole universe.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: All creation exists because of the Lord alone, not because of many gods.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The great King cares for his people like a shepherd cares for sheep (Isaiah 40:11). 

• The Lord, our Maker, the Creator of heaven and earth, also created a people for himself (Isaiah 45:9–12; Isaiah 51:12–16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: To harden your hearts means to be stubborn and resist the Lord's grace (see Numbers 20:2–13; see also Matthew 13:3–23; John 12:37–43; Ephesians 4:17–32; Hebrews 3:6–19; Hebrews 4:6–11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: If people want to enter into the Lord’s rest, they need to respond immediately (see Hebrews 3:7–4:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel's ancestors saw the Lord's wonders but did not understand their importance (see Psalm 92:5–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The generation of Israel that wandered in the wilderness for 40 years did not enter the place of rest that Israel enjoyed after conquering the land (1 Kings 8:56; see Deuteronomy 12:9). The Lord promised them the land and gave it to them (Isaiah 28:12), but they did not obey him (Isaiah 28:1). This warning reminds every generation of the need to obey with faith. 

• The rest that God provides includes peace, provision, and protection (Psalm 132:14–18). The author of Hebrews challenged a new generation to enter the rest provided by Jesus Christ (Hebrews 3:7–4:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Three psalms begin by urging people to sing a new song (Psalms 96, Psalms 98:98, Psalms 149:149). The song celebrates the Lord's universal kingship (see Psalm 33:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• This psalm establishes the Lord’s universal kingship (see Psalm 93) and prepares for the coming of the Lord to bring justice and righteousness to the world. The psalmist invites everyone to worship the Lord (Psalm 96:1–3), the glorious Creator of the earth (Psalms 96:4–6), because only he deserves worship (Psalms 96:7–9). The universe joins in praise as the righteous Judge establishes a new order (Psalm 96:10–13). 

• This psalm (along with Psalm 105:1–15; Psalms 106:1, Psalms 106:47–48) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in 1 Chronicles 16:1–43.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: great is the LORD … greatly to be praised: The poet praises the Lord above all gods (Psalm 95:3) and nations (Psalms 99:2). The Lord inspires more awe than anyone or anything else (Psalm 76:7, Psalms 76:12; Psalms 89:7; Psalms 99:3; Psalms 111:9). He is beyond human possession or comprehension. The story of what he does to redeem his people causes them to praise him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The gods of the nations are as nothing before the glorious and awesome Creator of the earth.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord made the heavens, an even greater task than creating the earth. The idols, made by human hands (Psalm 115:4), created nothing.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Splendor and majesty: The Lord is glorious (Psalm 96:6; Psalms 104:1; Psalms 148:13), and so are his works in nature (Psalms 8:1) and in redemption (Psalms 111:3; Psalms 145:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• families of the nations: Families and clans represent subdivisions of the nations (see Genesis 12:3). 

• The nations must respond to the Lord’s glory (Psalms 8:1; Psalms 19:1–4; Psalms 24:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The courts of God’s sanctuary were usually not open to non-Jewish people. In this psalm, the nations of the world (people who are not Jews) are invited to come in (Psalm 65:4; Psalms 84:2, Psalms 84:10; Psalms 100:4; Psalms 116:19; Psalms 135:2; Isaiah 1:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Worshipers should tremble in awe (Psalm 96:4; see Psalms 18:7–15; Psalms 97:4) at the splendor of the Lord’s great power and holiness (Hebrews 12:25).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Lord’s coming means the end of injustice. He rules fairly (Psalm 9:8; Psalms 96:13; Psalms 98:9). He brings a time of peace and order like the world has not known since Adam and Eve lived in the garden of Eden.

• The Lord’s rule over the world stands on the strong pillars of “righteousness and justice” (Psalm 89:14), so it cannot be shaken (compare Psalms 11:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist urges all of creation to respond with joy to the news of the Lord’s coming. Compare a similar theme in Psalm 98:7–9.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: All of nature will experience renewal in God’s presence (Psalms 65:13; Psalms 72:6, Psalms 72:16; Isaiah 44:23; Isaiah 55:12; Romans 8:21–22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The distant shores represent the most remote parts of the world.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God is greatly exalted over the gods and over all the earth. Awe-inspiring phenomena accompany his coming. Even the created order is visibly affected and the wicked perish, but the people of Zion love his coming and rejoice.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Clouds … Fire … lightning: This language shows that the Lord is coming to judge.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: All creation responds to the coming of its King. He alone deserves worship.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• When the Lord comes into the world, the heavens announce his righteousness (Psalm 50:6). 

• Every nation will see the clear display of the Lord’s glory (see Psalm 8:1; Psalms 19:1–4a; Psalms 24:7; Isaiah 40:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: At the Lord’s coming, when every god must bow to him, those who worship other gods will face their own foolishness (see Psalm 95:3–5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Jerusalem rejoices at the news of the Lord’s coming, for he brings justice and rescues the upright of heart.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Godly people who live with integrity (see Proverbs 2:7, Proverbs 2:21; Proverbs 3:32; Proverbs 11:6, Proverbs 11:11; Proverbs 14:2) have hearts that are right before the Lord. They maintain a relationship with the Lord and live rightly with others (Psalms 94:15; Psalms 125:4). 

The wicked plan to destroy the godly (Psalm 11:2), but the Lord rescues them (Psalms 11:1; Psalms 36:10). Then the sorrows of the godly turn into joy and praise (Psalms 32:11; Psalms 64:10; Psalms 111:1; Psalms 119:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This psalm celebrates the Lord as King. The Lord is the true King of Israel, its champion and savior. His people sing a new song to celebrate his victory and his faithfulness to them.

The Lord shows his righteous rule to all the nations of the earth. One day, this will lead to a worldwide kingdom of justice (Psalm 98:2, Psalms 98:9). Because of this, all the earth should worship and rejoice together, for the Lord is coming (Psalm 98:4–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord makes known his righteousness and faithfulness (see also Isaiah 52:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist invites the whole earth to worship the King (see Psalm 96:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The temple musicians played trumpets to gather people for meetings (compare Psalm 81:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalm speaks as if all creation rejoices when the righteous Judge comes (see Psalms 83:3–4; Psalms 96:11–13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• It is appropriate to tremble and quake in response to the Lord’s holiness (see Psalm 96:9). 

• The throne between the cherubim refers to the cover of the ark of the Testimony (Exodus 25:17–22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord is the holy and righteous King (Isaiah 6:1–5). Mount Zion, where the temple of the Lord is located, metaphorically stands as the highest point on earth (Psalm 113:4; Isaiah 2:2; Isaiah 6:1). From this high place, the "great King" (Psalm 47:2) can see, rule over, and receive praise from all nations and peoples.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist calls the nations to worship the Lord, the king of the earth who rules from Zion.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The qualities of the Lord’s rule include: 

• strength,

• justice,

• love,

• fairness, and

• righteousness (see Psalms 93:4; Psalms 97:2, Psalms 97:6–7, Psalms 97:12; Psalms 98:2–3, Psalms 98:9; Psalms 138:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Moses and Samuel were great models and leaders who had prayed on behalf of the Lord’s people (Exodus 32:31–32; 1 Samuel 12:23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God showed favor by responding to his people in the past, while holding sinners accountable.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron from the pillar of cloud (Exodus 33:9; Numbers 12:5–6). For a while, the people responded to the revelation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm calls all nations to come to Jerusalem to worship the Lord and acknowledge his goodness to Israel.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Lord is the one who determines who his people are.

• the sheep of His pasture: God will guide and protect his people (Psalm 23:1, Psalms 23:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Gates and courts were part of the temple in Jerusalem.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This song of praise expresses a commitment to live with integrity and to avoid evil. Jesus meets this ideal.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• in my house: This commitment to integrity might refer to private life at home. Some interpreters see my house as the king’s palace. The commitment would then refer to the policies of his administration. 

• Living with integrity means choosing a wise lifestyle.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist hates what the Lord hates (Proverbs 6:16–19; see Psalms 5:5; Psalms 11:4–5). 

• Perverse ideas come from corrupt human hearts (compare Psalm 18:26).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist surrounds himself with people who are also committed to integrity (Psalm 101:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist promises to remove all evil from his house and the city of the Lord, which represents the entire kingdom.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks the Lord not to turn away (or hide your face). Israel experienced God turning his face away when they were exiled.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A weak and suffering person prays for the Lord's mercy on Jerusalem and for his presence with its people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Smoke is an image of the temporary nature of life (Psalms 37:20; Psalms 68:2). 

• The psalmist’s bones represent his whole being (see Psalms 6:2; Psalms 34:19–22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Like withered grass, the psalmist senses his life fading away.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: skin hangs on my bones: The psalmist has become very thin due to his deep sorrow (see Psalm 102:9; Psalms 109:24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Owls often live in deserted places, such as ruined cities. Because of this, the Bible sometimes uses the owl as a sign of ruin and desolation (Isaiah 34:11, Isaiah 34:15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist cannot sleep (see Psalm 63:6–8). Like a lone bird on a housetop, he feels alone and separated from both friends (see Psalm 88:8) and enemies.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist blames the Lord for his troubles.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels that life is empty and short (Psalms 102:4; Psalms 109:23; Psalms 144:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: forever … to all generations: Human life is short and fragile (Psalm 102:3–11). In contrast, the Lord remains forever and rules through every generation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The topic changes from the psalmist’s troubles to the Lord’s glory. A vision of the Lord’s compassionate kingship gives him confidence in Zion’s future.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Now is the time for the Lord to restore Jerusalem from exile (see Psalm 75:2; Jeremiah 29:10; Daniel 9:1–19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: When the Lord arises (Psalm 102:13), the nations will tremble with fear because they will see his glory (see Psalm 8:1; Psalms 19:1–4a; Psalms 24:7). Rebuilding Zion and the temple shows God's glory and fulfills this promise. An even greater fulfillment will come with the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The people of Israel were very poor and vulnerable (destitute) during the exile.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Let this be written: The written record serves as a reminder of the Lord's goodness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord will show mercy. Both Jews and Gentiles will worship him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: His sanctuary refers to God's holy place in heaven (see Psalm 92:8–10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Many people (both Jews and non-Jews) will worship the Lord together (see Psalm 96:7, Psalms 96:9; Psalms 106:48; Isaiah 2:2–4; Isaiah 43:10–13; Isaiah 57:15; Isaiah 60:3–7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Although the psalmist suffers in the present, he bases his hope for the future on the Lord’s past faithfulness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist compares his short life (Psalm 102:23) to God's eternal existence (compare Psalms 90:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• wear out like a garment: Unlike the eternal Creator, the created world will wear out like a piece of clothing (see Isaiah 40:28). 

• The writer to the Hebrews describes this passage as having been addressed to Jesus, the Son (Hebrews 1:10–12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord’s presence provides the basis for the security and happiness of his people (Psalm 23:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: all that is within me, bless His holy name: Psalms 103 and Psalms 104:104 both start and end with this promise (Psalms 103:1–2, Psalms 103:22; Psalms 104:1, Psalms 104:35; see also Psalms 146:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist offers praise for the Lord’s goodness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm celebrates the Lord’s perfection, compassion, forgiveness, and goodness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord revealed himself to Moses in special ways to strengthen his relationship with his people (see Exodus 34:6–7; Numbers 14:18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: If the Lord were to constantly accuse or remain angry forever, no one would be left (see Isaiah 54:7–8; Isaiah 57:16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s love and forgiveness have no limits and are complete.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord is like a father to his children. This idea is central to the teachings of Jesus about God's fatherhood (see Matthew 5:43–48; Matthew 6:1; Matthew 10:19–20; Matthew 12:50; Luke 6:36; Luke 12:29–32; John 8:31–59; John 15:1–8; see also 2 Samuel 7:14; Jeremiah 3:19; Jeremiah 31:9; Malachi 1:6; 2 Corinthians 6:16–18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord compassionately cares for weak humans (see Psalm 37:2; Psalms 90:5; Psalms 92:7; Psalms 102:4; Isaiah 40:6–8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: from everlasting to everlasting the loving devotion of the LORD extends: The Lord’s kingdom is everlasting, so he commits himself to his people across many generations.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: To obey God means to be faithful and loyal to him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist urges the Lord's angels, servants, and messengers to praise the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God's kingdom extends over all things, so all things are called to praise the Lord. 

• The last phrase is similar to Psalm 103:1–2.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Bless the LORD, O my soul!: Psalms 103 and Psalms 104:104 both begin and end with this commitment to praise (Psalms 103:1–2, Psalms 103:22; Psalms 104:1, Psalms 104:35). 

• You are very great: These words praise God for rescuing his people (see also Psalms 35:27; Psalms 40:16; Psalms 70:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This creation hymn (see also Psalms 8, Psalms 33:33, Psalms 145:145) praises God's goodness and greatness. The psalmist thinks about the current world, the original creation, and a future new creation. He views both creations as wonderfully and wisely made (compare Psalm 139:14), as the work of the Lord's Spirit (Psalms 104:30; Genesis 1:2; 2 Corinthians 3:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist refers to two days of creation (see Genesis 1:1–8), when God created the heavens and the light.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This poetic description pictures the clouds as beams that support the heavens.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Wind and lightning (flames of fire) are described as God’s messengers. The Lord controls the wind, rain, and storms and uses them as he desires (Psalm 77:17–18; Psalms 78:26; Psalms 135:7; Psalms 148:5–6). 

• The psalmist refers to the third day of creation (Genesis 1:9–13). The Lord is master of water and earth.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: At first, water covered the earth.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord created dry ground on day three of creation (Genesis 1:9–13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The earth was made because God willed it.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord set a firm boundary for the seas to protect the land. This shows that the Lord rules both the sea and the land. This idea also challenged the beliefs of the Canaanites, who celebrated Baal as the god who defeated the sea (see Psalm 29).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord rules over all waters, including seas, rivers, and springs on the land. He brought order to the waters that were once chaotic. As a result, the earth became a rich place for animals and people. Water refreshes the ground and provides life for birds and other animals.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist celebrates animal, plant, and human life, as well as the Lord’s abundant provision for all of it (Genesis 1:9–30).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: for man to cultivate: People are the managers of the created order, and they receive nourishment from the work of their hands.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Both wine and olive oil can be misused (compare Proverbs 21:17), but the Lord gives them as gifts to improve life. Life is sustained by basic food, represented by bread.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The storks migrated from northern Europe and stayed in Palestine during the winter. 

• rock badgers: These animals are about the size of a rabbit and live in rocky areas.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• the moon to mark the seasons: Ancient Israel based its calendar on the cycles of the moon.

• the sun knows when to set: This poetic description reflects what people normally see. The sun goes down at a regular time each evening.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist rejoices in the order of night and day, marking day four of creation (Genesis 1:14–19). This cycle gives all creatures an opportunity to live.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Cycles of darkness and dawn mark the days on earth.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord’s works testify to his wisdom. All parts fit together (land and sea, night and day, land creatures and sea creatures). The Lord’s wisdom makes life orderly and wonderful.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: teeming with creatures beyond number: The ocean is full of all kinds of life (see Genesis 1:20–21). This shows the Lord's creative work.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• ships pass: Commercial ships used for sea trade were one of the wonders of the ancient Near East (see Isaiah 2:16; Isaiah 23:1, Isaiah 23:3). 

• Leviathan: The psalmist describes this feared sea creature as something the Lord created and controls.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: All living things depend on the Lord, who provides what they need and who has power over life and death (compare Matthew 6:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: When You send Your Spirit: Life on earth is only possible as the Lord’s gift, symbolized by his breath (Hebrew ruakh, which means "breath, wind, or spirit"). The Lord’s Spirit is the agent of renewal (Isaiah 32:15–20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord reveals his presence in the created order (see Psalms 8:1; Psalms 19:1–4; Psalms 24:7) and delights in his new creation (see Isaiah 65:19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist moves from describing the known creation to anticipating the new creation, when the Lord will renew the created order into a world without sinners.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The trembling earth and the smoking mountains represent the Lord’s coming in judgment against sinners and salvation for his faithful people (see Psalm 18:7–15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Lord will remove all forms of evil that defile his creation. 

• The final phrase returns to the opening words of Psalm 104:1 (see also Psalms 103:1–2, Psalms 103:22; Psalms 146:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The poet begins with a call to give thanks (see also Psalms 106:1; Psalms 107:1; Psalms 118:1; Psalms 136:1). The other psalms continue with the refrain "for He is good!" The rest of Psalm 105 tells of God's goodness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• This hymn praises the Lord’s faithfulness to Abraham and his descendants in all their journeys:

• from Ur to Canaan (Psalm 105:12),

• to Egypt (Psalm 105:17, Psalms 105:23),

• through the wilderness (Psalm 105:37, Psalms 105:41), and

• back to Canaan (Psalm 105:44).

These events fulfilled the Lord's promise to Abraham (Psalm 105:9, Psalms 105:42), which was the basis for Israel’s very existence. Joseph, whose suffering turned into glory, serves as a model of encouragement for Israel (Psalm 105:16–25). 

• Psalm 105:1–15 (along with Psalms 96:96; Psalms 106:1, Psalms 106:47–48) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in 1 Chronicles 16:1 Chronicles 16.

entries.title: Psalms
