entries.content: The story of Israel is based on the Lord’s commitment to Abraham. Even when a question arises about the future of God’s covenant with David (Psalm 89), God’s covenant with Abraham stands, as does the spiritual bond between God and Israel, Abraham’s descendants.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The covenant is the Lord’s unbreakable promise to be the Father of Abraham and his descendants (see Genesis 12:1–9; Genesis 15:1–21).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God promised the land of Canaan to Abraham's descendants as their special possession. They could live there as God's people (Psalm 105:44–45; Genesis 12:7; Genesis 15:7–21).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord protected Israel’s patriarchs, the early fathers of the nation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Abraham was one of the nation's prophets (Genesis 20:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These verses tell the story of Joseph (see Genesis 37–41).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• his prediction: Literally, his word.

• the word of the LORD proved him right: See Genesis 39:6–12.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Egypt (Hebrew Mitsrayim) is called the land of Ham.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These verses describe Israel's suffering in Egypt (see Exodus 1:1–14).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist tells the story of Moses and the plagues in Egypt (see Exodus 7:20–12:30).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: none … stumbled: The Lord protected all of his people (compare Psalm 9:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The exodus and the conquest of Canaan fulfilled God's promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Psalm 105:9–10). Unlike Psalm 78, the poet describes the Lord's goodness without mentioning Israel's history of rebellion (compare Psalm 106).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord’s presence was as evident to all as a fire in the darkness (Exodus 13:22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The story of redemption is also the story of the Lord’s faithfulness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Canaan was a land of pagan nations (see Psalm 111:6). The psalmist might also be thinking about God's promise to Abraham (Genesis 24:60) regarding the lands given to Isaac (Genesis 26:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord planned for Israel to show who he is by obeying him. Israel was to be his example among the nations.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Hallelujah! is a Hebrew word (haleluyah) that means “Praise the Lord.” This phrase appears in four small groups in the psalms: 

• Psalm 104–106

• Psalm 111–113

• Psalm 115–117

• Psalm 146–150

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Israelite community in exile confessed the Lord’s goodness and justice and their own past sins. From their humble state in exile, they asked for redemption and restoration. They hoped to be gathered back from all the places the Lord had scattered them in his anger. 

The psalm ends with a memory of the Lord’s past mercy and hope for renewed mercy (Psalm 106:44–48). Israel failed, but the Lord remains constant. 

• Verses 1, Psalms 47:47–48 (along with Psalms 96; Psalms 105:1–15) are included in David’s song of praise recorded in 1 Chronicles 16:1–43.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Wise people who practice justice and righteousness receive encouragement to proclaim the Lord’s great acts.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The poet prays individually for the Lord’s favor before leading the community confession that follows.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The story of Israel's redemption includes their sinful actions from the time of their ancestors to now (Psalm 106:43). The themes of sin and God's anger towards sin start and end Book Four (Psalms 90:1–9; Psalms 106:6, Psalms 106:23, Psalms 106:43).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The community joins together to confess their sins and their ancestors’ many acts of unbelief.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Red Sea: See Exodus 14:15–31.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: they … failed to wait: God’s impatient people did not trust him to work according to his will (for example, see Exodus 15:24; Exodus 16:2–3; Exodus 17:1–3; Numbers 14:26–45; Numbers 21:4–9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: He … sent a wasting disease: See Exodus 32:35 and Numbers 11:33.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The people became jealous because they wanted the same role as the priests God had chosen (see Numbers 16:1–35). 

• The earth opened up: See Numbers 16:28–33.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: they … worshiped a molten image: The people forgot their Savior and worshiped idols (see Exodus 32:1–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: the land of Ham: This means Egypt (Psalm 106:21).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The people disobeyed God’s command when they refused to enter the pleasant land (the promised land (see Jeremiah 3:19). 

• they did not believe His promise: See Numbers 13:25–14:12.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s judgment when Israel refused to obey was death and exile (Numbers 14:26–30). These judgments came because the people rejected God’s word (Psalm 106:24–25) and provoked the Lord's anger (Psalms 106:28–46).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: they yoked themselves to Baal of Peor: See Numbers 25:3; Deuteronomy 4:3.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: When the Israelites entered the land, they brought their idol worship with them. Their behavior stayed the same, and they angered the Lord with their actions.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Phinehas killed an Israelite man who openly turned away from the Lord (Numbers 25:3–8). Because his action stopped the plague, the psalm credits him with righteousness. In this psalm he is presented as a stronger example of zeal for the Lord than Moses, who failed at Meribah (Numbers 20:11–13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel continued to disobey the word of the Lord while living in the promised land. Instead of destroying the nations, Israel accepted them and their customs (see Judges 2:1–3, Judges 2:11–15; Judges 3:5–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The gods of other nations were really demons (see Deuteronomy 32:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Idolatry is like adultery. Both make God’s people unclean before the Lord (see Leviticus 18:24; Hosea 5:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God hated Israel's sin, just as he hates all sin.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist again talks about the Babylonian exile (Psalm 106:26–27). The Lord judged Israel harshly, but he also restrained his anger, remembering the covenant he had made with Abraham.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: When Israel fell, the destruction was not complete. The Lord had compassion on his people and left a remnant (a small group of people who remained).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: He remembered … and relented: Unlike Israel, the Lord is faithful to his covenant (Psalm 105:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Even though the exile was harsh, the Lord still protected his people (see 2 Kings 25:27–29).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: gather us: The community prays for God to bring them back from exile (see Psalms 102:19–22; Psalms 107:3; see also Isaiah 11:12; Isaiah 40:11; Isaiah 43:5; Isaiah 54:7; Isaiah 56:8; Isaiah 66:18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• This doxology (a short song of praise) ends Book Four (compare Psalms 41:13; Psalms 89:52). 

• from everlasting to everlasting: The reference to God’s eternal nature links to the opening of Book Four (Psalm 90:1–2). 

• Let all the people say, “Amen!”: The Hebrew word ’amen means “It is true.” The faithful accept the Lord’s will during exile and his promise to be their God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm is a hymn of praise to God the Redeemer. The psalmist begins by urging the redeemed to praise God for his goodness (Psalm 107:1–3). The psalmist then presents four examples of people whom the Lord saved from trouble (Psalm 107:4–32). He summarizes the Lord’s control over everything (Psalm 107:33–42) and ends with an invitation to recognize God’s loving devotion in all parts of life (Psalms 107:43).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The redeemed might be all who came out of exile.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: People came from all nations where the people of Israel and Judah had been scattered.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Those who were lost in the desert wastelands thank God for his rescue. The desert wastelands might be a metaphor for leaving the path of wisdom (Psalm 1:1; Proverbs 4:10–15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist does not say what caused his trouble and distress. Because the problem is not specific, people in many different situations can identify with the laments.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God led them like a shepherd (see Psalm 23:1). 

• Verse 8 is repeated in Psalm 107:15, Psalms 107:21, Psalms 107:31.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist calls for thanksgiving and praise from people in despair over the consequences of their rebellion.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s counsel includes his instruction and will.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Exhausted from their hard work (Lamentations 5:13), the people stumbled. While this might be expected of the wicked (Psalms 9:3; Psalms 27:2), it was different from the Israelites' escape from Egypt (Psalms 105:37).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Fools who received what they deserved but were rescued from death offer thanksgiving to the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord creates (Genesis 1:3) and sustains the universe (Hebrews 1:3) simply by speaking (Psalm 147:18). When God speaks, people are also healed (Matthew 8:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Sailors give thanks to the Lord when he saves them from the chaos and peril of the sea.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The same God who speaks and brings about the sailors’ distress can also calm the storm with just a word (compare Jonah 1:4; Matthew 8:26).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This call for public praise expands on the repeated phrases in Psalms 107:21–22 and Psalms 107:31.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord can choose to make the earth fertile or barren (Psalm 74:15; Isaiah 35:6–7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These two sections (Psalm 107:33–38, Psalms 107:39–42) expand the theme of the Lord’s complete authority and power over things that humans cannot control.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s presence can be seen in the abundance of his people’s families and herds (Psalms 127:3; Psalms 133:3; compare Psalms 109:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: People often become poor when their leaders are oppressive.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord rejects human rulers who act unjustly. He corrects their wrongdoing and brings justice on the earth.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The large families of the poor are evidence of God’s blessing.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Justice wins in God’s world (Psalm 1:6), and Israel’s history shows God’s loving devotion.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm combines two parts from David's other psalms (compare Psalms 57:5, Psalms 57:7–11; Psalms 60:5–12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist finds no evidence that God cares (see Psalm 28:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist starts this lament by accusing his accusers of repaying good with evil (Psalm 109:1–5). At the end of the psalm, he prays to the Lord, seeking protection (Psalm 109:21–25) and vengeance (Psalms 109:26–31).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist shows kindness and godliness (see Psalm 35:12–14), but faces stubborn opposition and hatred.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The NLT translates these verses as the words of the psalmist’s accusers; Hebrew lacks They say, which makes it unclear who is speaking.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked person apparently held a position of leadership. Peter referred to this psalm in regard to Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:20–26).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Family members of people guilty of capital crimes sometimes died with the offender (Numbers 16:1–33; Joshua 7:1–25) or had their property taken away (1 Kings 21:13–16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: If one’s family name was blotted out, it meant there was no offspring to continue the family name or remember its history (see Proverbs 10:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Children share in the sinful condition of their parents (Psalm 51:5; Exodus 20:5; Ephesians 2:3). The speaker asks the Lord to punish this guilty person also for the sins of his family who lived before him (compare Matthew 23:35–36).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The defendant committed very serious crimes that carried the death penalty and did not show even basic decency.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Cursing is the accused person’s whole way of life.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks God to act fairly and give people what they deserve (see Psalm 94:23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord's reputation is important. If the wicked win, people might think the Lord is also wicked and be tempted to act wickedly (Psalm 1:1).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Feeling vulnerable and miserable, the psalmist asks his Lord for help. The accusations have crushed his spirit and drained his physical strength.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A lengthening shadow suggests a temporary, empty life (Psalms 102:11; Psalms 144:4). A single locust can be easily brushed off clothing.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These verses form a prayer for God’s presence and for vindication. The psalmist wants everyone to see that he is vindicated by the Lord, not by any human agent.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord’s servant demonstrates loyalty and obedience.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist was accused of being clothed with disgrace (Psalm 109:18). Now, he asks that his accusers wear their shame like a piece of clothing.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The king of Israel had the great privilege of being the Lord’s adopted son (Psalm 2; 1 Chronicles 22:10), but he failed (Psalm 89). This decree restores and elevates his position. 

• The LORD: This title represents the Hebrew name Yahweh, which is God’s personal name (see Exodus 3:6–14; Exodus 6:2–8; Exodus 20:2). 

• my Lord: The Hebrew word ’adoni means “my master” or “my superior.” The psalmist understood God’s messianic ruler (the king chosen by God) to be greater than himself. The New Testament often quotes this psalm to show that Jesus is the Messiah (Matthew 22:44–45; Mark 12:36–37; Luke 20:42–44; Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 1:13). 

• The Lord’s right hand represents his authority, strength, presence, and benefits. The Lord chose the descendant of David and raised him up to be close to him (Psalm 80:17). 

Jesus claimed this position for himself (Matthew 26:64; Mark 14:62; Mark 16:19; Luke 22:69), and the apostles announced that Jesus, having gone up to heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father (Acts 2:33; Acts 5:31; Acts 7:55–56; Romans 8:34; Ephesians 1:20; Colossians 3:1; Hebrews 1:3; Hebrews 8:1; Hebrews 10:12; Hebrews 12:2). 

• Ancient Near Eastern kings were sometimes shown placing their feet on the backs of their defeated enemies as on a footstool (see Hebrews 10:12–13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Jesus and the apostles quote this psalm to explain the unique role and authority of Jesus as the Messiah (Matthew 22:43–45; Acts 2:32–36). The psalm also confirms God’s covenant with David. It gives hope that God will fulfill his promise in the future (see 2 Samuel 7:8–16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The kingdom will expand and increase, beginning from Jerusalem, until all enemies are conquered.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God had made an unbreakable oath and covenant with David. When the exile seemed to end the line of kings from David's family (Psalm 89:38), it created a crisis for God’s people. The placement of Psalm 110 in Book Five points again to the future of David’s line. David’s descendant must live according to God’s standard of integrity (Psalm 101). His rule will also be shaped by God’s kingship (Psalms 93–100). 

• You are a priest forever: The role of God’s messianic ruler changes. The kings from David’s family had a limited priestly role. They supported and organized the worship of the temple. For example, David brought the ark to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:15) and organized temple services (1 Chronicles 6:31–48; 1 Chronicles 15:11–26; 1 Chronicles 16:4–42; 1 Chronicles 23:4–32; 1 Chronicles 25:1). Solomon oversaw the construction of the temple (1 Kings 5:1–7:51). 

Even so, the offices of king and priest were separate in Israel. In the messianic kingdom, the king will also serve as a priest. He will be like Melchizedek, the king of Salem who was also a priest (Genesis 14:18). The New Testament explains that Jesus Christ fulfills this new order of priesthood (see Hebrews 5:6–10; Hebrews 6:20–7:25).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• at Your right hand: This position brings help and protection (see Psalms 16:7–8; Psalms 108:13). 

• The Lord will strike down rebellious kings. Rebellion against the Lord leads to death (Psalm 2; Romans 6:23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The new priestly role of David's descendant does not cancel his old role as a conquering ruler. He still needs to bring the nations under his rule (Psalm 110:2–3; see Psalm 2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s messianic ruler wins victory with renewed strength, like a traveler who drinks from streams along the way (Psalm 110:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly praise God and delight themselves in his great works. His mighty acts reflect his righteousness, grace, and compassion (see Psalm 116:5–7). All who submit themselves to him experience his glory.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This wisdom psalm contains many references to the works of the Lord that reveal his character. God is:

• righteous,

• gracious,

• compassionate,

• faithful,

• just,

• trustworthy,

• upright,

• holy, and

• awe-inspiring (Psalm 111:3, Psalms 111:4, Psalms 111:7, Psalms 111:8, Psalms 111:9).

God's character gives hope in the covenant relationship (Psalm 111:5). God rescued Israel from Egypt (Psalm 111:9). God gave them the land (Psalms 111:6). God provides for his people (Psalms 111:5). However, God expects those in this relationship to also be righteous and have integrity.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The word Hallelujah! is repeated throughout this group of psalms.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God takes care of his people’s needs, even providing food. He remembers his covenant with Abraham (see Psalm 105:8–11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Giving Israel the land of other nations was just and good. The Lord was judging those nations and showing grace to Israel. However, if the Israelites do not live faithfully and with integrity, they will also lose the land. The Lord’s people must reflect his character.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The people of the exodus generation went free because of God’s grace.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: True wisdom is the source of life (Proverbs 3:18; Proverbs 9:11; Ecclesiastes 7:12). It starts with the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 9:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The fear of the Lord leads to a wise life that honors God and brings blessing to the family and the community. The godly follow God with joy. Their obedience does not come from fear like a slave obeying a master.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm repeats the themes of wisdom and the fear of the Lord (Psalm 111). Wise people have reasons to be happy (Psalm 112:1–5) and strong (Psalms 112:6–10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: blessed: Everyone will recognize the children of godly people (see Psalm 127:4) because the godly leave a legacy for their children (see Psalms 1:3; compare Matthew 6:20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Godly people imitate God by being generous, compassionate, and righteous (Psalms 51:1; Psalms 111:1–10; 2 Corinthians 9:9). They lend money to the poor without charging interest (Psalms 15:5; Psalms 112:9; Exodus 22:25).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wise avoid mistakes because they are honest and compassionate (Psalms 15:5; Psalms 37:23–24). People will remember them for a long time (Proverbs 10:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Because the godly trust that God will rescue them and give them victory, they face their enemies with confidence (Psalms 59:10; Psalms 112:4; Psalms 118:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Paul quotes this verse in his instructions about generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The wicked gnash their teeth in anger due to their bitter envy (Psalms 35:16; Psalms 37:12). The strength and reputation of the godly create conflict with those who wish them harm. 

• The wicked will retreat in fear and shame.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: the name of the LORD: God's personal name (Hebrew Yahweh; see Exodus 3:15) reveals who he is (his nature, character, and reputation). He is exalted at all times (now and forever) and in every place (from east to west).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This song of praise celebrates the greatness of the Lord's name and glory. God is exalted and glorious in heaven (Psalm 113:4). He also stoops down to care for the lowly and needy on earth (Psalm 113:5–9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These psalms are called the Egyptian Hallel. Hallel means “praise.” Jewish people use these psalms during Passover, which began when God brought Israel out of Egypt in the exodus. The people recite Psalms 113–114 before the Passover meal, and Psalms 115–118 are recited afterward.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord’s glory extends to the heavens (Psalms 57:5, Psalms 57:11; Psalms 99:2; Psalms 108:5; Psalms 138:6; Isaiah 6:1; Isaiah 57:15) and throughout the world of human relationships.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord is unlike anyone else, yet he personally cares for people on earth.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord humbles himself to connect directly with his people (see Psalm 138:6; Philippians 2:6–8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These phrases are a quotation from Hannah’s prayer of praise (1 Samuel 2:8–9a).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• People in this culture often treated a woman without children with shame or contempt (Genesis 16:4). But the Lord has the power to make her a happy mother. For example: 

• Sarah (Genesis 21:2),

• Rebekah (Genesis 25:21),

• Rachel (Genesis 30:23), and

• Hannah (1 Samuel 1:20).

• God's greatness and goodness give people many reasons to praise him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• At the time of Israel’s exodus from Egypt and their entrance into the promised land, Israel was one holy kingdom (Exodus 19:5–6). 

• The mention of Judah and Israel as separate lands shows the psalm was written after the kingdom was divided (1 Kings 12:16–17; compare 1 Samuel 11:8; 1 Kings 1:35), and probably after the exile. Judah became God's sanctuary because the people worshiped God there. His tabernacle, and later his temple, were located there.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This song celebrates the Lord's power in nature. It remembers Israel's start as a nation during the exodus (Psalm 114:1–2) and their entry into the promised land (Psalms 114:3–6). It encourages respect for the God of Jacob (Psalm 114:7–8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• fled: God parted the waters so that Israel could escape Egypt (Psalm 77:17–18; Exodus 14). 

• The Jordan River turned back when Israel arrived to cross it (see Joshua 3). 

• skipped like rams: God's presence made the mountains quake (Exodus 19:16–20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord miraculously provided for his people in hard times after the exile, just as he had done in the wilderness after the exodus.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The community confesses their faith that God will rescue them for the glory of his name.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This is a song of thanksgiving for God's blessings. The community gives all glory to the Lord, the true source of hope and blessing. Those who trust in idols feel great disappointment. The Creator's blessing extends to future generations (Psalm 115:14), especially to the priests (Psalms 115:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Where is their God?: People question God's presence or power when he does not act as they expect (compare Psalms 14:1; Psalms 42:3, Psalms 42:10). However, God is in the heavens. He has all power, authority, and knowledge. He does as he wishes, not what people think he should do. He carries out his plans according to his will (Ephesians 1:11) and acts in his own time and ways.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• This entire section is repeated in Psalm 135:15–20. 

• Unlike the Lord (Psalm 95:3–5), idols cannot do anything. They are useless.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Worshiping idols leads one astray and corrupts those who trust in them (Isaiah 44:20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel … O house of Aaron … You who fear the LORD: The psalmist urges everyone in the God-fearing community to trust in the living God. This threefold address assures them that the Lord is their true helper and shield (compare Psalm 118:2–4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The groups mentioned in Psalm 115:9–11 receive assurance of the Lord's blessing, no matter their social status (see Psalms 113:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist blesses (Psalm 107:37–38, Psalms 107:41) all who trust in and fear the Lord. The Creator will care for the families of those who fear him. 

• the Maker of heaven and earth: This phrase speaks about how the Lord created everything and has power over all creation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The highest heavens belong to the LORD: God's exaltation starts in heaven (Psalm 113:4), far above the gods of other nations. The earth also belongs to him (Psalm 47:9; Psalms 95:4). 

• The dead cannot participate in God’s blessings. The living praise God in thanksgiving for his blessings (Psalm 79:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: I love the LORD: This unique opening expresses affection for and commitment to the Lord (see Psalm 18:1; Deuteronomy 6:5) on the basis of what the Lord has done.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist praises the Lord for answering his prayers and rescuing him from death.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This song of thanksgiving rejoices in God’s character and in rescue from death (Psalm 116:1–11). It gives an assurance of God’s protection in life and reminds the godly that the Lord watches over them even at death. The psalmist commits to living as God’s servant and resolves to honor him publicly (Psalm 116:12–19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Because the Lord responds to the cry of his people(Psalm 107:41; Psalms 113:6–8), the psalmist now strongly believes in prayer.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: It is not clear if the psalmist’s crisis was a literal near-death experience or if he was using the term figuratively.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This is the first of three times that the psalmist calls on the Lord’s name (which represents God's reputation).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The gracious, righteous, and compassionate Lord (see Psalm 111:1–5) rescued and gave rest to the psalmist.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: People with childlike faith readily receive God's wisdom and instruction (Psalm 19:7–11; Matthew 18:3–4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist’s near-death crisis made him more aware of life and of walking before the Lord. Though he had suffered, the Lord was faithful. However, people are all liars.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: I will walk before the LORD: The psalmist lived with integrity. After experiencing deep distress, he now enjoys open fellowship with the Lord (see Psalm 56:13; compare Job 42:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: I believed: Paul quotes this phrase in 2 Corinthians 4:13.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Lord’s gracious gifts are so great that the psalmist can do nothing to repay his debt. Keeping his promises publicly demonstrates his gratitude.

• All he has done for the psalmist includes answers to prayer, rescue, and life.

• The cup of salvation overflows with God’s blessings (Psalm 23:5), unlike the cup of judgment (Psalms 75:8). 

• The psalmist makes vows (Psalm 116:18) to praise the Lord publicly (Psalms 116:17–18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: No one lives or dies outside of God’s will. Having been given a second chance at life, the poet readily commits himself to the Lord with renewed acts of public devotion.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Paul quotes this verse to show that Gentiles would eventually praise the God of Israel (Romans 15:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm is the shortest in the Psalter. It invites all people of the earth to praise the Lord for his loving devotion and faithfulness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist joyfully thanks the Lord for his goodness and urges others to trust in his loving devotion (Psalm 118:1–4, Psalms 118:29). This poem is the last of the Egyptian Hallel (Psalms 113–118).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel … the house of Aaron … those who fear the LORD: These three groups represent the entire covenant community (compare Psalms 115:9–11; Psalms 135:19–20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord alone is the psalmist’s helper.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The LORD is on my side: Compare Romans 8:31;Hebrews 13:6. 

• God's presence removes the need to fear people (Psalm 56:11). The psalmist joyfully expects God’s rescue (Psalm 59:10; Psalm 112:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Trusting in the Lord is better than placing confidence in even the most powerful human leaders (Psalms 118:6; Psalms 146:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Strength comes from the name of the LORD. This is shown by the threefold repetition of the attackers, the name of the LORD, and the victory he gives.

• Even when hostile people surrounded the psalmist, the Lord extinguished them like burning thorns (see Isaiah 9:18; Isaiah 10:17).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist celebrates the victory of the Lord’s strong right hand, which kept him from death.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God has restored the psalmist from death to life, so he praises the Lord publicly (see Psalm 116:6, Psalms 116:12–19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The cornerstone shapes and supports a building or arch. It is the most important of all the stones. The Lord selects and places this stone for his sanctuary (Isaiah 28:16). 

Jesus referred to himself as this cornerstone (Matthew 21:42; Mark 12:10–11; Luke 20:17; see Acts 4:11; Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:6–7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist sees his own salvation as the beginning of a new day in which the Lord will do great things.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This is the day that the LORD has made: The Lord's victory has begun, but it will be completed on another day (Psalm 118:25).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist ends with prayer and thanksgiving, anticipating an even greater revelation of God’s victory and rescue.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The one who comes in the name of the Lord brings the Lord’s complete victory (see Psalm 118:10–12). 

• When Jesus triumphantly entered Jerusalem, the crowds shouted blessings. They used phrases from this verse (Matthew 21:9; Mark 11:9; Luke 19:38; John 12:13). 

Jesus quoted this passage as he wept over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:39; Luke 13:35).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Wise people are happy. They have integrity (see Psalm 84:11) and follow God's guidance. They obey God's teachings and seek them with complete devotion (see Psalm 27:7; Psalms 119:10, Psalms 119:45, Psalms 119:94, Psalms 119:155). They reject all evil forms. Compare Psalm 1:1–2.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Aleph (א) is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Psalm 119 is written as an acrostic poem. Each section has eight verses, and every verse in that section begins with the same Hebrew letter. The first section begins with Aleph.

God, the author of these instructions, commands that his followers live by them. The psalmist prays to be given the grace to live by that revelation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This psalm blends wisdom, lament, praise, thanksgiving, and confession. It often uses eight Hebrew words translated as: 

• “Instructions” 

• “law” 

• “words” 

• “commandments”

• “statutes”

• “judgments”

• “promises” 

• “precepts“

These words encourage love for and obedience to God's instructions in the Scriptures (see 2 Timothy 3:14–17). A deep commitment to these instructions unifies the psalm.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: To keep God’s commandments means to guard them by obeying them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• A young person often acts foolishly (Proverbs 22:15) and can easily make mistakes that ruin their life (Proverbs 7:6–23). However, youth is the best time to build self-discipline and seek wisdom (see Psalm 34:11; Proverbs 1:4). 

• keep his way pure: This means avoiding corruption by evil and sin and developing the integrity described in Psalm 15.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Beth (ב) is the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It makes the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist is determined to stay pure and encourages gaining wisdom through God's principles (Psalm 119:9) and instructions (Psalms 119:10–16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The student asks God the teacher to discipline him so that he will not stray.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God's wisdom is more valuable than any wealth people desire (Psalm 119:72, Psalms 119:127; Proverbs 3:14–15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The path of wisdom involves thinking deeply about God's teachings (see Psalm 119:1, Psalms 119:3). Wise people consider the meaning of God's word.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist wants to live a life full of praise and obedience to please the Lord (Psalms 118:17; Psalms 119:25, Psalms 119:77, Psalms 119:116, Psalms 119:144, Psalms 119:175). Only the Lord can remove his enemies and help him understand the wonderful truths in God's teachings.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Gimel (ג) is the third letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

Like a stranger in a hostile land, God's servant needs God's guidance.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The arrogant are probably those who mock the psalmist (Psalm Psalms 119:22–23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Those who meditate on God’s instructions receive wise advice from them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Daleth (ד) is the fourth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The poet feels deep pain and sadness but asks the Lord to give him strength. He wants to follow the Lord. Suffering and death may result from the Lord’s discipline (Psalms 118:17–18; Psalms 119:67, Psalms 119:71, Psalms 119:75), but his instruction renews the weary soul (see Psalms 119:12).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• path of deceit: Self-deception comes from sinful human nature (Jeremiah 17:9). It leads to foolishness. 

• Access to God’s word is a privilege, not a right.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
He (ה) is the fifth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

As a student, the poet asks his teacher, God, to renew life and to transform disgrace into righteousness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The love for money can lead to sin (compare Exodus 18:21; 1 Timothy 3:1–5; 1 Timothy 6:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks for protection from enemies who speak harshly (see Psalms 42:10; Psalms 44:16; Psalms 89:50–51; Psalms 102:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Waw (ו) is the sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm. 

The psalmist prays that God’s word would continue to be the source of his love and salvation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist is determined to obey the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist finds joy in God's word despite experiencing pain (Psalm 119:92, Psalms 119:143).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Zayin (ז) is the seventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist asks God to remember his word as the psalmist also remembers God’s word and his name. Remembrance expresses devotion.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: judgments of old: This refers to God’s just rulings or decisions (his laws). These are found in the Torah, the books of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Heth (ח) is the eighth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist seeks God’s favor and loving devotion. Although surrounded by evildoers, he remains a loyal servant of the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Wicked people try to lead him into sin, but the psalmist remembers God's word and stays strong (see Psalm 119:16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God's goodness fills the earth. The entire creation shows evidence of his goodness (see Isaiah 6:3; Isaiah 11:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Good judgment and knowledge come from wisdom (Psalm 111:10). 

• The psalmist admits he used to wander like a lost sheep (Psalm 119:176). 

• now I keep your word: See Psalm 119:25–29. 

• You are good, and You do what is good: God's character is perfect (Psalm 97:2; James 1:17; 1 John 1:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Teth (ט) is the ninth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm. 

The psalmist admits his sin and gratefully accepts the Lord's discipline.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: As God’s child, the psalmist asks for divine wisdom.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Yodh (י) is the tenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm. 

In this prayer for comfort and compassion, the psalmist commits himself to his Creator, who has afflicted him. He wants God to pay back his enemies for the wrongs they have done. He also prays to receive the gift of life. He not only prays for himself but also considers the whole community of the godly, asking that God’s answers to prayer would encourage them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Kaph (כ) is the eleventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist feels exhausted from waiting for the Lord, but he still hopes for God's future rescue.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God's word is trustworthy. This contrasts with the lies of the enemies who hunt the psalmist without reason (see Psalm 119:78).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Lamedh (ל) is the twelfth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The stability of God’s wisdom gives understanding. God’s word provides order and a framework for living, even when under pressure from adversaries.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The wicked planned to kill the psalmist, but they faced destruction themselves (Psalm 1:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: I have seen a limit to all perfection: Humans cannot fully understand God's ways (see Ecclesiastes 3:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: make me wiser: God’s word provides wisdom and perspective. God is the true source of wisdom.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Mem (מ) is the thirteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The instruction and wisdom of God through his word are far better than the best that human teachers can offer.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Wisdom is better than the finest food (Psalm 19:10; Psalms 81:16). 

• The psalmist had already turned away from the false promises of foolishness (see Psalm 119:18, Psalms 119:78, Psalms 119:86, Psalms 119:163).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord’s word is like a lamp. It offers perspective, hope, and guidance in darkness (Psalm 18:25–29; Psalms 119:130). This light also gives life (Proverbs 6:23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Nun (נ) is the fourteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist's deep commitment to God's word comes from within (Psalm 119:112) and directs his actions.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• freewill offerings of my mouth: This Hebrew expression is unique in the Old Testament (compare Psalm 50:23).

• The psalmist is vulnerable to his opponents because of his commitment to a wise life.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly hate the wicked and their actions (Psalm 5:4–6; compare Ezekiel 33:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Samekh (ס) is the fifteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist declares his hatred of evil and his love for God and his ways.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Ayin (ע) is the sixteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The servant of the Lord struggles to endure the evil around him. He confidently asks the Lord to rescue him right away!

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Simply possessing God’s law does not provide any benefits. The psalmist knows that only as the Lord gives discernment will he understand it.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Pe (פ) is the seventeenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist prays earnestly for God to speak to him as he suffers from his adversities.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Tsadhe (צ) is the eighteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

God is righteous, and his word is right and just, especially in contrast to the deceptions of the wicked.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels angry (compare Psalm 69:9) because he sees wicked people ignoring God's word.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels very troubled by those who oppress him (see Psalm 119:143; compare Isaiah 53).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: I rise and anticipate translate the same Hebrew verb.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Qoph (ק) is the nineteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

The psalmist prays to the Lord at night. Even when God seems distant, he is actually close.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Coming to attack me (or draw near) is a Hebrew wordplay on You are near. The wicked stay far from God's instructions, but the psalmist stays close, so he does not need to fear.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Resh (ר): This request for life appears throughout Psalm 119, but it is focused in this stanza.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• my heart fears … I rejoice: Fear, trembling, and joy show the psalmist’s devotion to God. 

• God’s word is a treasure (great spoil). 

• In the Old Testament, the number seven represents wholeness.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Shin (ש) is the twenty-first letter of the alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm. 

The psalmist looks beyond his adversaries to the peace of God. This perspective allows him to praise God throughout the day.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Taw (ת) is the twenty-second letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It marks the beginning of the next section of this psalm.

God's servant asks the Lord for help one last time. He still feels like a lost sheep.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God, the Great Shepherd, seeks out his lost sheep (Psalm 23:1; Luke 15:4–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist is surrounded by liars, so he makes his lament to the Lord, the only one who can help him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This short, individual lament expresses the psalmist’s trust that the Lord will deal with deceptive evildoers. It also laments living as a stranger among hateful liars. The psalmist’s picture of his life in a foreign land might have been a reality as he set out for Jerusalem, or it might depict his feelings and concerns as he begins his pilgrimage. Overwhelmed with injustice, he trusts God and looks forward to arriving in the Lord’s presence.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These short and memorable songs were sung by pilgrims as they traveled to Jerusalem for the national festivals held three times each year (Deuteronomy 16:16). The title of these psalms includes a Hebrew word that can mean “steps” or “stairs.” Some scholars understand it to mean “going up to Jerusalem.” These psalms, often called the Songs of Ascents, lead the listener on a journey to Jerusalem to praise God for his goodness to Israel through history.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist speaks with the liars around him. He feels confident that the Lord will judge them. 

• The Divine Warrior (see Psalms 7:12–13; Psalms 11:4–6) will attack the liars with sharp arrows and burning coals.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Meshech was a Japhethite territory far to the north of Canaan. Kedar was an Ishmaelite territory in Arabia. Violent people lived in both places. 

Meshech was known for its slave trade (Ezekiel 27:13; see also Exodus 21:16), and Kedar was known for its warriors (Isaiah 21:16–17). These places represented the rebellious and violent land where the psalmist suffered.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels the pain of being alone, isolated, and in constant conflict.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: peace: See Psalms 37:11; Psalms 122:6–9; Psalms 125:5; Psalms 128:6.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The mountains were known for idol worship (Deuteronomy 12:2), and Israel was drawn to the hilltop shrines (Hosea 4:13). This verse can be seen as a rhetorical question expecting a "no" answer: The gods of the hilltop shrines cannot save anyone. 

Others understand the mountains to be a symbol of the Lord’s strength (Psalm 95:4). In that case, the question would be taken literally (From where does my help come?), with the answer in the next verse.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The leader of the group of pilgrims uses word pictures to assure the group of the Lord’s presence during the journey.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God watches over his own, even and especially when they face many troubles (Psalms 12:5, Psalms 12:7; Psalms 69:29; Psalms 91:14; Psalms 146:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Maker of heaven and earth (Psalm 121:2) protects Israel. 

• God stands with Israel, offering support and care to the faithful (see Psalm 16:7–8). 

• Both the sun and the moon were worshiped as gods in the ancient Near East. But God limits their power. They are part of creation and also praise the Lord (Psalm 148:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The central sanctuary was the house of the LORD. This phrase first referred to the tabernacle (Exodus 23:19; Exodus 34:26).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Jerusalem is presented here as the city of God, the city of David, and the center of faith. A group of pilgrims joyfully arrives in the city (Psalm 122:1–2). The psalmist praises Jerusalem (Psalm 122:3–5) and prays for the city’s peace (Psalms 122:6–9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Several psalms celebrate or look forward to being inside the gates of the city (Psalms 9:14; Psalms 87:2; Psalms 100:4; Psalms 118:19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In the time of David and Solomon, people knew Jerusalem as a safe place (1 Kings 10:6–7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Jerusalem can represent God’s heavenly dwelling place. David became the model for the rulers God chooses.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Each person in Israel belonged to a tribe, and all tribes belonged to the Lord. 

• Giving thanks means presenting an offering acceptable to the Lord (Psalms 50:14, Psalms 50:23; Psalms 100:4; Psalms 118:19). 

• as a testimony for Israel: See Exodus 23:17; Deuteronomy 16:16.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: the thrones of judgment stand: In the time of David and Solomon (1 Kings 3:28), Jerusalem was known for wisdom and justice. It will be like that again (Isaiah 9:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Prayers for the peace of Jerusalem are motivated by love of family and God’s sanctuary.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This lament about the psalmist's humble position shows strong trust in the Lord (Psalm 123:1–2). The psalmist prays for God's favor on the community because evil surrounds them (Psalm 123:3–4). The poet looks beyond Jerusalem (Psalm 122) to God's throne in heaven.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The negative rhetorical questions emphasize the positive idea that the Lord was indeed on their side.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This thanksgiving song describes what might happen if the Lord were not present with his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: the raging waters: The enemies could have defeated the Israelites and destroyed them if the Lord had not supported his people (compare Psalm 69:15; Jeremiah 46:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The enemies of God's people were like lions or bears that tear prey with their teeth (see Psalm 57:4; Proverbs 28:15). The Lord shut their mouths (Daniel 6:22).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist expresses the community's trust in the Lord's protection (Psalm 125:1–2) and prays for peace (Psalms 125:3–5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: surrounds: God guards and protects like a wall of fire (Zechariah 2:5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly may be tempted to abandon God’s ways because of pressure from others or from the surrounding culture.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: People who do not follow the "straight paths" are foolish (Proverbs 2:12–15). God gives his goodness to the godly (see Psalm 122:6–9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord brought about Israel’s restoration from exile, just as he had brought Israel out of Egypt (Psalm 114:1). The restoration transformed the weeping of the Lord’s people into laughter and showed the Lord’s character to the nations (Psalm 9:11; Psalms 64:9; Isaiah 12:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This psalm celebrates Israel's return from exile (Psalm 126:1–3). The psalmist then prays that God will fully restore the people (Psalm 126:4–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The prophets had spoken of the restoration as a time when the wilderness would change into the garden of Eden (Isaiah 51:3; Ezekiel 47). However, the reality was far from paradise. Here, the restoration community prays for complete redemption (see Haggai 2:19). 

• like streams in the Negev: Seasonal rains filled the dry riverbeds (wadis), making the land green again. The prayer seeks a similar change in Israel’s fortunes, fulfilling the imagery of the "Second Exodus" in Isaiah (see "The Promise of a Second Exodus" Theme Note). 

• carrying sheaves of grain: This harvest represents God's complete restoration.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Unless: These conditional statements emphasize that the Lord is the one who protects the city (compare Psalm 124:1–2). 

• Human effort achieves nothing unless the Lord blesses it (see Psalm 44:3). 

• you rise early and stay up late: This phrase describes people who work constantly and live with pressure and competition.

• Those whom God loves can rest and sleep in peace (Psalm 3:5; Psalms 4:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Blessings and protection come from God. Without his presence, success is not possible (Psalm 127:1–2). This is especially true for children, who are gifts from God (Psalm 127:3–5).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Children are one of God’s blessings. In Hebrew, the word for children (banim) sounds like the word for builders (bonim; Psalm 127:1). This wordplay shows that having children helps build a family.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Like arrows: The image compares children to arrows in a warrior’s hand. Children strengthen and support the family and help defend its honor when others accuse or oppose them (compare Psalms 120:4; Psalms 7:12–13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: eating the fruit of your labor: This means gaining benefit from whatever work one does.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The godly, who fear the Lord, will know true happiness (Psalm 128:1–2). The Lord is with them (see Psalm 127:1–2), strengthens their family life (Psalms 128:3–4), and blesses them for generations (Psalms 128:5–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Children are like strong young olive trees because they are full of potential. Olive oil symbolizes God's blessing (Psalm 104:15; Numbers 18:12; Jeremiah 31:12; Haggai 2:19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God will continually bless those who fear him (Psalm 133:3) from his dwelling in Zion (Psalms 20:2; Psalms 50:2; Psalms 110:2), no matter where they live. 

• children's children: God's blessings continue through generations for those who are faithful (Psalms 79:12–13; Psalms 89:1; Psalms 100:4–5; Psalms 103:17–19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel’s earliest years as a nation took place while the people were living in Egypt.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist briefly reviews Israel’s history of trouble (Psalm 129:1–2) and redemption (Psalms 129:3–4). He ends with curses against the enemies and blessings on the godly (Psalm 129:5–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The LORD is righteous: He rescued Israel from Egypt, from many enemy attacks, and from the Babylonian exile.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Grass on a rooftop had shallow roots and would scorch easily. A crop was ignored by the harvester when the yield was low. The enemies who had sown hurt among God’s people would gain little.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: A cry from the depths comes from a place of deep distress (compare Psalm 69:2, Psalms 69:14; Isaiah 51:10; Ezekiel 27:34). Feeling weak, the psalmist prays for God's favor.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Beginning with himself as a representative of the community, the psalmist cries for God’s mercy (Psalm 130:1–3) out of deep distress. He places his hope in the Lord (Psalm 130:4–6), trusting that the Lord will rescue in his own time and way. With this confidence, the psalmist invites Israel to wait for the Lord (Psalm 130:7–8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist knows that his sins make him guilty and deserving of God’s judgment.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The good news comes in God’s readiness to forgive sinners. His grace encourages people to fear him and hope in him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God's word gives hope (Psalms 119:42–43, Psalms 119:49; Psalms 147:11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Israel is encouraged to hope in the Lord (Psalms 9:18; Psalms 27:14; Psalms 131:3) because the Lord pays the high price for redemption and removes the sin that separates humans from him (see also Psalm 111:9; Exodus 6:6–8; 2 Samuel 7:23–24; Isaiah 43:1–4; Titus 2:14; Hebrews 9:12; 1 Peter 1:18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The heart represents the entire person (see Psalm 27:8). 

• God hates arrogance, which is a foolish way of life (Proverbs 6:16–19). 

• The psalmist does not trouble himself with matters that properly belong to the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Out of his contentment in the Lord, the psalmist invites Israel to seek their rest in God (Psalm 131:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist has calmed and quieted himself. He has given up his ambitions and pride (Galatians 2:20). 

• like a weaned child: The psalmist compares himself to a contented child who rests quietly with its mother.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This psalm celebrates the Lord’s faithfulness to David. When David wanted to bring the ark to Jerusalem (Psalm 132:1–5), the Lord agreed and made Jerusalem his earthly home (Psalms 132:6–10). God’s choice of Jerusalem also shows his choice: 

• of David's family line (Psalm 132:11–13),

• of Zion (Psalm 132:14–17), and

• of the priesthood (Psalm 132:9, Psalms 132:16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Ephrathah is another name for Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19; Genesis 48:7). 

• Jaar is the singular form of the plural Jearim. The ark was at Kiriath-jearim for 20 years in Samuel’s time (1 Samuel 7:1–2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These verses recall David moving the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:1–15) and the Lord's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:4–16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These verses are a quotation from Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the temple (2 Chronicles 6:41–42).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The priests were to show righteousness by the way they live (Psalm 132:16; Malachi 2:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The LORD swore an oath to David (2 Samuel 7:4–16): God's promise is unconditional, but the covenant depends on conditions (If … then). Those who break God's covenant should expect God's judgment as discipline (see Psalm 89:30–37).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist remembers how God chose Jerusalem and appointed the priests.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: anointed one: God chose and established this ruler (see Psalms 1–8) to always provide light for the Lord’s people. This light would shine continuously (see 1 Kings 11:36; 2 Kings 8:19; compare John 8:12; Revelation 21:23–24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The enemies will feel shame, while the king will be honored (Psalm 132:9, Psalms 132:16).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Brothers are connected by family, by work, or by loyalty. In this psalm, brothers means all members of the community, including men and women, who live in unity.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist speaks about the joy of relationships dedicated to God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this wisdom psalm (see Psalm 1), peaceful and harmonious relationships show that God is present.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The fine oil was used to appoint and set apart Aaron for his role as priest (see Exodus 29:7). 

• head … beard … collar of his robes: The oil set Aaron apart completely for God’s service.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The dew represents the richness of God’s blessings (his goodness and care). In Jerusalem, this moisture comes from winds off the Mediterranean Sea. Mount Hermon, which has snow on its peak, is known for its abundant moisture.

• A blessing is God’s life-giving power. It shows his provision (care for needs) and protection (Psalm 5:12; Psalms 41:2). It also comes from his presence (Psalms 21:6; Psalms 67:1). In the end, all nations will receive God’s blessing (Psalms 67; Psalms 72:17). Zion is the central place of God's blessing (Psalms 134:3; Psalms 147:13). 

• God gives everlasting life to people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Those who serve by night were the priests and Levites (see also Psalm 135:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In the last of the pilgrims’ songs (Psalms 120–134), the travelers ask the temple workers to praise the Lord. In return, they will receive a long-awaited blessing.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God is the Creator and the Lord of history, the “Maker of heaven and earth” (Psalm 134:3). He deserves praise because, unlike idols, he saves his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The names Jacob and Israel represent all twelve tribes. The Lord loves his chosen people. They are his treasure among all the world's kingdoms (Exodus 19:5–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord is greater than any real or imagined supernatural being (see Psalms 95:3–5; Psalms 115:4–8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• God has complete authority and power over the whole created order. God does whatever pleases him.

• The phrase in the heavens and on the earth refers to all of creation.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist tells of God’s complete power and authority over the weather (Psalms 29; Psalms 77:17–18; Psalms 78:26; Psalms 104:4; Psalms 147:8–9; Psalms 148:5–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• In the tenth and final plague against Egypt, God destroyed the firstborn of each family.

• The signs and wonders refer to the ten plagues (see Exodus 7–11; Deuteronomy 4:34; Nehemiah 9:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord had complete authority and power over the exodus and the conquest of the promised land.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God’s name and character are very different from idols.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Idols lead people to think wrongly because they are only things humans make. They cannot speak, see, hear, or breathe (Isaiah 41:22–24; Isaiah 44:9, Isaiah 44:18; Romans 1:21–23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This entire section is repeated in Psalm 115:4–11.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The groups mentioned here formed the covenant community (see Psalm 115:9–11).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist calls the community to praise the Lord, who is good and full of love. He is the true Lord over all people. Verse 1 echoes the poetic line in 2 Chronicles 5:13.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This is the last of the Great Hallel psalms (Psalms 120–136). It uniquely repeats the phrase His loving devotion endures forever in every verse. 

The hymn begins and ends with a call to praise (Psalm 136:1–3, Psalms 136:26). It declares the Lord as the Creator of everything and the Redeemer of Israel, both in ancient times (Psalm 136:10–22) and in the recent past (Psalms 136:23–24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist tells the early history of Israel's redemption.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist tells the recent story of Israel's redemption, but does not specify the details.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord provides for all of his creatures.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
The phrase God of heaven is a name for the Lord used during and after the exile (when many Israelites were taken from their land). It appears in:

• Ezra (Ezra 1:2; Ezra 5:11, Ezra 5:12; Ezra 6:9, Ezra 6:10; Ezra 7:12), 

• Nehemiah (Nehemiah 1:5; Nehemiah 2:4, Nehemiah 2:20), and

• Daniel (Daniel 2:18, Daniel 2:19, Daniel 2:37, Daniel 2:44).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In response to the pain of exile (Psalm 137:1–4), the psalmist decides to remember Jerusalem, even though the memories cause him pain (Psalms 137:4–6). He also speaks a strong prayer asking God to bring justice on his enemies (Psalm 137:7–9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
Because the music of Jerusalem was connected to the joy of life in the promised land, the exile took away any reason to sing joyful songs. The Babylonians asked the Judeans to sing and dance for them, but the people were so full of grief that they could not do it.

The songs about the Lord celebrate his power and goodness, but his people were now filled with doubt and questions. They hung their harps in the trees, which may show that their joy had come to an end under God’s judgment (Deuteronomy 21:23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist pledges his loyalty to Jerusalem, the city at the center of God’s reign and the location of fellowship with him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The poet saw how the Edomites betrayed the people of Judah, so he calls on God to judge Edom. The long conflict between Edom and Judah reached its worst point near the end of Judah’s history. At that time, the Edomites handed the Judeans over to the Babylonians (Obadiah 1:10–11) and celebrated Jerusalem's fall. 

• This prayer asking God to bring justice uses strong language and can be shocking.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord receives praise before the gods of the nations.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this wisdom psalm, the Lord is presented as the God of gods. He rescued his people and has a perfect plan for them as individuals. The nations will join Israel in glorifying God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this final group of psalms of David, psalms of praise and wisdom (Psalms 138–139, Psalms 145:145) form a frame around five psalms of lament (Psalms 140–144).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: As the Lord's glory fills the earth, people must willingly submit to him. Every king (compare Psalm 2) will join in praise when they learn the Lord's ways of truth and love.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God is holy and great, far beyond human understanding (see Psalms 99:2; Psalms 113:4; Isaiah 6:1; Isaiah 57:15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The exalted God cares for the humble (Psalm 138:6), especially his servant, the psalmist (Psalms 138:7–8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist trusts in the Lord's perfect plans and prays for God's continued involvement. The psalmist sees himself as part of God’s plans (see Psalms 9:10; Psalms 139:14).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord knows the psalmist well. God has examined him closely, in a thorough examination that can be painful at times (Job 7:17–19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
In this wisdom psalm, the psalmist opens every part of his life to God. He invites God to examine his thoughts, actions, and words. Even though life is difficult, he wants to grow in wisdom so that he does not share in the judgment of the wicked (Psalm 141:5; Psalms 142:3; Psalms 143:8, Psalms 143:10; Psalms 144:3–4). 

The psalmist also knows that he cannot escape from the Lord. His stress fades as he remembers that God has cared for him with love, even before he was born (Psalm 139:13–18). He ends by asking God to keep examining him and to guide him on the path of wisdom (Psalm 139:23–24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The phrase when I sit and when I rise refers to everyday activities (compare Deuteronomy 6:6–9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord's all-knowing and all-powerful nature provides comfort to the godly, but it troubles the wicked (Psalm 2:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord’s wonderful understanding lies beyond the psalmist’s ability to comprehend (see Judges 13:18).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist shows wonder at God being everywhere at all times.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: if I make my bed in Sheol: God has complete access to all he has created, even the most hidden or hard-to-reach places.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• rise on the wings of the dawn: This poetic expression describes traveling eastward, as far as the sunrise, if that were possible.

• the farthest sea: This expression takes the traveler in the opposite direction, far to the west.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• my inmost being: The delicate inner parts of the body include a person's very being. 

• Even when hidden in his mother’s womb, the psalmist was guided by the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: How precious to me are Your thoughts: God’s careful examination shows his loving care. Life with the Lord brings blessings that are beyond words.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist’s sense of awe leads him to consider the wicked and to reflect on himself. The Lord, as the examiner of all people, judges the wicked for their destructive acts and speech. So, the psalmist prays that he will not be among them.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Do I note hate those who hate You: Rejecting evil shows wisdom (see Psalms 1:1; Psalms 5:4–6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: As the psalmist prays about the wicked, he also reflects on himself. He does not assume that he is righteous. This prayer has been spoken again and again by God’s people over many generations.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The path of wisdom leads to eternal life (see Psalm 1:6; Proverbs 4:18; Proverbs 6:23).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays for the Lord to rescue him from wicked people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this personal lament, the psalmist describes God's enemies and their evil plans. He prays for the Lord's protection and rescue, trusting in God's strength and justice. He predicts that fire will judge the evil (Psalm 140:9–11) and that he will be proven right and live in the Lord's presence (Psalms 140:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: snakes … vipers: These creatures portray the wicked as very corrupt people (see Proverbs 23:32; Isaiah 14:29; Romans 3:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays for God's protection (see Psalm 121), asking the Lord to keep him safe from the wicked's many plans.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: O GOD the Lord: This title comes from combining the name Yahweh with the title Adonai (which means Master). See also Psalms 68:20; Psalms 69:6; Psalms 71:16; Psalms 73:28; Psalms 109:21; Psalms 141:8.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays for God’s judgment on the wicked.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks for burning coals to fall on his enemies and for them to be thrown into the miry pits, so that they cannot attack again. This language hints at the New Testament teachings on hell (see Matthew 5:22, Matthew 5:29–30; Matthew 10:28; Matthew 18:9; Mark 9:43–47; Luke 12:5; James 3:6; 2 Peter 2:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist urgently prays for rescue. He does not have incense or an evening offering (Exodus 29:38–39), but his prayers and devotion represent those elements (see Isaiah 1:13; Revelation 5:8). 

• uplifted hands: This is a posture of prayer (Psalms 28:2; Psalms 88:9; Psalms 143:6; Exodus 9:29; 1 Timothy 2:8).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays for rescue and for wisdom. He also looks ahead to the end of evil. The idea that people receive what they deserve (Psalm 141:10) holds the psalm together.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• Wisdom sometimes requires protection from oneself. People might say or think things that lead to a harmful path (Proverbs 13:3; Proverbs 21:23). 

• Wisdom accepts correction from godly people (see Proverbs 3:11; Proverbs 9:8; Proverbs 15:31; Proverbs 19:25).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Although overwhelmed by his persecutors (Psalm 142:6), the psalmist seeks wisdom from the Lord.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
when he was in the cave: Compare Psalm 57:1.

The psalmist faces severe persecution, so he cries to the Lord, and the Lord will rescue him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist feels deep despair (see Psalm 77:3), and the Lord helps him in his distress. The psalmist trusts in the Lord's wisdom (see Psalm 139) but mourns being trapped by evil people (Psalms 5:9–10; Psalms 140:5; Psalms 141:9; Psalms 142:3).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Even when alone, the psalmist trusts the Lord, who is his life (see Psalms 9:9; Psalms 16:5; Psalms 27:13).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Though overwhelmed by loneliness and trouble, the psalmist focuses on the Lord’s goodness and protection. He knows that the Lord alone is his Redeemer, so he offers his praise.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: He feels trapped and stressed, similar to being in prison (see Psalm 107:10).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist prays for God’s love and mercy.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: In this lament, the psalmist feels overwhelmed by constant trouble from his enemies, so he turns to the Lord’s love, righteousness, and faithfulness. He remembers what God has done in the past and longs for God to renew his love. He opens himself to God’s wisdom because he knows that God’s instruction leads to life.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Everyone has sinned and is guilty before God (Romans 3:20–24).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: My spirit grows faint within me: The psalmist admits his desperation as his life seems to slip away under cruel and powerful enemies.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Remembering God’s acts from the past reassures the psalmist of God’s faithfulness (Psalms 42:4; Psalms 63:6; Psalms 77:3, Psalms 77:6; Psalms 119:55).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist’s thirst is a deep longing for God’s redemption (see Psalm 42:1–2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist experiences depression. He describes himself as close to death from sorrow (Psalms 31:10; Psalms 119:87). He feels worn out (Psalms 39:10; Psalms 71:9; Psalms 119:81). He is weak from longing (Psalm 84:2). He feels overwhelmed by the burdens of life (Psalm 90:7, Psalms 90:9).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks the Lord to renew his love.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The psalmist prays for wisdom (see Psalms 5:8; Psalms 25:4–6; Psalms 138:138; Psalms 143:10). 

• Your good Spirit: The Spirit brings God's goodness (see Psalm 23:6).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: revive: Here, it means to bring someone out of despair and restore them to life (Psalms 80:19; Psalms 85:6; Psalms 138:7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalm ends with a prayer for God to show that the psalmist is in the right and to restore his life.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: my Rock … my steadfast love … my deliverer … my shield: The psalmist’s descriptive names for the Lord reveal his deep love for him.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This lament begins with an exclamation of love for the Lord. The community then reflects on the temporary nature of life (Psalm 144:3–4). The psalmist asks for God's help and anticipates victory (Psalm 144:5–11). 

A new song (Psalm 144:9–10) and a prayer for rescue (Psalms 144:11) introduce the theme of the Lord’s blessings through his care and protection (Psalm 144:12–15).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
what is man: The same question in Psalm 8:4–6 leads to the answer that humans are only mortal (they do not live forever), yet God gives them honor and responsibility to rule. 

The psalmist focuses on how brief and fragile human life is. He describes it as temporary and passing quickly (see Psalms 90:3, Psalms 90:7–10; Psalms 102:11; Psalms 109:23; Psalms 146:4).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist asks God to act against his enemies (compare Psalm 18:7–19).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist compares sons and daughters to plants and pillars, which are images of strength and beauty.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This prayer for the Lord’s blessing brings the laments of Psalms 140–144 to a close. It describes God’s provision (care for needs) and protection (keeping people safe; see Psalm 127), not only for the psalmist but also for his children and for all who follow God.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: no going into captivity, and no cry of lament: These images show peace and safety.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist praises God, the Great King who reigns over all other rulers (see Psalm 47:2).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
This psalm of praise is the last in this collection of the psalms of David (Psalms 138–145). Praise continues in the last five psalms (Psalms 146–150). 

This psalm celebrates the Lord as the King of all (Psalm 145:1–3, Psalms 145:10–13). God's actions show his royal qualities (Psalm 145:4–7). He cares for all creatures (Psalm 145:14–17) and for those who fear him (Psalms 145:18–20).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This litany (a repeated form of praise, often with the same line said again and again) celebrates God’s character and his mighty deeds. Each generation will continue to tell others about God’s power (Psalm 22:30).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: God consistently demonstrates his character toward all his creation (see Psalm 136:25).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: These verses form a description of the Lord’s kingdom.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord cares for his creatures.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Lord cares for those who love him and fear him. God-fearers love the Lord and find refuge in him (Psalm 5:11). They seek him as their only true Savior (Psalms 40:16; Psalms 70:4). They will experience a good future (Psalm 69:36) and enjoy the peace that God gives (Psalms 119:165).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This verse is similar to Psalm 103:1, Psalms 103:2, Psalms 103:22; Psalms 104:1, Psalms 104:35.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The call to praise (Psalm 146:1–2) leads to a warning against foolishness and false confidence (Psalms 146:3–4). The psalm ends with a blessing for everyone who places their hope in the Lord (Psalm 146:5–7).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The Psalter ends with five hallelujah psalms, so named because each begins and ends with Praise the LORD! (Hebrew haleluyah).

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: Repeating the Lord’s name (shown as LORD in the Berean Standard Bible) four times emphasizes that he alone heals, lifts burdens, loves, and protects.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: This verse is a call to worship.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist calls for the Lord to be praised for restoring and blessing Zion, caring for the poor, displaying his power over nature, and revealing himself to his people.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content: The psalmist remembers how the Lord restored Jerusalem and brought back his people who had suffered in exile.

entries.title: Psalms
entries.content:
• The Lord created the heavens.
